manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Tangent Function y=tanx Graph Visualization (One Period)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Tangent Function y=tanx Graph Visualization (One Period)2. Subject: Mathematics - Trigonometric Functions3. Experiment Objective: To visualize the graph of the tangent function over one period, identify its zeros, asymptotes, and periodicity, and understand the mathematical relationship between the function expression and its graphical behavior.II. Experimental ToolsCoordinate grid (digital graphing software or drawing board), white background canvas, axis scale markers, curve plotting tool, colored pens or digital colors (orange, red, blue, green).III. Experimental Procedure1. Coordinate System Setup: Prepare a white background and draw a Cartesian coordinate system. Set the x-axis range to [-π/2, 3π/2] and the y-axis range to [-5, 5], ensuring uniform scaling.2. Asymptote Marking: Draw vertical red dashed lines at x=-π/2 and x=π/2 to represent the vertical asymptotes of y=tanx.3. Curve Plotting: Using an orange color, plot the curve y=tanx between the asymptotes, ensuring the curve approaches but never touches the asymptote lines.4. Zero Marking: Mark the zeros of the function with blue dots at the points (0,0) and (π,0).5. Annotation: Add a green text label near the curve reading y=tanx (period 2π).IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The tangent curve increases monotonically between each pair of asymptotes.2. Near x=-π/2 and x=π/2, the curve rises or falls sharply, indicating divergence toward infinity.3. The curve crosses the x-axis at (0,0) and (π,0).4. The overall shape demonstrates periodic repetition with period 2π.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe tangent function is defined as tanx = sinx/cosx. When cosx approaches zero at x=±π/2, the function value grows without bound, creating vertical asymptotes. Zeros occur where sinx=0 while cosx≠0, resulting in x=0 and x=π within the observed interval. The repeating nature of sine and cosine leads to the periodicity of tanx with period 2π.VI. Notes1. Ensure asymptotes are dashed to distinguish them from the function curve.2. Maintain consistent scaling for accurate visual interpretation.3. Do not connect the curve across asymptotes.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Visualization of the tangent function y=tanx over one period, emphasizing asymptotes, zeros, and periodicity. Visibility constraints: axes, asymptotes, curve color, and labeled points must remain clearly visible and spatially consistent for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Centrifugation of Cell Culture Lysate to Separate Cell DebrisI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Centrifugation of Cell Culture Lysate to Form Cell Debris PelletSubject: Natural Science – Cell & Developmental BiologyObjective: To demonstrate how centrifugation separates insoluble cell debris from soluble components in a cell lysate, and to observe pellet formation and supernatant clarification.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentBench-top microcentrifuge; microcentrifuge tube (1.5 mL); cloudy cell culture lysate; tube rack; gloves and lab coat.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the microcentrifuge tube containing cloudy cell culture lysate into a balanced position in the bench-top centrifuge. Ensure the tube cap is securely closed.2. Centrifugation: Close the centrifuge lid and spin the sample at appropriate speed (e.g., 12,000 × g) for a short duration (about 1–2 minutes).3. Removal: After the centrifuge stops completely, open the lid and carefully remove the microcentrifuge tube.4. Observation: Hold the tube upright at eye level without shaking and observe the contents.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before centrifugation: The lysate appears uniformly cloudy, with suspended cell debris.2. After centrifugation: A compact, opaque pellet of cell debris is visible at the bottom of the tube, while the liquid above becomes clear or lightly translucent (supernatant).V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCentrifugation separates components based on density under centrifugal force. Dense and insoluble cell debris sediments to the bottom of the tube to form a pellet, while lighter, soluble molecules remain in the supernatant, resulting in a clear liquid above the pellet.VI. PrecautionsAvoid disturbing the pellet when handling the tube after centrifugation; always wait until the centrifuge fully stops before opening the lid.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Temperature Change Shown by a Liquid Thermometer During Heating and CoolingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Temperature Change Shown by a Liquid Thermometer During Heating and Cooling2. Subject: Natural Science – Biophysics3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand how a liquid-in-glass thermometer responds to heating and cooling, recognize the delayed response of temperature measurement, and relate the observed scale change to thermal expansion and contraction of liquids.II. Experimental EquipmentGlass liquid thermometer (alcohol or mercury type), two transparent glass beakers (500 mL), hot plate, water, cold water or water with ice, thermometer clamp or holder (optional), camera or mobile phone with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Pour room-temperature water into the first beaker (about 2/3 full) and place it on the hot plate. Pour cool water (or ice water) into the second beaker and place it nearby. Ensure the thermometer is clean and intact.2. Heating Stage: Place the glass liquid thermometer vertically into the first beaker so that the bulb is fully submerged but not touching the beaker bottom or sides. Turn on the hot plate and heat the water gently.3. Observation During Heating: Fix the camera focus on the thermometer scale and begin time-lapse recording. Observe the liquid column in the thermometer gradually rising as the water temperature increases.4. Transfer Stage: After the thermometer reading becomes stable at a higher value, carefully remove the thermometer from the hot water and immediately place it into the second beaker containing cool water.5. Cooling Stage Observation: Keep the thermometer vertical and continue recording. Observe the liquid column gradually falling as the thermometer cools.6. Completion: When the thermometer reading stabilizes at a lower value, stop recording. Turn off the hot plate and allow all equipment to cool.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The liquid column in the thermometer is at a stable level corresponding to room temperature.2. During Heating: As the water is heated, the thermometer liquid rises slowly and continuously, showing a gradual increase in temperature rather than an instant change.3. During Cooling: After transferring to cool water, the liquid column falls gradually, again showing a delayed response before stabilizing at a lower level.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleA liquid-in-glass thermometer works based on thermal expansion and contraction. When the thermometer bulb is heated, the liquid inside absorbs heat and expands, causing the liquid column to rise in the narrow capillary tube. When cooled, the liquid releases heat and contracts, causing the column to fall. The gradual change demonstrates heat transfer between the water and the thermometer and shows that temperature measurement requires time to reach thermal equilibrium.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not allow the thermometer bulb to touch the hot plate or beaker bottom to avoid damage.2. Heat the water slowly to prevent sudden temperature changes.3. Handle the thermometer carefully, especially when transferring between beakers.4. Turn off the hot plate immediately after the experiment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Liquid thermometer response to heating and cooling based on thermal expansion and contraction. Minimum assumptions: water temperature changes through heating and cooling; the thermometer exchanges heat with water and responds gradually.Phased storyline: (1) Initial stable thermometer reading at room temperature; (2) Heating phase where water temperature increases and the liquid column rises; (3) Transfer to cool water as a causal action; (4) Cooling phase where the liquid column falls and stabilizes. Visibility constraints: thermometer scale and liquid column must remain clearly visible and centered to verify directional changes.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Soap Bubbles Tracing Rotating Air EddiesI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Soap Bubbles Tracing Rotating Air Eddies in Gentle Indoor AirflowSubject: Natural Science – Atmospheric ScienceExperiment Objective: To visualize airflow patterns and rotating air eddies formed when gentle airflow passes a narrow vertical obstacle, using soap bubbles as tracers.II. Experimental EquipmentSmall desk fan with adjustable low speed; narrow vertical obstacle (e.g., ruler or thin cardboard strip fixed upright); soap bubble solution and bubble wand or bubble machine; table or desk; neutral indoor background.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the desk fan on a table and set it to the lowest steady speed. Fix the narrow vertical obstacle upright about 20–30 cm in front of the fan, aligned perpendicular to the airflow.Airflow Setup: Turn on the fan and allow the airflow to stabilize for several seconds, ensuring the air moves gently past both sides of the obstacle.Bubble Release: Release soap bubbles slowly upstream of the obstacle or just at the fan outlet, allowing them to enter the airflow naturally.Observation Operation: Continue releasing bubbles steadily while observing their paths as they pass the obstacle and move downstream.Completion: Stop bubble release, turn off the fan, and clean up the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Soap bubbles move smoothly with the airflow toward the obstacle.Near the Obstacle: As bubbles pass the sides of the vertical obstacle, some deviate from straight paths.Downstream Region: Behind the obstacle, bubbles trace curved and rotating paths, forming visible swirling patterns that indicate rotating air eddies.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhen a gentle airflow encounters a narrow vertical obstacle, the flow separates around the obstacle edges. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Binary Tree Level-order Traversal DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Binary Tree Level-order Traversal Demonstration2. Subject: Engineering – Computer Science – Data Structures3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the level-order (breadth-first) traversal of a binary tree, help learners understand the visiting order of nodes from top to bottom and left to right, and connect the traversal process with the generated output sequence.II. Experimental Materials and Environment1. A simple binary tree diagram with 7 nodes labeled 1–7.2. Light-colored background to ensure clear contrast.3. Bright highlight color (e.g., red) and glow animation effect.4. A horizontal output list area displayed at the bottom of the screen.III. Experimental Operation Process1. Initialization: Display a complete binary tree with node 1 as the root, nodes 2 and 3 as the second level, and nodes 4, 5, 6, and 7 as the third level. All nodes are shown in a neutral color on a light background. The output list at the bottom is initially empty.2. Start Traversal: Begin level-order traversal from the root node.3. Level 1 Operation: Highlight node 1 using a bright color and brief glow effect to indicate it is being visited. Append the value ‘1’ to the output list from left to right.4. Level 2 Operation: Move to the next level. First highlight node 2 with the same glow effect and append ‘2’ to the output list, then highlight node 3 and append ‘3’.5. Level 3 Operation: Continue to the third level. Highlight nodes 4, 5, 6, and 7 sequentially from left to right. Each node briefly glows when visited, and its value is appended to the output list in order.6. Completion: After node 7 is visited, stop the traversal. The final output list shows the complete traversal result.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: All nodes are visible but unhighlighted; the output list is empty.2. During Traversal: Nodes are highlighted one by one level by level. Each highlighted node briefly glows, clearly indicating the visiting sequence. Simultaneously, numbers appear in the output list in the same order as the traversal.3. Final State: All nodes have been visited once. The output list displays the sequence: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Core Principle: Level-order traversal (also called breadth-first traversal) visits nodes of a binary tree level by level, starting from the root and proceeding from left to right within each level.2. Algorithmic Logic: The traversal conceptually uses a queue data structure. A node is visited, its value is recorded, and then its left and right child nodes are enqueued for subsequent visits.3. Visual Mapping: Highlighting nodes and appending values to the output list directly maps the abstract traversal algorithm to an intuitive visual process, reinforcing understanding of traversal order.VI. Experimental Notes1. Highlight color should contrast clearly with the background and unvisited nodes.2. The visiting order must strictly follow top-to-bottom and left-to-right rules.3. Each node should glow only once to avoid confusion about repeated visits.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Binary tree level-order (breadth-first) traversal. Minimum assumptions: a static binary tree with seven labeled nodes, clear parent–child relationships, and a traversal that visits nodes level by level from left to right.Phased Storyline: (1) Initial display of a complete binary tree and empty output list; (2) Root node highlighted and recorded; (3) Second-level nodes highlighted sequentially and recorded; (4) Third-level nodes highlighted sequentially and recorded; (5) Final state showing complete output sequence. Key causal link: highlighting a node directly causes its value to appear in the output list. Visibility constraints: entire tree and output list must remain on screen throughout for verification.

Impact Compaction (Tray B): Place the same flat loading plate on the sand surface of Tray B. Apply the same weight X in the form of impact loading (e.g., dropping or striking once or several times from a fixed height). Ensure the total applied weight is equal to X.4. Observation and Recording: Measure and record the final sand height in both trays. Observe the surface condition and apparent compactness. Take a focused demonstration photograph showing both trays for comparison.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Sand in both trays is loose, with similar height and low density.2. After Static Compaction: The sand in Tray A shows a slight reduction in height and moderate densification.3. After Impact Compaction: The sand in Tray B shows a more明显 reduction in height and higher densification than Tray A.4. Comparative Result: Under the same weight X, impact compaction produces a denser sand structure and smaller final height compared with static compaction.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the principle of soil compaction in geotechnical engineering. Static compaction mainly relies on slow particle rearrangement under constant stress, resulting in limited densification. Impact compaction introduces dynamic energy, causing sand particles to overcome inter-particle friction and rearrange more efficiently into a denser configuration. Therefore, for the same applied weight, impact compaction generally achieves greater density and lower void ratio than static compaction.

Subject: Natural Science – Neuroscience (Plant Structure Observation as Biological Foundation)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the internal structure of a celery stalk by slicing it lengthwise and exposing its vascular bundles, and to understand the basic transport system in plants through direct visual evidence.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentFresh celery stalk (1 piece, green and intact), cutting board (flat and stable), kitchen knife (clean and sharp), paper towel or cloth (for moisture), camera or smartphone (fixed focus, time-lapse mode optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the cutting board on a stable surface. Wash the celery stalk with clean water and dry the surface with a paper towel. Adjust focus so the celery stalk is clear, and keep the focus fixed throughout the experiment.3. Core Operation: Hold the celery steady with one hand. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCelery is a vascular plant containing xylem and phloem tissues arranged in vascular bundles. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Laser Pointer vs LED Flashlight on a Rough WallI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Speckle Patterns from a Laser Pointer and an LED Flashlight2. Subject: Physics – Optics3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare speckle and interference effects produced by coherent laser light and incoherent LED light when reflected from a rough surface, and to understand the role of coherence in optical interference.II. Experimental EquipmentRed laser pointer (low-power, eye-safe), white LED flashlight, rough wall (painted or plaster surface), camera or smartphone with manual focus, tripod or stable support, darkened room.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Darken the room and fix the camera on a tripod facing the rough wall. Set the camera focus manually on the wall and keep it fixed.Alignment: Place the red laser pointer and white LED flashlight side by side, aiming both at nearby spots on the same rough wall.Core Operation: Turn on both light sources. Gently wiggle the laser pointer for several seconds while keeping the flashlight steady, then gently wiggle the flashlight while keeping the laser steady, or wiggle both slightly.Recording: Use time-lapse or continuous video recording while ensuring the wall and camera remain stationary.Completion: Turn off the light sources and stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The LED flashlight produces a smooth, uniform bright spot on the wall, while the laser produces a granular, grainy speckle pattern.During Wiggling: When the laser pointer is gently wiggled, the speckle pattern rapidly changes and appears to shimmer. When the LED flashlight is wiggled, the illuminated area moves smoothly without forming a stable speckle pattern.Comparison: The speckle from the laser has high contrast and fine structure, while the LED illumination remains diffuse and low-contrast.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesLaser light is highly coherent and nearly monochromatic. When it reflects from a rough wall, light scattered from different microscopic points interferes, producing a speckle pattern. Small changes in angle cause large changes in the interference pattern. In contrast, LED light is incoherent and contains many wavelengths, so interference averages out, resulting in smooth illumination without stable speckle.VI. Experimental PrecautionsDo not aim the laser at eyes or reflective surfaces. Keep the camera focus fixed. Ensure the wall and camera do not move during the experiment.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Moving a Bar Magnet In and Out of a Copper Wire Coil Connected to a GalvanometerI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Electromagnetic Induction with a Moving Bar Magnet2. Subject: Physics – Electricity and Magnetism3. Experiment Objective: To observe electromagnetic induction by pushing a bar magnet in and out of a copper wire coil connected to an analog galvanometer, and to understand the relationship between changing magnetic flux and induced current.II. Experimental EquipmentBar magnet (clearly marked N and S poles), copper wire coil (insulated wire wound into multiple turns), analog galvanometer with zero-centered needle, connecting wires.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the galvanometer on a stable surface and ensure its needle points to zero. Connect the two ends of the copper coil to the galvanometer terminals.2. Initial Observation: Keep the bar magnet stationary and away from the coil. Observe that the galvanometer needle remains at zero.3. Core Operation (Push In): Hold the bar magnet and slowly push one pole into the center of the copper coil while observing the galvanometer needle.4. Core Operation (Pull Out): Pull the bar magnet out of the coil and observe the change in the needle direction.5. Stop Motion: Hold the magnet stationary inside or outside the coil and observe the needle.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. When the magnet is stationary, the galvanometer needle stays at zero.2. When the magnet is pushed into the coil, the galvanometer needle deflects to one side.3. When the magnet is pulled out of the coil, the galvanometer needle deflects to the opposite side.4. When the magnet stops moving, the needle returns to zero.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates electromagnetic induction. When the bar magnet moves relative to the coil, the magnetic flux through the coil changes, inducing an electric current that causes the galvanometer needle to deflect. The direction of deflection depends on whether the magnetic flux is increasing or decreasing. When there is no change in magnetic flux, no induced current is produced.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure secure wire connections to the galvanometer.2. Move the magnet smoothly to make needle deflection clearly observable.3. Avoid striking the coil or galvanometer with the magnet.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Water Droplet Behavior on Smooth and Hairy Leaf SurfacesSubject: Healthcare – Pharmacy (Plant Surface Properties and Hydrophobicity)Experiment Objective: To observe and compare how water droplets interact with different leaf surface structures (smooth waxy vs hairy), and to understand the role of surface microstructure in water retention and repellency.II. Experimental EquipmentFresh smooth, glossy leaf (e.g., camellia or magnolia)Fresh fuzzy, hairy leaf (e.g., lamb’s ear or tomato leaf)Spray bottle filled with clean waterFlat tray or tabletopCamera or smartphone with fixed focus (for time-lapse recording)Good lighting sourceIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the flat tray on a stable surface under good lighting. Select two intact leaves of similar size, one smooth and glossy, the other fuzzy with fine hairs.2. Placement: Lay the two leaves side by side on the tray, with the upper (adaxial) surfaces facing upward. Ensure they are at the same height and orientation.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera directly above or at a slight angle. Fix the focus and frame so both leaves are fully visible. Do not adjust the camera during the experiment.4. Core Operation: Using the spray bottle, mist both leaves evenly from the same distance, applying a fine spray until water droplets are clearly visible.5. Initial State: Both leaves are dry, with clearly visible differences in surface texture.2. After Misting: On the smooth, waxy leaf, water forms round, bead-like droplets that may roll or merge easily. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Enrichment of Suspected Vibrio cholerae Using Alkaline Peptone WaterSubject: Healthcare – Pathology (Medical Microbiology)Objective: To enrich suspected Vibrio cholerae from a clinical or environmental sample using alkaline peptone water, and to understand the role of selective enrichment in bacterial detection.II. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear protective equipment. Place the alkaline peptone water test tube upright in a rack and label it clearly.2. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Verifying that the Harmonic Mean Is Less Than the Arithmetic MeanI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Marking Arithmetic Mean and Harmonic Mean on the Same Number Line2. Subject: Natural Science – Statistics & Data Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate, through calculation and visualization, that for two positive numbers the harmonic mean is always less than the arithmetic mean.II. Experimental MaterialsPaper or spreadsheet software, pen or keyboard, calculator (optional), ruler or digital chart tool.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Create a simple table with two positive numbers, for example a = 2 and b = 6.2. Arithmetic Mean Calculation: Add the two numbers (2 + 6 = 8), then divide by 2 to obtain the arithmetic mean AM = 4.3. Harmonic Mean Calculation: Take the reciprocals (1/2 and 1/6), compute their average: (1/2 + 1/6) ÷ 2 = (2/3) ÷ 2 = 1/3, then take the reciprocal to obtain HM = 3.4. Plotting: Draw a number line covering the range from 0 to at least 6. Mark the arithmetic mean point at 4 and the harmonic mean point at 3 using distinct labels or colors.5. Comparison: Observe the relative positions of the two points on the number line.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The arithmetic mean point appears to the right of the harmonic mean point on the number line.2. The harmonic mean point is closer to the smaller of the two original numbers.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleFor any two positive numbers, the arithmetic mean represents simple averaging, while the harmonic mean emphasizes smaller values through reciprocals. This leads to the general inequality HM ≤ AM, with equality only when the two numbers are equal. The visualization confirms that the harmonic mean is always less than the arithmetic mean for unequal positive numbers.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Milk Protein Film Forming on a Heated Stainless Steel SurfaceI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Milk Protein Film Formation on a Heated Stainless Steel Surface2. Subject: Engineering – Nuclear Engineering (Thermal-hydraulic fouling and heat transfer analogy)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the formation of a milk protein fouling film on a heated stainless steel surface under continuous flow, and to relate the phenomenon to heat transfer degradation and surface fouling mechanisms.II. Experimental EquipmentStainless steel plate (polished, flat), electric heating plate or cartridge heater (mounted beneath the plate), temperature controller and thermocouple, transparent tray (heat-resistant), peristaltic pump, silicone tubing, fresh milk, reservoir beaker, support frame, camera with fixed focus and tripod, power supply, heat-resistant gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Mount the stainless steel plate horizontally and attach the heater beneath it. Place the plate inside the transparent tray. Connect the thermocouple to monitor plate temperature.2. Circulation Setup: Fill the reservoir with milk. Connect tubing so that milk is pumped uniformly across the top surface of the stainless steel plate and returned to the reservoir, forming a closed loop.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera above or at an oblique angle to the tray. Fix focus, framing, and exposure. Start time-lapse recording.4. Heating and Operation: Turn on the pump to establish steady milk flow. Switch on the heater and maintain constant heating from below (e.g., 80–100 °C plate temperature).5. Observation Stage: Allow the system to run continuously while recording. Do not adjust focus or flow during operation.6. Shutdown: After clear film formation is observed, turn off the heater first, then stop the pump. Allow the system to cool before disassembly and cleaning.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Milk flows smoothly over a clean, shiny stainless steel surface with no visible deposits.2. Early Heating Stage: Slight cloudiness appears near the plate surface; small whitish patches begin to form.3. Film Formation Stage: A continuous whitish to yellowish protein film develops on the heated stainless steel surface, thickening over time, especially in hotter regions.4. Later Stage: The film becomes more opaque and adherent, while milk above continues to flow.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhen milk contacts a hot stainless steel surface, proteins (mainly whey proteins and casein) denature due to elevated temperature. Denatured proteins aggregate and adhere to the metal surface, forming a fouling film. Continuous heating accelerates denaturation, while flow supplies fresh proteins. This process is analogous to fouling on heat transfer surfaces in nuclear and thermal engineering, where deposited layers reduce heat transfer efficiency and alter surface characteristics.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure stable heating and flow before recording; avoid overheating that may burn milk; handle hot surfaces with protective gloves; clean the stainless steel plate promptly after the experiment to prevent permanent fouling.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Deflection of an Analog Magnetometer Needle by an Approaching Bar Magnet2. Subject: Natural Science – Geology & Geophysics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that a magnetic field exerts a torque on a magnetized needle, causing deflection; to observe how the magnitude and direction of needle deflection change as a bar magnet approaches, moves away, and reverses polarity; to support visual recording via fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Equipment1. Handheld analog magnetometer (or compass-style magnetometer) with a clearly visible needle and marked scale.2. Bar magnet with distinct red (north pole) and blue (south pole) ends.3. Flat tabletop surface (non-magnetic).4. Camera or smartphone mounted on a tripod; focus fixed manually.5. Optional: tape or stand to hold the magnetometer steady.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the magnetometer flat on the tabletop, ensuring it is level and free from nearby metal objects. Allow the needle to settle so it aligns with Earth’s magnetic field.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera above or at a slight angle to the tabletop so the magnetometer needle and bar magnet path are clearly visible. Lock exposure and fix focus for time-lapse recording.3. Initial State Recording: Start recording. Confirm the needle is stable and pointing in a constant direction.4. Approach of Magnet: Slowly move the bar magnet from the side toward the magnetometer, keeping the magnet parallel to the tabletop. Do not touch the magnetometer.5. Withdrawal: Pause briefly near the closest approach, then slowly pull the magnet away to its starting position.6. Polarity Reversal: Flip the bar magnet end-for-end so the opposite colored pole faces the magnetometer.7. Repeat: Repeat steps 4 and 5 with the reversed magnet orientation.8. Completion: Stop recording, remove the magnet, and allow the needle to return to its original alignment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: With no nearby magnet, the needle points steadily along Earth’s magnetic field direction.2. Magnet Approaching: As the bar magnet approaches from the side, the needle deflects toward or away from the magnet depending on the pole facing it. The closer the magnet, the larger the deflection angle.3. Magnet Withdrawing: As the magnet is pulled away, the needle gradually returns toward its original direction.4. Magnet Flipped: When the magnet is flipped end-for-end and re-approached, the needle deflects in the opposite direction compared with the first approach.5. Repeatability: The same approach–withdraw–flip sequence produces consistent, repeatable needle motions.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. The magnetometer needle is itself a small magnet that experiences a torque in an external magnetic field.2. A nearby bar magnet produces a magnetic field that superposes with Earth’s magnetic field, changing the net field direction at the needle.3. The needle rotates to align with the net magnetic field; stronger fields (closer magnet) produce larger deflections.4. Reversing the bar magnet reverses the direction of the applied magnetic field, causing opposite needle deflection.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Keep the magnetometer away from other magnetic or metallic objects.2. Move the bar magnet slowly to ensure smooth, observable needle motion.3. Do not touch or jar the magnetometer during the experiment.4. Fix camera focus and framing before starting to ensure consistent time-lapse results.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Emulsification Stability Test (Oil–Water Emulsion)Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food HygieneExperiment Objective: To observe the formation and stability of an oil–water emulsion using an edible emulsifier, understand the role of emulsifiers in food systems, and master basic operations of mixing, shaking, and visual observation.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsTransparent test tube (1), test tube rack, stopper or sealing film, measuring cylinder or dropper, distilled water, edible oil (e.g., soybean oil), edible emulsifier (e.g., lecithin or egg yolk solution).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean transparent test tube on the rack. Ensure all materials are at room temperature.2. Liquid Addition: Measure equal volumes of water and edible oil (e.g., 5 mL each) and carefully pour them into the test tube. Observe the clear layering, with oil floating above water.3. Emulsifier Addition: Add a small amount of emulsifier (2–3 drops) into the test tube.4. Sealing and Shaking: Seal the test tube tightly with a stopper or film. Hold the tube firmly and shake vigorously for 5–10 seconds.5. Standing and Observation: Place the test tube upright on the rack. Observe immediate changes, then continue observing over time (can be shown with time-lapse photography).IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before Shaking: Water and oil form two distinct layers with a clear interface.2. After Shaking: The mixture becomes uniformly cloudy or milky, indicating emulsion formation.3. Standing Over Time: The emulsion gradually separates into layers; with emulsifier, separation is slower and less distinct compared to no emulsifier.V. An emulsifier contains both hydrophilic and lipophilic groups, allowing it to reduce interfacial tension and stabilize dispersed oil droplets in water. Over time, gravity causes partial separation, demonstrating emulsification stability.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Protein Detection in Food (Biuret Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Protein Detection in Food by Biuret Method2. Subject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To detect the presence of protein in soybean milk using the Biuret reaction, observe characteristic color changes, and understand the chemical principle of protein–copper complex formation.II. Experimental Materials and ReagentsTest tube (1), test tube rack, measuring cylinder or pipette, dropper, soybean milk (protein-containing sample), Biuret reagent A (alkaline solution, usually NaOH), Biuret reagent B (copper sulfate solution), gloves and safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Sample Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack. Use a pipette to add 2 mL of soybean milk into the test tube.2. Addition of Reagent A: Add 1 mL of Biuret reagent A to the test tube. Gently shake the test tube to mix thoroughly.3. Observation: Place the test tube on the rack and observe the color change of the solution.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe Biuret method is based on the reaction between peptide bonds in proteins and copper ions (Cu2+) under alkaline conditions. Add reagent B dropwise and mix gently to avoid splashing.2. Observe color changes under good lighting for accurate judgment.3. Dispose of waste solutions according to laboratory safety regulations.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Thermal Camera Showing Handprint Cooling on a TabletopI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Thermal Camera Observation of Handprint Cooling on a Tabletop2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Geography (Thermal Environment Perception)3. Experiment Objective: To observe heat transfer between the human body and a solid surface using a handheld thermal infrared camera, and to understand surface heat dissipation over time.II. Experimental EquipmentHandheld thermal infrared camera (with temperature color scale enabled), smooth tabletop surface (wood, plastic, or stone), bare human hand, indoor environment with stable temperature.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the thermal camera above the tabletop and adjust focus so the surface is clearly visible in the thermal image. Ensure no strong airflow or sunlight affects the table.2. Initial Observation: Observe and record the initial uniform temperature of the tabletop using the thermal camera.3. Core Operation: Press the bare hand flat onto the smooth tabletop for about 3–5 seconds, ensuring full contact.4. Release: Lift the hand vertically away from the surface.5. Observation and Recording: Keep the thermal camera fixed on the tabletop and record the thermal image as the handprint gradually changes and fades (time-lapse recording optional).IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The tabletop shows a relatively uniform thermal color, indicating even temperature.2. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates heat transfer by conduction. When the warmer human hand contacts the cooler tabletop, thermal energy flows from the hand to the surface. Keep the camera steady to ensure clear observation of temperature changes.2. Avoid touching the surface multiple times, which may interfere with the cooling pattern.3. Conduct the experiment in a stable indoor environment for clearer results.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Reaction Between Carbon and Concentrated Sulfuric AcidI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Reaction Between Carbon and Concentrated Sulfuric Acid2. Subject: Natural Science - Chemistry - Inorganic Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To observe the oxidation-reduction reaction between carbon and concentrated sulfuric acid, understand the oxidizing and dehydrating properties of concentrated sulfuric acid, and verify the production of sulfur dioxide gas through its effect on fuchsine solution.II. Experimental EquipmentHard glass test tube, test tube clamp and stand, alcohol lamp, rubber stopper with delivery tube, glass tubing, black carbon powder, concentrated sulfuric acid (colorless), fuchsine solution (reddish-purple), beaker or test tube for fuchsine solution, safety goggles and gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Put on safety goggles and gloves. Fix the hard test tube on the test tube stand at a slight incline.2. Addition of Reactants: Place a small amount of black carbon powder at the bottom of the hard test tube. Slowly add a small volume of colorless concentrated sulfuric acid along the tube wall.3. Apparatus Setup: Immediately seal the test tube with a rubber stopper fitted with a delivery tube. Insert the other end of the glass tube into a container holding fuchsine solution, ensuring the tube end is below the liquid surface.4. Heating: Light the alcohol lamp and gently heat the bottom of the test tube. Maintain steady heating.5. Gas Introduction: Allow the generated gas to pass through the delivery tube into the fuchsine solution.6. Completion: After clear phenomena are observed, stop heating, remove the delivery tube from the fuchsine solution, extinguish the alcohol lamp, and allow the apparatus to cool.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Black carbon powder and colorless concentrated sulfuric acid remain unchanged at room temperature; fuchsine solution is reddish-purple.2. During Heating: The mixture in the test tube produces gas, and the carbon gradually reacts.3. Gas Effect: As the gas bubbles into the fuchsine solution, the reddish-purple color gradually fades and becomes colorless.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleConcentrated sulfuric acid acts as a strong oxidizing agent when heated with carbon. Carbon is oxidized to carbon dioxide, while sulfuric acid is reduced to sulfur dioxide. The produced sulfur dioxide is a reducing agent that decolorizes fuchsine solution.Core Reaction Equation: C + 2H2SO4 (conc, heat) = CO2 + 2SO2 + 2H2OPrinciple Explanation: Heating provides the energy required for the redox reaction. The sulfur dioxide gas generated enters the fuchsine solution and reduces its colored structure, causing decolorization.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Glass Etching with Hydrofluoric AcidI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Glass Etching with Hydrofluoric Acid2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the selective etching of glass by hydrofluoric acid using a paraffin wax mask, and to recognize the reaction between silicon dioxide and hydrofluoric acid.II. Experimental EquipmentGlass microscope slide, paraffin wax, metal needle or glass rod for drawing, hydrofluoric acid solution (teacher demonstration only), plastic dropper, plastic tray, running water or wash bottle, safety goggles, gloves, lab coat.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear goggles, gloves, and lab coat. Place the clean glass slide flat in a plastic tray.2. Wax Coating and Pattern Drawing: Evenly coat one surface of the slide with molten paraffin wax. After solidification, use a needle to draw a simple pattern, exposing the glass where lines are drawn.3. Acid Treatment: Using a dropper, carefully add hydrofluoric acid solution to cover the patterned area. Allow the slide to stand for a short, fixed time.4. Washing: Pour off the acid into a designated waste container. Rinse the slide thoroughly with running water.5. Wax Removal: Remove the paraffin wax with warm water or gentle wiping, exposing the etched surface.6. Observation: Observe the slide surface. Focus the image on the slide and record a time-lapse sequence showing the appearance of etched patterns.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before reaction: The glass surface under wax appears smooth and transparent.2. After acid treatment and washing: Areas not protected by wax appear rough or frosted, while wax-covered areas remain smooth and clear. The drawn pattern becomes visible on the glass surface.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesGlass mainly contains silicon dioxide (SiO2). Hydrofluoric acid reacts with silicon dioxide to form soluble fluorosilicates, causing the glass surface to be etched. Paraffin wax acts as a protective mask, preventing contact between acid and glass in covered areas, resulting in selective etching.Core reaction concept: SiO2 + HF → soluble silicon fluoride compounds.VI. Experimental PrecautionsHydrofluoric acid is highly corrosive and toxic; this experiment is for demonstration only. Avoid skin contact and inhalation. All waste must be disposed of according to safety regulations.

Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how wetland plants and soil can filter sediments from muddy water by comparing water clarity after passing through planted and bare soil trays.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo shallow soil trays of equal size, wetland plants with intact roots (e.g., reeds or sedges), clean soil, muddy water (water mixed with fine soil), two identical clear containers, measuring cup, support stand or slight slope for trays, camera fixed for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fill both trays with the same depth of soil. Plant wetland plants evenly in one tray; leave the other tray bare. Place trays side by side at the same slight angle so water can drain from one end.2. Setup: Position a clear container under the drainage end of each tray to collect outflow. Ensure both containers are empty and clean.3. Core Operation: Measure equal volumes of muddy water. Slowly pour the muddy water onto the upper end of the planted tray and the bare tray at the same rate.4. Recording: Keep the camera fixed and record the entire process, allowing water to flow through the soil and drain into the containers.5. Completion: Stop pouring once the same volume has passed through each tray. Allow drainage to finish before final observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Summary of Experimental PrincipleWetland plants and their root systems slow water flow and physically trap suspended sediments. Soil particles adhere to roots and settle as water movement decreases. Experiment Title: Cold Surface Plate with Warm Humid Air Forming Visible Fog Layer2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the condensation of water vapor when warm, humid air encounters a cold surface, and to visually understand the concept of dew point and fog formation.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Peroxidase–Guaiacol Reaction Showing Rapid Initial BrowningI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Peroxidase–Guaiacol Reaction with Hydrogen Peroxide2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Biochemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the catalytic action of horseradish peroxidase on hydrogen peroxide using guaiacol as a chromogenic substrate, and to understand the phenomenon of rapid initial reaction followed by a slowdown.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsClear glass cuvette (1 cm path length), plastic or glass pipette, guaiacol solution (colorless or pale yellow), dilute hydrogen peroxide solution, horseradish peroxidase solution, cuvette holder or stable surface, safety gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, dry clear glass cuvette on a stable surface. Add guaiacol solution to fill about two-thirds of the cuvette. Then add a measured amount of hydrogen peroxide. Gently mix so the solution is uniform and remains clear.2. Initial Observation: Observe from the side. The solution should be colorless or very light yellow, with no brown coloration.3. Enzyme Addition (Core Operation): Using a pipette, draw horseradish peroxidase solution. Carefully add several drops directly into the cuvette.4. Mixing: Immediately and gently swirl the cuvette to mix the enzyme evenly, avoiding bubbles.5. Observation: Keep observing from the side as the reaction proceeds.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Immediately after enzyme addition and swirling, the solution rapidly turns brown, starting near the point of mixing and spreading throughout the cuvette.2. After the initial rapid browning, the rate of color deepening gradually slows, and the color change becomes less pronounced over time.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesHorseradish peroxidase catalyzes the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water while oxidizing guaiacol. Oxidized guaiacol forms a brown-colored product. At the beginning, substrate concentrations are high, so the reaction rate is fast, causing rapid browning. As guaiacol or hydrogen peroxide is consumed, the reaction rate decreases, leading to a visible slowdown in color change.VI. Experimental PrecautionsAvoid skin contact with hydrogen peroxide and enzyme solutions. Use gentle swirling to prevent splashing. Dispose of reaction mixtures according to laboratory waste guidelines.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Visualization of Fluorescently Stained DNA Bands After Agarose Gel ElectrophoresisI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visualization of Fluorescently Stained DNA Bands Under Blue or UV Light2. Subject: Biology – Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To observe and record DNA fragments separated by agarose gel electrophoresis using a transilluminator. Through direct visualization of fluorescent DNA bands under blue or UV light, learners understand the principles of DNA separation by size, fluorescence-based staining, and standardized observation and imaging methods, including fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsAgarose gel containing electrophoresed DNA samples, clear gel tray, electrophoresis buffer (already used), transilluminator (blue light or UV), fluorescent DNA stain (e.g., SYBR Safe, GelRed, or ethidium bromide – pre-stained), protective goggles (UV-rated if UV light is used), digital camera or imaging system with tripod, darkroom or light-shielding cover (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: After electrophoresis is completed, ensure the agarose gel remains intact and submerged or moist with buffer. Put on appropriate protective goggles, especially when using UV light. Turn off ambient room lighting if necessary to improve fluorescence contrast.2. Placement of Gel: Carefully transfer the agarose gel together with the clear tray onto the center of the transilluminator surface. Ensure the gel lies flat and is correctly oriented, with wells positioned consistently for observation.3. Illumination Setup: Switch on the transilluminator and select the appropriate light source (blue or UV) according to the fluorescent stain used. Allow a few seconds for the fluorescence to stabilize.4. Observation Operation: Observe the gel directly or through a protective viewing window. Identify discrete fluorescent DNA bands within each lane. Avoid prolonged exposure to UV light.5. Imaging and Recording: Position the camera directly above the gel. Adjust framing so the entire gel is visible. Fix the camera focus and exposure settings to avoid refocusing during recording. Start time-lapse or continuous photography to document the fluorescent bands under constant illumination.6. Experiment Conclusion: After observation and imaging, switch off the transilluminator. Remove the gel for proper disposal or downstream processing. Turn on room lights and store all equipment properly.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before illumination, the agarose gel appears transparent or slightly opaque, with DNA bands not visible to the naked eye.2. Under Illumination: When blue or UV light is applied, bright fluorescent bands appear in the gel lanes. Each band corresponds to a group of DNA fragments of similar length.3. Comparative Observation: Smaller DNA fragments appear farther from the wells, while larger fragments remain closer to the wells, forming a clear banding pattern.4. Imaging Result: The fixed-focus camera captures stable, high-contrast images of fluorescent bands without shifts in position or focus over time.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe experiment is based on agarose gel electrophoresis and fluorescence detection. DNA molecules carry a negative charge and migrate toward the positive electrode in an electric field. The agarose gel acts as a molecular sieve, separating DNA fragments by size, with smaller fragments moving faster. Fluorescent dyes intercalate into DNA or bind to it, emitting visible light when excited by blue or UV illumination. The transilluminator provides the excitation light, enabling direct visualization and documentation of DNA band patterns.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Always use appropriate eye and skin protection when working with UV light.2. Avoid excessive exposure of DNA to UV light to prevent DNA damage.3. Ensure the gel does not dry out during observation.4. Fix camera focus and exposure before recording to ensure consistent documentation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Spectrogram Visualization of Sustained Vowel versus Stop ConsonantI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Spectrogram Visualization of Sustained Vowel versus Stop Consonant2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences - Linguistics - Phonetics3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare spectrogram characteristics of a sustained vowel and a stop consonant using live phonetic analysis software, and to understand the acoustic principles underlying different speech sounds.II. Experimental EquipmentComputer with phonetic analysis software supporting live spectrogram display, external or built-in microphone, quiet recording environment, camera with fixed focus for continuous recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Open the phonetic analysis software and set it to display a live spectrogram with time on the horizontal axis and frequency on the vertical axis. Vowel Production: The speaker sustains a single vowel sound steadily into the microphone for several seconds, maintaining constant pitch and loudness.3. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Borax Detection (Curcumin Color Method)Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food HygieneExperiment Objective: To detect the presence of borax in food samples by observing the characteristic color change of curcumin reagent after mixing and heating, and to master basic operations such as dropwise addition, gentle stirring, and controlled heating.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsBeaker or test tube, dropper, glass rod, hot plate or alcohol lamp (low flame), curcumin reagent, prepared food sample extract (suspected of containing borax), test tube rack, safety gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a small amount of the food sample extract into a clean test tube or beaker and fix it on a rack. Ensure the solution is clear enough for color observation.2. Reagent Addition: Use a dropper to add several drops of curcumin reagent into the sample solution. Keep the dropper vertical and add the reagent slowly.3. Mixing: Use a glass rod to gently stir the mixture for several seconds to ensure uniform contact between the reagent and the sample.4. Heating: Place the container on a hot plate or gently heat it with a low flame for a short time (a few seconds), avoiding boiling or splashing.5. Completion: Remove the heat source and place the container on the rack for observation. Dispose of waste according to laboratory rules and clean all equipment.IV. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Urban Heat Island Effect Using Concrete and GrassI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Urban Heat Island Effect Using Concrete and Grass Under a Heat Lamp2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences - Geography3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how different surface materials absorb and release heat differently, helping students understand the urban heat island effect by comparing concrete and grass.II. Experimental EquipmentConcrete slab (1 piece, flat and dry), grass tray or turf tray (1 piece, fresh or artificial grass with soil), identical ice cubes (2 pieces, same size and shape), heat lamps (2 lamps with equal power), lamp stands, tabletop, camera or smartphone with tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the concrete slab and the grass tray side by side on a stable tabletop, ensuring both surfaces are level and exposed to similar surroundings.2. Placement of Ice Cubes: Place one identical ice cube at the center of the concrete slab and one at the center of the grass tray.3. Heat Source Setup: Position one heat lamp directly above the concrete slab and one directly above the grass tray at the same height and angle to ensure equal heating conditions.4. Recording Setup: Fix the camera on a tripod, adjust the focus to include both surfaces and ice cubes clearly, and set it for time-lapse photography.5. Core Operation: Turn on both heat lamps at the same time and begin recording. Allow heating to continue for a set period or until a clear difference in ice melting is observed.6. Completion: Turn off the heat lamps, stop recording, and observe the final state of both ice cubes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both ice cubes are solid, transparent, and of equal size on their respective surfaces.2. During Heating: The ice cube on the concrete slab melts faster, forming water more quickly, while the ice cube on the grass melts more slowly.3. Final State: After the same heating time, the concrete surface shows significantly more melted water than the grass surface.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesConcrete has a higher heat absorption and lower evapotranspiration compared to grass. Under the same heat input, concrete heats up faster and transfers more heat to the ice, causing faster melting. Grass remains cooler due to moisture evaporation and lower heat storage. This difference explains the urban heat island effect, where cities with more concrete and asphalt are hotter than areas with vegetation.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure heat lamps have equal power and are placed at the same distance.2. Use identical ice cubes to ensure fairness.3. Avoid touching hot lamps during or after the experiment.4. Keep the camera stable to ensure clear time-lapse results.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Urban heat island effect, assuming that different land surfaces have different heat absorption and release properties under equal energy input.Minimum mechanistic assumptions: Concrete absorbs and stores more heat; grass cools through evapotranspiration; equal heat lamps provide comparable energy to both surfaces.Expected phased storyline: Phase 1 shows two identical ice cubes placed on concrete and grass. Phase 2 begins with heat lamps turning on, causing both surfaces to warm. Phase 3 shows a clear divergence, where ice on concrete melts faster than on grass. Phase 4 ends with visibly more meltwater on concrete. The camera remains fixed with a clear top or angled view to verify side-by-side comparison and causal heat differences.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Erosion Simulation – Water Flowing Over Soil and PebblesI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Erosion Simulation Using Flowing WaterSubject: Natural Science – Geology & GeophysicsExperiment Objective: To simulate surface erosion by flowing water, observe how water transports soil and interacts with pebbles, and understand the basic mechanism of water-driven erosion.II. Experimental EquipmentShallow tray, soil, small pebbles, water source (cup or bottle with spout), support to tilt tray slightly, collection container for runoff, camera fixed on tripod (for time-lapse observation).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Spread an even layer of soil in the shallow tray and scatter small pebbles on the surface. Place the tray on a support so it is slightly tilted, with one end higher than the other. Position a container at the lower end to collect runoff.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera facing the tray from the side or above, ensuring the entire tray is in frame. Lock focus and keep the camera position unchanged.3. Core Operation: Slowly pour a steady, continuous stream of water onto the soil at the higher end of the tray. Maintain a consistent flow so water travels downslope across the tray and exits at the lower edge.4. Observation and Completion: Allow water to flow for a short period, then stop pouring. Turn off the camera and dispose of wet soil appropriately. Clean and store equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Soil and pebbles remain stationary on the tray surface.2. During Water Flow: Water forms small streams that move downslope, carrying fine soil particles. Shallow channels or rills appear in the soil layer. Pebbles remain mostly in place or shift slightly.3. After Flow Stops: Accumulated soil is visible at the lower edge or in the runoff container; erosion channels remain on the tray surface.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleFlowing water exerts shear stress on the soil surface. Fine particles are detached, transported, and deposited downslope, while heavier pebbles resist movement. This demonstrates basic water erosion processes such as detachment, transport, and deposition, which shape natural landscapes.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse a gentle, steady water flow to avoid splashing. Ensure the tray is only slightly tilted to simulate natural erosion. Keep electrical equipment away from water.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Wind Transport of Sand versus Dust in a Simple Fan-Driven SetupI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Wind Transport of Sand versus Dust2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Archaeology (Environmental Archaeology)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how wind differentially transports coarse sand and fine dust, helping explain archaeological patterns such as site burial, erosion, and dust deposition.II. Experimental Equipment- Two shallow trays of equal size- Coarse sand (visible grains, dry)- Fine dust or very fine silt (dry, light-colored)- Household electric fan (with steady speed setting)- Tabletop or flat surface- Camera or phone mounted on a fixed support (for time-lapse or fixed focus recording)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two empty trays side by side on a flat tabletop. Ensure the surface is dry and free of obstacles.2. Material Placement: Evenly spread coarse sand in one tray and fine dust in the other, keeping layer thickness similar.3. Fan Positioning: Place the household fan at the same height as the trays, directly facing them, about 50–80 cm away.4. Camera Setup: Fix the camera focus and angle so both trays are fully visible; do not adjust during the experiment.5. Core Operation: Turn on the fan at a steady, moderate speed and let it blow across both trays for several seconds.6. Completion: Turn off the fan and allow particles to settle before stopping recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both sand and dust lie flat and motionless in their trays.2. During Blowing: Fine dust is lifted into the air, forming a visible cloud and traveling farther downwind; coarse sand mainly vibrates, creeps, or hops short distances.3. Final State: Dust shows noticeable loss or redistribution, while most sand remains in the tray with limited displacement.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWind transport depends strongly on particle size and mass. Fine dust particles have low weight and large surface-area-to-mass ratios, allowing airflow to lift them into suspension. Coarse sand particles are heavier and require stronger wind to move, typically traveling by rolling or short hops (saltation). This principle helps archaeologists interpret sediment layers, site exposure, and dust accumulation in past environments.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Differential wind transport of sediments based on particle size, illustrating aeolian processes relevant to archaeology.Minimum Assumptions: Airflow from a fan simulates wind; sand and dust differ mainly by grain size and mass; gravity and airflow act normally.Phased Storyline: (1) Static setup with two contrasting materials; (2) Fan activates, generating airflow; (3) Fine dust becomes airborne and travels farther, while coarse sand shows limited movement; (4) Airflow stops and materials settle, revealing contrasting transport outcomes. Visibility must keep both trays and downwind area in frame for causal comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Cloud-in-a-Bottle Caused by Pressure ReleaseI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Cloud-in-a-Bottle Pressure Release Causing Condensation2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To simulate cloud formation through pressure change, observe condensation caused by rapid pressure release, and understand the role of adiabatic cooling in atmospheric processes.II. Experimental EquipmentClear plastic bottle with cap (1–2 L), small amount of water (about 5–10 mL), human hands for squeezing, camera or smartphone with fixed focus (for time-lapse or continuous recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Pour a small amount of clean water into the clear plastic bottle. Cap the bottle tightly to ensure it is sealed. Gently shake the bottle so the inner wall is moistened, forming water vapor inside.2. Setup: Place the bottle in a well-lit environment. Fix the camera position and focus on the bottle to avoid changes during recording.3. Core Operation: Hold the sealed bottle with both hands and squeeze it firmly for several seconds, increasing the internal air pressure.4. Pressure Release: Suddenly release the squeezing force while keeping the bottle sealed.5. Observation: Continue recording and observe the changes inside the bottle immediately after release.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The bottle is transparent, and the air inside appears clear with no visible cloud.2. During Squeezing: The bottle deforms slightly, but the air inside remains mostly clear.3. After Sudden Release: A white, cloud-like mist quickly appears inside the bottle and may gradually dissipate after a short time.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhen the bottle is squeezed, the air pressure and temperature inside increase. Upon sudden release, the air rapidly expands, causing a drop in temperature (adiabatic cooling). The cooling air cannot hold as much water vapor, so excess water vapor condenses into tiny droplets, forming a visible cloud. This process is analogous to cloud formation in the atmosphere when air rises and pressure decreases.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the bottle is well sealed to allow pressure change; avoid over-squeezing to prevent damage; keep the camera fixed to clearly capture the condensation phenomenon.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Anti-seepage Performance Test of Geosynthetic Clay Liners (GCL)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Anti-seepage Performance Test of Geosynthetic Clay Liners (GCL)2. Subject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the anti-seepage performance of GCL by comparing water penetration in a beaker lined with GCL and an unlined beaker using a colored aqueous solution.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent beakers (2, same size), geosynthetic clay liner (GCL) sample cut to fit beaker bottom, colored aqueous solution (water with dye), measuring cup, tweezers or gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Clean and dry two transparent beakers. Label them as Beaker A (with GCL) and Beaker B (without GCL).2. Laying GCL: Place the GCL flat at the bottom of Beaker A, ensuring full coverage and close contact with the beaker bottom. Do not place anything in Beaker B.3. Pouring Solution: Slowly pour an equal volume of colored aqueous solution into both beakers at the same time or in the same order, keeping the pouring height and speed consistent.4. Observation: Place both beakers on a flat surface and observe the bottom and side walls for seepage or leakage of colored water.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both beakers contain colored water; the bottoms are clearly visible.2. Beaker B (without GCL): Colored water seeps downward quickly and may be seen spreading along the bottom.3. Beaker A (with GCL): Little to no colored water seeps through; seepage is significantly delayed or absent.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesGCL contains bentonite clay, which swells upon contact with water and forms a low-permeability barrier. This swelling reduces hydraulic conductivity and prevents water from seeping through. In contrast, the unlined beaker lacks this barrier, allowing free seepage of water.VI. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Laser Beam Passing Through Horizontally Layered Sugar-Water TankI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Laser Beam Refraction in a Horizontally Stratified Sugar-Water Tank2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To simulate atmospheric refraction by observing how a laser beam propagates through a liquid with horizontally layered refractive indices, and to understand how density and refractive index gradients affect light paths.II. Experimental EquipmentRectangular transparent tank; sugar and water solutions of different concentrations; measuring cup or syringe; stirring rod; narrow green laser pointer; tripod-mounted camera (side view); darkened room or shaded background.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation of Stratified Solution: Prepare several sugar-water solutions with increasing sugar concentration. Slowly pour the densest solution into the tank first, then carefully add lower-density solutions along the tank wall to form stable horizontal layers without mixing.2. Setup: Place the tank on a stable surface. Darken the background to enhance laser visibility. Fix the camera on a tripod facing the side of the tank and lock the focus for time-lapse photography.3. Laser Alignment: Position the green laser so that it enters horizontally through the side wall of the tank at mid-height. Ensure the beam is narrow and level.4. Core Operation: Turn on the laser and allow it to pass through the layered sugar-water. Keep all equipment stationary during observation.5. Recording: Use the fixed-focus camera to record or capture time-lapse images of the laser path through the layers.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The sugar-water forms distinct, horizontal transparent layers; the laser enters as a straight beam.2. During Propagation: As the laser passes through layers of different concentrations, its path gradually bends or changes direction at layer boundaries.3. Overall Effect: The laser beam appears segmented or smoothly curved, with deviations corresponding to the refractive index differences between layers.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates refraction caused by spatial variations in refractive index. Sugar concentration affects water density and refractive index. When light travels through media with different refractive indices arranged in horizontal layers, its speed changes at each boundary, causing bending according to Snell’s law. This is analogous to atmospheric refraction, where light bends due to temperature- and density-dependent refractive index gradients in the atmosphere.VI. Experimental PrecautionsPour solutions slowly to avoid mixing; do not look directly into the laser beam; ensure the tank and camera remain stable; conduct the experiment in a dim environment for clear observation.

Experiment Title: Electric Stove Burner Coil Heating Up and Changing Color2. Subject: Natural Science – Astrophysics & Astronomy (Thermal Radiation and Energy Transfer)3. Experiment Objective: To observe how an electric stove burner coil heats up and changes color as electrical power increases, and to understand the relationship between temperature and thermal radiation. Experimental EquipmentElectric stove with exposed metal burner coil, power control knob, heat-resistant surroundings, camera or smartphone with tripod, stable power supply.III. Initial State Recording: Start recording or set time-lapse mode while the burner is still off, capturing the initial dark color of the coil.3. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Dish Soap Forms a Stable Oil–Water EmulsionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effect of Dish Soap on an Oil–Water Mixture2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To observe how dish soap enables oil and water to form a stable emulsion, and to understand the role of surfactants in reducing interfacial tension.II. Experimental MaterialsTwo identical transparent jars with lids, water, cooking oil, liquid dish soap, measuring spoon or dropper, camera or phone with fixed focus (for time-lapse observation).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical empty jars side by side on a flat surface. Pour equal volumes of water into each jar (about half full), then gently add an equal volume of oil to form a clear oil layer above the water in both jars.2. Soap Addition: Add a small amount of dish soap (about 3–5 drops) to the right jar only. Do not add soap to the left jar (control).3. Sealing: Tightly seal both jars with their lids to prevent leakage.4. Shaking: Shake both jars vigorously for the same duration (about 5–10 seconds).5. Observation Setup: Place the jars back side by side, fix the camera focus, and observe immediately and over time.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before shaking, both jars show two distinct layers, with oil floating on water.2. Immediately After Shaking: Both jars appear cloudy as oil droplets are temporarily dispersed in water.3. After Standing: In the left jar (no soap), the oil droplets gradually rise and separate, reforming a clear oil layer. In the right jar (with soap), the mixture remains cloudy for a much longer time, showing a stable or semi-stable emulsion.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleOil and water are immiscible due to differences in polarity. Shaking breaks oil into small droplets, but without soap these droplets quickly recombine and separate. Dish soap contains surfactant molecules with hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails. These molecules surround oil droplets, reduce interfacial tension, and prevent droplets from merging, forming a stable emulsion.VI. PrecautionsEnsure both jars are identical and shaken equally for fair comparison. Do not overfill jars. Clean up spills promptly and wash hands after the experiment.

Visibility constraints: jars must remain side by side in frame, with clear view of layer separation and cloudiness differences over time.

manual: Experiment Title: Demonstration of the Brachistochrone (Cycloidal Curve)Subject: Physics – Classical MechanicsI. Experiment ObjectiveTo demonstrate that, between the same starting and ending points under gravity and negligible friction, a ball traveling along a cycloidal (brachistochrone) track reaches the end faster than a ball traveling along a straight track.II. Experimental EquipmentStraight track, cycloidal (inverted cycloid) track, two identical solid balls, adjustable stand or frame, release mechanism or manual release, marked common starting point and ending point.III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Fix the straight track and the cycloidal track on a frame so that they share the same starting height and the same ending point.2. Preparation: Place one identical ball at the starting point of each track. Ensure both balls are at rest.3. Release: Release both balls simultaneously without giving any initial push.4. Observation: Observe and compare the motion of the two balls as they roll along their respective tracks until they reach the ending point.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. At release, the ball on the cycloidal track drops more steeply and accelerates rapidly.2. The ball on the straight track accelerates more slowly due to its gentler slope.3. Although the cycloidal path is longer, the ball on the cycloidal track reaches the ending point first.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe cycloidal curve is the brachistochrone, the path of shortest descent time under gravity without friction. Its steep initial section provides greater initial acceleration, allowing the ball to gain speed early, while the later, flatter section uses this high speed to complete the horizontal displacement. As a result, the total travel time is less than that along a straight path between the same points.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Zinc Plate on Electroscope Illuminated by Ultraviolet LightI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Discharge of a Negatively Charged Gold-Leaf Electroscope by Ultraviolet Light2. Subject: Physics – Modern Physics (Photoelectric Effect)3. Experiment Objective: To observe that ultraviolet light can cause a negatively charged zinc plate on a gold-leaf electroscope to discharge, while visible light cannot, and to understand the photoelectric effect.II. Experimental EquipmentGold-leaf electroscope (with metal knob), clean zinc plate attached to the knob, charging rod (for negative charging), lamp capable of alternating between visible and ultraviolet light, fixed stand to keep lamp at constant distance, camera fixed for time-lapse photography.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the electroscope on a stable surface. Attach a clean zinc plate to the metal knob. Fix the camera focus and position.2. Charging: Use a charging rod to give the electroscope a negative charge. Observe that the gold leaves diverge clearly.3. Visible Light Illumination: Turn on the lamp in visible-light mode and illuminate the zinc plate from a fixed distance. Keep the illumination for a short time.4. Observation: Observe and record the state of the gold leaves under visible light.5. Ultraviolet Illumination: Switch the same lamp to ultraviolet mode without changing the distance or position. Illuminate the zinc plate.6. Observation: Observe and record the change in the gold-leaf divergence over time.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: After negative charging, the gold leaves are clearly diverged.2. Under Visible Light: The gold leaves remain diverged, with no obvious change.3. Under Ultraviolet Light: The gold leaves gradually close, indicating discharge of the electroscope.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleUltraviolet light has a higher frequency than visible light. When ultraviolet light shines on the zinc plate, it provides sufficient energy to eject electrons from the zinc surface (photoelectric effect). The loss of electrons reduces the negative charge of the electroscope, causing the gold leaves to close. Visible light does not have enough energy to eject electrons, so no discharge occurs.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the zinc plate surface is clean.2. Keep lamp distance constant during visible and UV illumination.3. Avoid touching the electroscope during observation to prevent charge leakage.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: photoelectric effect on a zinc plate causing discharge of a negatively charged electroscope. Minimum assumptions: ultraviolet light has higher frequency than visible light and can eject electrons from zinc; electroscope leaf divergence represents charge. Phased storyline: (1) show negatively charged electroscope with diverged gold leaves; (2) illuminate with visible light—no change; (3) switch to ultraviolet light at same distance—electrons emitted from zinc; (4) electroscope discharges and leaves close. Visibility constraints: clear view of gold leaves, zinc plate, and lamp state changes; camera fixed to verify temporal causality.
