manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Laser Pointer Scattering in a Milk–Water TankI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Laser Pointer Scattering in a Milk–Water Tank2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To simulate atmospheric light scattering by suspended particles, observe how increasing particle concentration enhances laser beam visibility, and understand the relationship between aerosols and light scattering.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent rectangular tank (glass or acrylic), clean water, fresh milk, red laser pointer, measuring dropper or spoon, stirring rod, darkened room or shaded background, camera or smartphone on tripod (focus fixed).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the empty tank on a stable table and fill it with clear water. Darken the surroundings to improve beam visibility. Fix the camera on a tripod and lock the focus and exposure.2. Laser Setup: Turn on the red laser pointer and align it so the beam shines horizontally through the center of the tank from one side to the other.3. Initial Observation: Observe and record the beam path in clear water; it should be faint and only weakly visible from the side.4. Particle Addition: Add a small amount of milk to the water using a dropper. Gently stir until the milk is evenly mixed.5. Progressive Addition: Repeat the milk addition and mixing several times, each time increasing particle concentration slightly while continuously recording.6. Completion: Stop adding milk when the beam is clearly visible along its entire path. Turn off the laser and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: In clear water, the laser beam is barely visible from the side.2. With Small Milk Addition: The beam becomes faintly visible as a thin red line.3. With Increased Milk Concentration: The beam grows brighter and more continuous, clearly visible throughout the tank.4. High Concentration: Strong scattering makes the entire beam path vivid and well-defined.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMilk contains tiny fat and protein particles suspended in water, acting as analogs of atmospheric aerosols. As particle concentration increases, incident laser light is scattered more strongly (mainly by Mie scattering). This enhanced scattering redirects light toward the observer, making the beam path visible. The experiment models how haze or aerosols in the atmosphere increase light scattering and visibility of light beams.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Lucas Test – Comparison of tert-Butanol and EthanolI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Lucas Test – Reactivity of tert-Butanol vs Ethanol2. Subject: Chemistry – Organic Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To compare the reactivity of a tertiary alcohol (tert-butanol) and a primary alcohol (ethanol) with Lucas reagent through visual observation of turbidity formation, and to understand alcohol classification and reaction mechanisms.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tubes (2, identical), test tube rack, dropper or pipette, Lucas reagent (concentrated HCl saturated with anhydrous ZnCl2), tert-butanol, ethanol, labels or marker, safety goggles and gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, dry test tubes in a rack. Label the left tube as tert-butanol and the right tube as ethanol. Put on safety goggles.2. Addition of Reagent: Add an equal volume (about 2 mL) of Lucas reagent to each test tube.3. Addition of Alcohols: Using separate droppers, add 3–5 drops of tert-butanol to the left test tube and 3–5 drops of ethanol to the right test tube.4. Mixing: Gently swirl each test tube for 2–3 seconds to mix the contents, avoiding vigorous shaking.5. Standing and Observation: Place both test tubes back into the rack and leave them undisturbed at room temperature. Fix the camera focus and record the process for time-lapse observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both mixtures are colorless and transparent immediately after mixing.2. Short Time Standing: The left test tube containing tert-butanol rapidly becomes cloudy or milky due to formation of insoluble tert-butyl chloride.3. Continued Standing: The right test tube containing ethanol remains clear within the same observation period or shows very slow/no turbidity.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe Lucas test distinguishes alcohol classes based on their reactivity with Lucas reagent. Tertiary alcohols react rapidly via an SN1 mechanism to form insoluble alkyl chlorides, producing immediate turbidity. Primary alcohols, such as ethanol, react very slowly or not at room temperature, so no immediate cloudiness is observed. This difference allows visual identification of alcohol types.VI. PrecautionsHandle Lucas reagent carefully as it is corrosive. Use separate droppers to avoid cross-contamination. Perform the experiment in a well-ventilated area and dispose of waste according to laboratory rules.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: The Lucas test demonstrates how alcohol structure affects reactivity with Lucas reagent, assuming basic SN1 reaction knowledge and phase separation visibility. Minimum assumptions include correct reagent identity, correct alcohol classification, and room-temperature conditions.Expected phased storyline: (1) Two labeled test tubes with clear Lucas reagent are shown side by side; (2) tert-butanol is added to the left and ethanol to the right, followed by brief swirling; (3) during standing, the left tube transitions from clear to cloudy, while the right remains clear within the short time window. Visibility constraints: camera remains fixed, test tubes stay in frame, and turbidity difference is clearly observable for verification.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Copper Pipe Sleeve Joint Brazing with Silver FillerI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Copper Pipe Sleeve Joint Brazed with Silver Filler by Capillary ActionSubject: Engineering - Mechanical EngineeringExperiment Objective: To demonstrate silver brazing of copper pipes and observe capillary action drawing molten filler into a sleeve joint.II. Experimental EquipmentCopper pipes (2, cleaned), copper sleeve fitting (1), silver brazing rod, gas torch, heat-resistant work surface, flux suitable for silver brazing, wire brush or abrasive cloth, safety gloves, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Clean the outer surface of one copper pipe end and the inner surface of the sleeve using a wire brush or abrasive cloth until shiny; clean the mating pipe end. Apply a thin, even layer of flux to the joint surfaces.2. Assembly: Insert the two cleaned copper pipes into the sleeve fitting to form a proper sleeve joint with a uniform gap.3. Heating: Place the assembled joint on a heat-resistant surface. Ignite the torch and heat the joint evenly, moving the flame around the sleeve to raise the temperature uniformly.4. Brazing: When the joint reaches brazing temperature, gently touch the silver brazing rod to the seam without directly heating the rod. Allow the molten silver filler to be drawn into the joint.5. Completion: Remove the torch and allow the joint to cool naturally. Do not disturb the joint during cooling.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Copper pipes and sleeve are solid, metallic, and unchanged in color.During Heating: The joint area becomes hot and may show slight color change due to heating; flux becomes active and flows.During Brazing: The silver brazing rod melts upon contact with the heated joint, and molten filler is visibly drawn into the seam, flowing along the joint by capillary action.After Cooling: A smooth, continuous silver fillet is visible around the joint, indicating successful brazing.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSilver brazing relies on heating the base metals (copper pipes and sleeve) to a temperature above the melting point of the silver filler but below that of copper. When molten, the silver filler is drawn into the narrow gap of the sleeve joint by capillary action, driven by surface tension and wetting of the copper surfaces. Proper cleaning, flux application, and uniform heating are essential for effective capillary flow and joint strength.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure surfaces are thoroughly cleaned before brazing; heat the joint evenly rather than the filler rod; wear protective equipment to avoid burns.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Silver brazing of a copper sleeve joint using capillary action. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: cleaned copper surfaces, a narrow joint gap, sufficient heating to melt silver filler, and surface tension-driven flow.Phased Storyline: (1) Initial setup shows two cleaned copper pipes assembled in a sleeve joint; (2) torch heating raises joint temperature uniformly; (3) silver brazing rod touches the seam and melts; (4) molten filler is drawn smoothly into the joint by capillary action; (5) heating stops and the joint cools with a visible silver fillet. Visibility requirement: close, fixed camera focus on the joint area to clearly verify filler melting and inward flow.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Beam Bridge Model Progressively Loaded with Small WeightsI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Progressive Loading Test of a Simply Supported Beam Bridge ModelSubject: Engineering – Structural EngineeringObjective: To observe the bending behavior and deflection characteristics of a simply supported beam under progressively increasing concentrated load at midspan, and to understand basic beam bending principles.II. Experimental EquipmentBeam bridge model (uniform cross-section, elastic material), two rigid piers (supports), identical small weights (multiple pieces), flat tabletop, ruler or scale (optional), camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two rigid piers on the tabletop at a fixed distance. Lay the beam horizontally on the piers to form a simply supported beam. Ensure the beam is initially level and unloaded.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera position and focus so the entire beam and supports are clearly visible. Do not adjust during the experiment.3. Initial Observation: Record the initial state of the beam with no load applied.4. Progressive Loading: Place one identical small weight gently at the center of the beam deck. After the beam stabilizes, place the next identical weight at the same center position. Repeat until a clear deflection trend is observed or the safe load limit is reached.5. Completion: Stop loading, keep recording briefly, then remove weights and end the experiment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The beam remains straight with no visible deflection.2. During Loading: With each additional weight at midspan, the beam shows increasing downward deflection at the center while supports remain stable.3. Overall Trend: Deflection increases progressively as load increases, forming a smooth bending curve.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleA simply supported beam subjected to a concentrated load at midspan experiences bending due to internal moments. As identical weights are added, the bending moment at the center increases, causing greater elastic deflection. Within the elastic range, deflection increases approximately proportionally to the applied load, demonstrating fundamental beam bending behavior in structural engineering.VI. PrecautionsEnsure supports are rigid and stable; apply weights gently to avoid impact effects; do not exceed the beam’s safe load capacity.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Infrared Comparison of Asphalt Pavement and Grass Lawn HeatingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Infrared Comparison of Asphalt Pavement and Grass Lawn Heating2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To compare the heating characteristics of asphalt pavement and grass lawn under direct midday sunlight using an infrared camera, and to understand how surface properties influence surface temperature and local thermal environments.II. Experimental EquipmentInfrared thermal camera (with time-lapse function), tripod or fixed mount, stopwatch or timer, outdoor site with adjacent asphalt pavement and grass lawn, notebook or data recorder.III. Experimental Procedure1. Site Preparation: Select an outdoor location where dark asphalt pavement and green grass lawn are directly adjacent and unobstructed by shade. Ensure clear midday sunlight.2. Camera Setup: Mount the infrared camera on a tripod facing both surfaces simultaneously, with asphalt on the left and grass on the right. Fix the focus, angle, and field of view so they remain unchanged.3. Initial Recording: Start the infrared camera and record the initial surface temperatures of both asphalt and grass.4. Time-Lapse Recording: Allow the camera to record continuously or in time-lapse mode for a set period (e.g., 10–30 minutes), without moving the camera.5. Completion: Stop recording after sufficient heating is observed. Save the infrared images or video and note the observation time.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Experiment Objective: To simulate and visually compare the antioxidative effect of different selenium doses by observing lipid oxidation in hydrogen peroxide using an oxidation indicator, and to understand the dose-dependent antioxidative role of selenium.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentTest tubes (3 identical tubes), test tube rack, dropper or micropipette, hydrogen peroxide solution (same concentration), lipid oxidation indicator (colorimetric), selenium solution (low-dose and high-dose), gloves and goggles (simulation safety).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place three clean test tubes on a rack and label them Tube 1 (No Se), Tube 2 (Low Se), Tube 3 (High Se).2. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Laser Beam Through Clear Water vs Milk-Diluted Water (Tyndall Scattering)I. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Laser Beam Through Clear Water vs Milk-Diluted WaterSubject: Natural Science – Marine ScienceObjective: To demonstrate Tyndall scattering by comparing the visibility of a laser beam in clear water and in water containing fine particles, and to understand how suspended particles in seawater scatter light.II. EquipmentTwo identical transparent tanks; clear water; water diluted with a small amount of milk (uniformly mixed); narrow green laser pointer; darkened room; stable support for laser; camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse or continuous recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical transparent tanks side by side on a level table. Fill one with clear water and the other with milk-diluted water of equal depth.2. Setup: Darken the room to enhance visibility. Fix the camera on a tripod and lock focus and exposure.3. Operation: Position the green laser so it enters both tanks horizontally at the same height. Slowly sweep the laser beam through both tanks along a straight horizontal line.4. Observation: Record the process continuously or as time-lapse while maintaining constant camera settings.IV. Observation of PhenomenaIn clear water, the laser path is faint or nearly invisible. In milk-diluted water, a bright, continuous green beam is clearly visible along the laser path. The contrast between the two tanks is obvious when viewed side by side.V. Experimental PrincipleMilk-diluted water contains fine suspended particles that scatter incident light. When the laser passes through this colloidal mixture, light is scattered in many directions, making the beam path visible (Tyndall effect). Clear water lacks sufficient particles, so little scattering occurs and the beam is not easily seen. This models how light scatters in particle-rich seawater.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Tyndall scattering—visibility of a light beam increases in a medium containing fine suspended particles compared with a clear medium. Minimum assumptions: two identical transparent containers, equal liquid depth, same laser color and height, stable camera viewpoint.Phased storyline: (1) Initial static setup—two side-by-side tanks, one clear, one milk-diluted, camera fixed. (2) Action—narrow green laser sweeps horizontally through both at the same height. (3) Causal transition—beam remains faint in clear water but becomes bright and continuous in milk-diluted water due to scattering. (4) Verification—simultaneous comparison in a single frame; visibility contrast is the key observable. Perspective constraints: tanks fully visible, laser path unobstructed, stable lighting and framing throughout.

manual: Instructions for the Sport Demonstration Experiment: Swimming Freestyle Forward Flip TurnI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Swimming Freestyle Forward Flip Turn DemonstrationSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – SportExperiment Objective: To demonstrate and understand the standard technical process and biomechanical principles of the freestyle forward flip turn, including approach, rotation, wall push-off, and continuation of swimming.II. Experimental Conditions and EquipmentStandard swimming pool with a vertical wall and lane markings; swimmer wearing standard swimwear, goggles, and swim cap; safe pool environment with adequate water depth.III. Experimental Operation Process1. Preparation: The athlete starts swimming freestyle in a straight line toward the pool wall at moderate speed, maintaining a stable body position and rhythmic arm-leg coordination.2. Approach to Wall: As the swimmer nears the wall (about one arm length away), the last freestyle stroke is completed and the head begins to lower.3. Forward Flip: The swimmer tucks the chin toward the chest, contracts the core, bends the hips and knees, and pulls the legs inward to initiate a forward somersault.4. Wall Contact and Push-Off: After rotation, both feet contact the wall simultaneously; the swimmer forcefully extends the legs to push off the wall.5. Post-Turn Adjustment: The swimmer aligns the body into a streamlined posture, glides briefly, then resumes freestyle kicking and arm strokes to continue swimming forward.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The swimmer approaches the wall in a horizontal freestyle position with continuous forward motion.2. During the Turn: The head lowers, legs tuck, and the body rotates smoothly forward; water disturbance increases briefly around the rotation.3. After Push-Off: The swimmer leaves the wall with increased forward speed in a streamlined posture and then transitions back into normal freestyle swimming.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe forward flip turn is based on biomechanical and physical principles of momentum, rotation, and force application. Forward swimming speed provides angular momentum for the flip when the head lowers and legs tuck. Compact body posture reduces rotational inertia, enabling faster rotation. The wall push-off applies a reaction force that propels the swimmer forward, conserving energy and maintaining speed during the turn.VI. PrecautionsEnsure sufficient distance judgment to avoid collision with the wall; keep movements compact to prevent injury; perform the turn smoothly without holding breath excessively.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstration of a correct freestyle forward flip turn in swimming. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: a human swimmer in water, forward momentum from freestyle swimming, body rotation via head-lowering and leg tuck, solid wall providing reaction force for push-off.Phased storyline: (1) Freestyle approach toward pool wall with steady speed; (2) Head lowers and last stroke finishes, initiating rotation; (3) Legs tuck and body performs a forward flip; (4) Feet contact wall and push-off occurs, causing acceleration away from wall; (5) Body straightens into streamline and resumes freestyle swimming. Visibility requirements: the wall, swimmer orientation, leg tuck, foot-wall contact, and post-turn forward motion must be clearly observable from a side or slightly angled underwater/above-water perspective.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Mineral Fluorescence Under Ultraviolet LampI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Mineral Fluorescence Under Ultraviolet Lamp (Calcite or Fluorite)2. Subject: Natural Science - Geology & Geophysics3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the fluorescence phenomenon of minerals such as calcite or fluorite under ultraviolet (UV) illumination, recognize the visual characteristics of mineral fluorescence, and relate the observed phenomena to the physical principles of crystal structure and electronic transitions.II. Experimental Equipment1. Calcite or fluorite mineral specimen (clean, dry, palm-sized)2. Handheld ultraviolet lamp (long-wave UV preferred, ~365 nm)3. Dark room or light-proof enclosure4. Table or flat surface5. Camera or smartphone with fixed focus (tripod recommended)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Darken the room completely by turning off ambient lights or using a light-proof enclosure. Place the calcite or fluorite specimen flat on the center of the table.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera facing the mineral. Adjust framing so the mineral is clearly visible. Fix the focus and exposure; do not change settings during the experiment.3. Initial Observation: With the ultraviolet lamp turned off, observe and record the natural appearance of the mineral under darkness or very dim light.4. Core Operation: Turn on the handheld ultraviolet lamp and shine it steadily onto the mineral from a short distance (10–30 cm). Keep the lamp position stable.5. Alternating Illumination: Switch the ultraviolet lamp on and off several times at regular intervals to clearly show the difference between non-illuminated and UV-illuminated states.6. Recording: Use time-lapse or continuous recording to capture the mineral’s appearance during the lamp on/off cycles.7. Completion: Turn off the ultraviolet lamp, stop recording, and restore normal lighting conditions.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: When the ultraviolet lamp is off, the mineral appears its natural color (usually white, transparent, or pale) and does not emit visible light.2. Under UV Illumination: When the ultraviolet lamp is turned on, the calcite or fluorite emits visible fluorescent light. Calcite commonly glows red, orange, or pink; fluorite often glows blue, purple, or green.3. On-Off Contrast: The fluorescence appears immediately when UV light is on and disappears almost instantly when the UV light is turned off.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesMineral fluorescence is a physical optical phenomenon. When ultraviolet light irradiates certain minerals, electrons in impurity atoms or defects within the crystal lattice are excited to higher energy states. As these electrons return to lower energy states, they release energy in the form of visible light. The color of the fluorescence depends on the mineral’s chemical composition, crystal structure, and the type of activator elements present.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Avoid direct exposure of eyes or skin to ultraviolet light; do not shine the lamp toward people.2. Keep the lamp at a stable distance to ensure consistent illumination.3. Ensure the room is sufficiently dark to enhance contrast and visibility of fluorescence.4. Handle mineral specimens carefully to avoid damage.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: mineral fluorescence under ultraviolet light, requiring only the assumption that UV photons excite electrons in certain minerals causing visible emission. Phased storyline: (1) dark room with inert-looking mineral; (2) UV lamp switched on causing immediate visible glow; (3) UV lamp switched off and glow disappears; (4) repetition reinforces causal link. Visibility constraints: camera remains fixed, mineral centered, and darkness maintained so fluorescence contrast is clearly verifiable.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Sedimentation Gradually Burying Objects in a JarI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Sedimentation Gradually Burying Objects in a Jar2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Archaeology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how sediment carried by water settles as water movement slows, gradually burying objects, and to help understand archaeological site formation processes.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass jar with lid (1), clean water, mixed sediment (sand, silt, clay), several small stones or beads, table or flat surface, camera or phone fixed on a tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place small stones at the bottom of the empty glass jar. Add mixed sediment (sand, silt, clay) on top of the stones. Slowly pour water into the jar until it is nearly full.2. Mixing: Close the lid tightly. Gently shake the jar to fully mix water and sediment, making the water visibly cloudy and suspending particles.3. Settling: Place the jar on a stable table. Stop all movement and allow the water to become still. Fix the camera focus and begin time-lapse recording.4. Observation Period: Leave the jar undisturbed while particles gradually settle and layers form.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: After shaking, the water is cloudy, and sediment particles are evenly suspended.2. During Settling: As the water becomes still, larger and heavier particles (stones and coarse sand) settle first to the bottom, followed by finer sand and silt.3. Final State: Very fine clay particles settle last, forming thin upper layers. The stones at the bottom appear gradually buried by accumulated sediment layers.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates sedimentation. When water movement slows, gravity causes particles to settle according to size and weight: larger, heavier particles settle faster, while finer particles remain suspended longer. Over time, repeated sedimentation can bury objects, explaining how artifacts become layered and preserved at archaeological sites.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Shake gently to avoid breaking the jar.2. Place the jar on a stable surface to prevent disturbance during settling.3. Do not open the jar during observation to maintain still water conditions.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation (NMES) Inducing Visible Forearm Muscle ContractionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation Inducing Visible Muscle Contraction in the Forearm2. Subject: Healthcare – Occupational Therapy3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the application of neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) on the volar side of an adult forearm, observe visible muscle contractions, and understand the basic therapeutic principle of NMES in activating skeletal muscles. The experiment also aims to document the contraction process using a fixed-focus camera suitable for time-lapse recording.II. Experimental Equipment1. Neuromuscular electrical stimulation device (with adjustable intensity and pulse settings)2. Two adhesive surface electrodes3. Conductive gel (if required by electrodes)4. Treatment table or flat table surface5. Adult participant (forearm exposed, no contraindications to NMES)6. Camera mounted on a tripod (focus fixed, positioned above or obliquely toward the forearm)7. Alcohol swabs or skin-cleaning wipesIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   (1) Ensure the NMES device is powered off and intensity is set to zero.   (2) Ask the adult participant to sit comfortably beside the table and rest the forearm supinated (palm facing upward) on the table.   (3) Clean the volar side of the forearm with alcohol swabs and allow the skin to dry.   (4) Fix the camera position, adjust framing so the entire forearm and electrode area are visible, and lock the focus for time-lapse photography.2. Electrode Placement:   (1) Apply two adhesive electrodes to the volar side of the forearm along the muscle belly, typically over the wrist and finger flexor muscles.   (2) Ensure electrodes are parallel to muscle fibers, firmly attached, and spaced appropriately according to device guidelines.3. Core Operation:   (1) Connect the electrode leads to the NMES device.   (2) Turn on the NMES device and gradually increase stimulation intensity.   (3) Observe the forearm while slowly adjusting intensity until visible muscle contraction is achieved.4. Observation and Recording:   (1) Maintain stimulation for several contraction–relaxation cycles.   (2) Keep the camera recording with fixed focus, capturing repeated muscle contractions over time.   (3) Ensure the participant remains relaxed and the forearm stays stationary on the table.5. Completion:   (1) Gradually reduce intensity to zero and turn off the NMES device.   (2) Remove electrodes from the forearm.   (3) Stop camera recording and save the time-lapse footage.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The forearm muscles are relaxed, with no visible movement.2. During Stimulation: Upon activation of NMES, the muscles on the volar forearm visibly contract, causing subtle flexion or tightening of the wrist and fingers. Contractions occur rhythmically in response to electrical pulses.3. After Stimulation Stops: Muscle contractions cease, and the forearm returns to a relaxed resting state.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesNeuromuscular electrical stimulation works by delivering controlled electrical impulses through surface electrodes placed on the skin. These impulses depolarize peripheral motor nerves, triggering action potentials that cause skeletal muscle fibers to contract. The visible forearm muscle contractions observed in this experiment are not voluntary but are externally induced by electrical stimulation. In occupational therapy, NMES is used to facilitate muscle activation, prevent disuse atrophy, improve motor control, and support functional recovery.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Screen participants for contraindications to electrical stimulation (e.g., pacemakers, skin lesions).2. Always start with the lowest intensity and increase gradually.3. Ensure electrodes maintain full contact with the skin to avoid discomfort.4. Monitor participant comfort throughout the procedure and stop immediately if pain occurs.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Vitamin E Detection by Phosphomolybdic Acid Colorimetric MethodI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Vitamin E Detection (Phosphomolybdic Acid Colorimetric Method)2. Subject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To qualitatively detect vitamin E in vegetable oil extract through a colorimetric reaction, and to understand the reducing property of vitamin E and its application in food analysis.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (15×150 mm), test tube rack, dropper, measuring pipette, boiling water bath, beaker, thermometer (optional), vegetable oil extract (prepared in advance), phosphomolybdic acid ethanol solution, heat-resistant gloves, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, dry test tube on the test tube rack and wear safety goggles.2. Sample Addition: Use a measuring pipette to transfer 2 mL of vegetable oil extract into the test tube.3. Reagent Addition: Using a dropper, carefully add 2 drops of phosphomolybdic acid ethanol solution into the test tube.4. Mixing: Gently shake the test tube to ensure the reagent and oil extract are evenly mixed.5. Heating: Place the test tube into a boiling water bath and heat for 1 minute, ensuring the liquid level in the bath is above the level of the solution in the test tube.6. Completion: Remove the test tube using heat-resistant gloves and place it back on the rack for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The vegetable oil extract appears light yellow and transparent or slightly turbid.2. After Reagent Addition: No obvious color change or only slight yellowing is observed before heating.3. After Heating: The solution gradually develops a blue-green or bluish coloration, indicating a positive reaction for vitamin E.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleVitamin E (tocopherols) is a strong reducing agent. In this experiment, phosphomolybdic acid is reduced by vitamin E under heating conditions, forming reduced molybdenum species that exhibit a characteristic blue-green color. The intensity of the color is related to the amount of vitamin E present, forming the basis of qualitative and quantitative colorimetric analysis in food engineering.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Strictly control the volume (2 mL) and number of drops (2 drops) to ensure comparability.2. Avoid overheating or heating for too long, which may cause solvent evaporation or interfere with color development.3. Handle phosphomolybdic acid carefully, as it is corrosive.4. Dispose of experimental waste according to laboratory regulations.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Aquarium Water Aeration Increases Activity of Brine ShrimpI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effect of Water Aeration on Brine Shrimp Activity2. Subject: Natural Science - Paleontology3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare the activity level of brine shrimp in aerated and non-aerated aquarium water, and to understand the relationship between dissolved oxygen and organism activity.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo clear aquariums of equal size; brine shrimp of similar size and quantity for each aquarium; aquarium water of the same source and volume; air pump with tubing and air stone; stable table; camera with fixed focus for continuous or time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clear aquariums side by side on a stable table. Add equal volumes of the same aquarium water to each tank. Introduce an equal number of brine shrimp into each aquarium and allow them to acclimate for a short time.2. Setup: Install the air pump so that the air stone is placed at the bottom of the right aquarium. Ensure the left aquarium has no aeration device and remains still.3. Core Operation: Turn on the air pump to produce continuous bubbles in the right aquarium while keeping the left aquarium undisturbed.4. Observation and Recording: Fix the camera focus and angle so that both aquariums are clearly visible in the same frame. Observe and record the activity of brine shrimp in both tanks continuously or using time-lapse photography.5. Completion: After sufficient observation, turn off the air pump and end the recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Brine shrimp in both aquariums show similar, relatively low levels of movement.2. During Aeration: In the right aquarium, rising bubbles are visible and brine shrimp gradually show increased swimming speed and frequency. In the left aquarium, the water remains still and shrimp activity changes little.3. Comparative Result: Over time, brine shrimp in the aerated aquarium are noticeably more active than those in the non-aerated aquarium.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAeration increases the dissolved oxygen content of water. Brine shrimp rely on dissolved oxygen for respiration. When oxygen levels increase due to bubbling, their metabolic activity rises, resulting in more frequent and vigorous movement. In still water with lower oxygen exchange, shrimp activity remains lower. This experiment demonstrates the relationship between oxygen availability and organism activity.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Paper Chromatography of Black Marker Ink on Filter PaperI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Paper Chromatography of Black Marker Ink Using WaterSubject: Natural Science – ChemistryExperiment Objective: To observe the separation of different dye components in black marker ink using paper chromatography, and to understand the principles of capillary action and differential solubility.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentWhite filter paper strip (one strip, clean and dry)Black water-soluble markerClear transparent container (beaker or glass)Clean water (used as solvent)Clip or tape (to fix paper position, optional)Camera or phone with fixed focus (for time-lapse recording)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Cut a strip of white filter paper. Using a black marker, draw a small solid dot about 1–2 cm from the bottom edge of the paper. Allow the ink to dry completely.2. Solvent Setup: Pour a small amount of clean water into the clear container. The water level should be below the black ink dot.3. Placement: Place the filter paper vertically into the container so that its lower edge touches the water, ensuring the ink dot is above the water surface. Keep the paper upright and not touching the container walls.4. Recording: Fix the camera focus and position. Begin time-lapse or continuous recording.5. Development: Allow the water to slowly rise up the filter paper by capillary action. Do not disturb the setup.6. Completion: Stop the experiment when the water front has moved near the top of the paper or when clear color separation is visible.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The filter paper is white, and the black ink dot is concentrated at a single position near the bottom.During the Experiment: Water rises upward along the paper. The black ink begins to spread and separate into several colored bands, such as blue, green, or yellow, moving at different speeds.Final State: Distinct colored bands appear at different heights on the filter paper, showing clear separation of ink components.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePaper chromatography is based on capillary action and differential solubility. Water moves upward through the tiny pores of the filter paper by capillary action, carrying dissolved ink components with it. Different dye components have different solubilities in water and different attractions to the paper, so they travel at different speeds. As a result, the mixed black ink separates into individual colored components.VI. PrecautionsThe ink dot must remain above the water level.Do not shake or tilt the container during the experiment.Use water-soluble marker ink for clear separation.Ensure the filter paper does not touch the container wall.

Phase 2 – Causal transition: water wicks upward, dissolving the ink. Phase 3 – Separation: the black ink splits into multiple colored bands that move upward at different rates. Visibility Constraints: the container must be transparent, the paper fully visible, and color bands clearly distinguishable for verification.

Smoke Source Setup: Light the incense stick and allow it to burn steadily. Use tweezers to place the lit incense vertically at the bottom center of the beaker so that smoke can rise freely.3. Covering the Beaker: Gently cover the mouth of the beaker with a glass slide, leaving the inside air relatively enclosed while still visible.4. Heating Operation: Light the alcohol lamp and place it directly under the bottom of the beaker. Heat the bottom evenly and continuously.5. Observation: Observe the movement of the incense smoke inside the beaker during heating.6. Ending the Experiment: After clear phenomena are observed, remove the alcohol lamp first, then carefully remove the glass slide. Extinguish the incense and alcohol lamp. Clean up the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before heating, the incense smoke inside the beaker rises slowly and irregularly, with no obvious directional airflow.2. During Heating: After the bottom of the beaker is heated, the smoke near the bottom becomes more concentrated and begins to rise rapidly in a clear upward column along the central region of the beaker.3. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWhen the air at the bottom of the beaker is heated by the alcohol lamp, its temperature rises, causing the air to expand and its density to decrease. The incense smoke acts as a visible tracer, clearly showing the direction and existence of the upward airflow caused by thermal convection.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Handle the alcohol lamp carefully and keep flammable materials away from the flame.2. Do not touch the hot beaker or glass slide directly after heating.3. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Water Wave Tank Showing Overlapping Circular Waves from Two SlitsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Water Wave Interference from Double Slits2. Subject: Physics – Waves and Interference3. Experiment Objective: To observe diffraction and interference of water waves by allowing plane waves to pass through two narrow slits, and to understand the principle of wave superposition.II. Experimental EquipmentShallow water wave tank, transparent tank walls, ripple generator or vibrating bar, flat barrier with two narrow slits of equal width and spacing, water (depth about 5–10 mm), overhead light source, white screen or bottom plate for clear observation.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fill the wave tank with a shallow, uniform layer of water. Place the barrier vertically in the tank so that it divides the tank into two regions, with two narrow slits at the center.2. Wave Generation: Position the ripple generator on one side of the barrier to produce straight, periodic water waves moving toward the slits.3. Core Operation: Turn on the ripple generator and adjust it until clear, parallel incoming waves travel steadily toward the barrier.4. Observation Setup: Ensure the light source illuminates the water surface so wave patterns are clearly visible on the bottom or screen.5. Observation: Observe the waves as they pass through both slits and spread into the region beyond the barrier.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before the barrier: Straight, parallel wavefronts move uniformly toward the two slits.2. At the slits: Each slit acts as a new wave source, and the waves diffract upon passing through.3. After the barrier: Two sets of circular waves spread outward from the slits and overlap.4. Interference pattern: Regions of stronger waves (constructive interference) and weaker or nearly still water (destructive interference) appear in a stable, repeating pattern.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates wave diffraction and interference. When water waves pass through narrow slits, each slit becomes a secondary source of circular waves. According to the principle of superposition, overlapping waves add together. Where wave crests meet crests, constructive interference occurs; where crests meet troughs, destructive interference occurs, forming an interference pattern characteristic of double-slit wave behavior.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Keep the water depth uniform to avoid distortion of wave patterns.2. Ensure the slits are narrow and of equal width for clear interference.3. Minimize vibrations and air disturbances around the tank during observation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Color Change of Cobalt(II) Chloride During Hydration and DehydrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Hydration and Dehydration Color Change of Cobalt(II) Chloride2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Inorganic Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the reversible color change of cobalt(II) chloride caused by hydration and dehydration, and to understand the relationship between coordination structure, water content, and color.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsEvaporating dish or watch glass, dropper, glass rod, alcohol lamp or hot plate (for mild heating), cobalt(II) chloride crystals (anhydrous or partially hydrated, blue), water, tripod and wire gauze (if using alcohol lamp), safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean evaporating dish on the lab bench. Add a small amount of blue cobalt(II) chloride crystals to the dish. Fix the camera focus for time-lapse recording.2. Hydration Operation: Use a dropper to add water dropwise onto the crystals while gently swirling the dish to ensure even contact between water and crystals.3. Observation During Hydration: Continue adding water slowly until a clear color change is observed.4. Dehydration Operation: After the crystals are fully wetted and color change is complete, gently heat the dish using mild heating to evaporate water. Avoid overheating.5. Observation During Heating: Continue heating until the color changes again and no visible moisture remains.6. End of Experiment: Stop heating, allow the dish to cool, and record the final state.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The cobalt(II) chloride crystals are blue and solid.2. During Water Addition: As water is added, the blue crystals gradually turn pink, indicating hydration.3. During Heating: Upon gentle heating, moisture evaporates and the pink color gradually fades, returning to blue.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAnhydrous cobalt(II) chloride has a tetrahedral coordination structure and appears blue. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that warm surfaces heat the air above them, causing faster upward convection compared with cold surfaces, by observing the rising speed of incense smoke.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Sulfonamide Antibiotic Residue Detection in Milk (Test Strip Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Detection of Sulfonamide Antibiotic Residues in Milk Using Test Strip Method2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food Hygiene3. Experiment Objective: To qualitatively determine the presence or absence of sulfonamide antibiotic residues in milk using a rapid test strip, understand the basic principle of immunochemical detection, and master the standardized operation and result interpretation.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentMilk sample (prepared or commercial liquid milk), sulfonamide antibiotic test strip, dropper or disposable pipette, small clean container for sample solution (if needed), timer or stopwatch, standard color card provided with the test kit.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the milk sample, test strip, dropper, timer, and standard color card on a clean working surface. Ensure the test strip is at room temperature and within its validity period.2. Sample Addition: Use the dropper to draw the prepared milk sample solution. Add the specified number of drops (usually 2–3 drops) onto the reaction area or sample pad of the sulfonamide test strip.3. Reaction Waiting: Start the timer immediately after adding the sample. Keep the strip flat and undisturbed. Wait for the required reaction time indicated by the kit (typically 3–5 minutes; in demonstration, this may be accelerated or shown via time-lapse).4. Result Reading: After the reaction time, compare the color intensity or band appearance on the test strip with the standard color card.5. Judgment: Determine whether sulfonamide residues are present (positive) or absent (negative) according to the comparison result.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The test strip shows its original background color or control line only.2. After Sample Addition: Liquid migrates along the strip by capillary action.3. After Reaction Time: One or more colored lines or color intensity appears in the detection area. The color depth is compared with the standard card.4. Interpretation: A color matching the negative standard indicates no sulfonamide residue; a lighter color or disappearance of the test line compared with the standard indicates presence of sulfonamide residues.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on an immunochromatographic competitive inhibition principle. Sulfonamide molecules in the milk sample compete with labeled antigens on the test strip for binding sites on specific antibodies. When sulfonamide residues are present, they inhibit the formation of the colored test line, resulting in a weaker or absent color signal. By comparing the strip color with a standard color card, the presence or absence of sulfonamide antibiotic residues in milk can be qualitatively determined.VI. Precautions1. Operate strictly according to the test strip instructions and observe the specified reaction time.2. Avoid touching the reaction area of the test strip.3. Do not interpret results after the maximum reading time.4. Dispose of used strips according to laboratory waste regulations.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Rapid qualitative detection of sulfonamide antibiotic residues in milk using a test strip based on immunochromatographic competition. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Comparative Experiment of Bearing Capacity between Pile Foundation and Non-Pile Foundation under Seismic LoadSubject: Engineering – Geotechnical EngineeringObjective: To visually compare the settlement behavior and bearing capacity of pile foundations and non-pile foundations under simulated seismic loading, and to understand the reinforcing effect of piles on soil stability.II. Experimental EquipmentVibration table; two identical sand tables; dry uniform sand; three model piles; two identical weights; fixing clamps; measuring scale (optional for reference).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical sand tables on a flat surface. Label them as sand table A and sand table B.2. Model Construction: In sand table A, vertically embed three model piles evenly spaced, then fill the table with sand to the same height as sand table B. Fill sand table B with sand only, without piles. Level the sand surfaces.3. Loading: Place identical weights centrally on top of the sand surface of both sand tables.4. Installation: Secure both sand tables firmly onto the vibration table to prevent sliding.5. Vibration: Start the vibration table and apply continuous vibration to simulate seismic loading.6. Observation: Observe and compare the settlement of the weights in sand tables A and B during vibration. Use focused, time-lapse observation to highlight differences.7. Completion: Stop vibration after clear settlement differences are observed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before vibration, both weights rest stably on the sand surfaces with no visible settlement.2. During Vibration: Under vibration, the weight on sand table B (non-pile foundation) settles faster and deeper, while the weight on sand table A (pile foundation) shows smaller and slower settlement.3. Comparative Result: The non-pile foundation exhibits明显 larger deformation and instability compared with the pile foundation.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleUnder seismic loading, vibration causes soil particles to rearrange and densify, leading to settlement. In a non-pile foundation, the load is carried mainly by the soil, so vibration significantly reduces bearing capacity, resulting in large settlement. In a pile foundation, part of the load is transferred through piles to deeper, more stable soil layers, and soil–pile interaction enhances overall stiffness and seismic resistance. Therefore, pile foundations demonstrate higher bearing capacity and smaller settlement under seismic conditions.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Comparing Strong and Weak Negative Correlation Scatter PlotsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visual Comparison of Strong and Weak Negative Correlation2. Subject: Natural Science – Statistics & Data Science3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare strong and weak negative correlations using scatter plots, understand how point dispersion affects correlation strength, and learn how trend lines summarize data relationships.II. Experimental Materials and ToolsComputer or tablet, data visualization software or programming environment (e.g., spreadsheet, Python, or plotting tool), prepared coordinate axes with labeled X and Y.III. Experimental Procedure1. Axes Setup: Create a 2D coordinate system with fixed X and Y axes. Keep axes identical for all plots.2. Strong Negative Correlation Plot:   (1) Gradually add data points that decrease in Y as X increases, keeping points close to a straight downward path.   (2) Observe that points cluster tightly around an imagined line.   (3) Fit and display a linear trend line after most points are added.3. Weak Negative Correlation Plot:   (1) Using the same axes, clear only the points and trend line.   (2) Gradually add new data points showing a slight overall decrease in Y as X increases, but with wide vertical dispersion.   (3) Fit and display a linear trend line after points are added.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. In the strong negative correlation plot, points are closely aligned along a clear downward trend, and the trend line fits tightly.2. In the weak negative correlation plot, points are widely scattered, the downward trend is less obvious, and the trend line fits loosely.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCorrelation describes the strength and direction of a relationship between variables. A strong negative correlation occurs when data points closely follow a downward linear pattern. NotesEnsure axes remain unchanged between plots to allow fair comparison. Focus on point dispersion rather than slope alone when judging correlation strength.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Steel Wool Rapid Oxidation in Hydrogen PeroxideI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Accelerated Oxidation of Steel Wool by Hydrogen Peroxide2. Subject: Engineering – Biomedical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate accelerated oxidative reactions by comparing steel wool oxidation with and without hydrogen peroxide, and to understand how oxidizing agents increase reaction rates.II. Experimental EquipmentSteel wool pads (2 identical pieces), ceramic plates (2), hydrogen peroxide solution (3–6%), dropper or small beaker, protective gloves and goggles, camera or smartphone on tripod.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical ceramic plates side by side on a stable surface. Put one steel wool pad on each plate. Label them left and right.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera on a tripod directly facing both plates from the same angle. Lock focus and exposure for continuous or time-lapse recording.3. Core Operation: Start recording. Slowly pour an equal amount of hydrogen peroxide onto the steel wool pad on the left plate only. Do not add any liquid to the right pad.4. Observation Period: Continue filming both pads simultaneously without moving the camera until clear changes are observed.5. Completion: Stop recording after the reaction on the left pad becomes evident. Dispose of materials safely and clean the area.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Summary of Experimental PrincipleHydrogen peroxide is a strong oxidizing agent. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Circular Drum Membrane Vibrating in One Normal Mode Pattern2. Subject: Physics – Waves and Vibrations3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the normal mode vibration of a circular membrane by visualizing nodal patterns formed by fine sand under fixed-frequency mechanical driving.II. Experimental EquipmentCircular drum membrane with rigid frame, mechanical shaker with frequency controller, signal generator and power amplifier, fine dry sand, clamp/stand for fixing the shaker, camera with tripod (fixed focus), uniform lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Stretch and fix the circular membrane tightly on its frame. Place it horizontally and ensure the surface is clean and dry.2. Sand Sprinkling: Evenly sprinkle a thin layer of fine sand over the membrane surface.3. Driving Setup: Attach the mechanical shaker to the membrane at a fixed point near the edge or center. Set the shaker to a chosen fixed frequency.4. Camera Setup: Position the camera above the membrane, fix focus and framing, and keep the camera stationary for time-lapse recording.5. Core Operation: Turn on the shaker and maintain continuous driving at the fixed frequency. Allow the membrane to vibrate steadily for several seconds.6. Summary of Experimental PrincipleA circular membrane supports standing waves at specific resonant frequencies. When driven at a fixed frequency matching one normal mode, regions called nodes remain stationary while antinodes oscillate with large amplitude. Fine sand is shaken away from antinodes and settles along nodal lines, making the normal mode pattern visible.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Visual Verification of Mean Balance Using a Line ChartSubject: Natural Science - Statistics & Data ScienceExperiment Objective: To draw a 2D coordinate chart, plot five discrete data points with left-right symmetry, connect them with straight line segments, draw and mark the mean value, and visually verify that the mean represents the balance point of the data.II. Experimental MaterialsGraph paper or digital plotting software, ruler or straight-line tool, pen or stylus, calculator (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Draw a horizontal x-axis and vertical y-axis to form a 2D coordinate system.2. Select five x-values that are symmetric about the center (e.g., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2).3. Assign y-values so that the data are symmetric left to right around the center point.4. Plot the five discrete data points clearly on the coordinate system.5. Use a ruler or straight-line tool to connect adjacent points with straight line segments.6. Calculate the mean of the five y-values.7. Draw a horizontal line across the chart at the height of the mean value.8. Mark the mean point where the mean line intersects the central vertical line.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The plotted data points form a left-right symmetric shape around the central x-value.2. The connecting line segments create a balanced visual pattern.3. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe mean is a measure of central tendency representing the average value of a dataset. For symmetric data, the mean lies at the geometric center and acts as a balance point. When plotted on a line chart, a correctly calculated mean visually divides the data so that deviations above and below it are balanced, demonstrating the statistical concept of equilibrium.VI. PrecautionsEnsure data symmetry when selecting values; use straight lines for clarity; label axes and the mean line clearly.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Turning a Rotary Potentiometer to Vary Lamp BrightnessI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Turning a Rotary Potentiometer to Smoothly Vary a Lamp’s BrightnessSubject: Engineering – Electrical EngineeringExperiment Objective: To observe how changing resistance using a rotary potentiometer affects current in a series circuit and thereby smoothly controls the brightness of a small incandescent lamp.II. Experimental EquipmentDC power supply (low-voltage), rotary potentiometer, small incandescent lamp, connecting wires, tabletop surface, camera fixed on a tripod (focus fixed).III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the power supply, potentiometer, and lamp on a tabletop. Ensure the power supply is turned off. Fix the camera focus and framing so the entire circuit is visible.Circuit Connection: Connect the potentiometer in series with the incandescent lamp and the power supply using wires, forming a closed series circuit.Initial State: Set the potentiometer knob to one extreme position. Turn on the power supply and observe the initial brightness of the lamp.Core Operation: Slowly rotate the potentiometer knob in one direction with your hand. After reaching the other extreme, slowly rotate it back.Completion: Turn off the power supply after observation.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The lamp emits dim or bright light depending on the initial resistance setting.During Rotation: As the knob is turned, the lamp brightness changes smoothly and continuously, gradually becoming brighter or dimmer.Reverse Rotation: Turning the knob back causes the brightness to change smoothly in the opposite manner.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA rotary potentiometer changes the resistance in a series circuit. According to Ohm’s law (I = V/R), increasing resistance reduces current, dimming the lamp, while decreasing resistance increases current, making the lamp brighter. The smooth mechanical rotation results in a continuous change in resistance, producing a smooth variation in brightness.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse a low-voltage power supply to avoid overheating the lamp. Ensure secure wiring connections. Rotate the knob slowly to clearly observe gradual changes.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Reaction Between Sodium Peroxide and WaterI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Reaction Between Sodium Peroxide and Water2. Subject: Engineering – Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe the reaction of sodium peroxide with water, verify oxygen generation and alkalinity of the solution, and understand the reaction principle.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube, test tube rack, dropper, distilled water, small amount of sodium peroxide (pale yellow powder), glowing wooden splint, phenolphthalein solution, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Put on safety goggles. Place a clean, dry test tube on the rack.2. Adding Reagent: Add a small amount of pale yellow sodium peroxide powder into the test tube.3. Reaction with Water: Use a dropper to slowly add distilled water into the test tube.4. Oxygen Test: Immediately insert a glowing splint into the mouth of the test tube.5. Alkalinity Test: Add 1–2 drops of phenolphthalein solution into the test tube and gently observe.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Upon adding water, vigorous bubbling occurs and heat may be released.2. The glowing splint re-ignites or becomes brighter, indicating oxygen generation.3. After adding phenolphthalein, the solution turns pink, indicating an alkaline environment.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSodium peroxide reacts with water to produce sodium hydroxide and oxygen. The released oxygen supports combustion, causing the glowing splint to brighten. The generated sodium hydroxide makes the solution alkaline, turning phenolphthalein pink.Core reaction equation: 2Na₂O₂ + 2H₂O → 4NaOH + O₂↑VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use only a small amount of sodium peroxide to avoid excessive reaction.2. Add water slowly to control the reaction rate.3. Do not look directly into the test tube during the reaction.4. Dispose of waste according to laboratory regulations.

manual: Experiment Title: Scissor Linkage Vertical Lift Driven by Hand CrankI. Basic Experiment InformationSubject: Engineering – Mechatronics & RoboticsObjective: To observe and understand how a metal scissor linkage lift converts rotary motion from a hand crank into vertical linear motion of a top platform.II. Experimental EquipmentMetal scissor linkage lift model, base plate, top platform, side-mounted hand crank, fixed camera (tripod), uniform background and lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the scissor linkage lift on a stable surface. Ensure the base plate is fixed and the top platform can move freely. Adjust the camera to face the side of the mechanism and fix the focus.2. Initial State Observation: Confirm that the scissor linkage is in its lowest collapsed position and the hand crank is stationary.3. Extension Operation: Slowly turn the side hand crank forward at a steady speed. Continue rotating until the scissor linkage fully extends and the top platform reaches its maximum height.4. Collapse Operation: Reverse the direction of the hand crank. Observe the linkage collapsing smoothly until it returns to the lowest position.5. Completion: Stop turning the crank, ensure the mechanism is stable, and end the recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The scissor arms are crossed at small angles, and the top platform is close to the base plate.2. During Forward Crank Rotation: The scissor arms open symmetrically, joint angles increase, and the top platform rises vertically.3. During Reverse Crank Rotation: The scissor arms close, joint angles decrease, and the top platform descends vertically back to the base level.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe scissor linkage lift operates on the principle of kinematic transformation. Rotational motion from the hand crank is transmitted through a screw or gear mechanism to the scissor arms. As the arms rotate about their pivot joints, changes in their angles cause a change in vertical height. Increasing the angle between the arms results in vertical extension, while decreasing the angle causes vertical collapse. This demonstrates the conversion of rotary motion into linear vertical motion, a common mechanism in lifting devices.VI. Experimental NotesEnsure smooth crank rotation to avoid sudden motion. Keep the camera focus fixed to clearly record the vertical displacement over time.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: LED Shift Register Driven by a Visible Clock PulseI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: LED Shift Register Driven by a Visible Clock Pulse2. Subject: Engineering – Control & Automation3. Experiment Objective: To understand the basic working principle of a digital shift register by visually observing how a row of LEDs changes state in response to manual clock pulses, and to master the relationship between clock signals, data input, and output states.II. Experimental EquipmentShift register integrated circuit (e.g., 74HC595 or equivalent), LED array (8 LEDs) with current-limiting resistors, fixed data source (logic HIGH or LOW), visible clock input device (push button or rotary pulse knob), power supply (5V), breadboard, connecting wires.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Power off the circuit. Insert the shift register IC into the breadboard. Connect the power and ground pins correctly. Connect each output pin of the shift register to an LED in series with a resistor.2. Data Source Setup: Connect the data input pin of the shift register to a fixed logic level (e.g., HIGH) so that the same data bit is loaded on each clock pulse.3. Clock Setup: Connect the clock input pin to a visible clock device such as a push button or manual pulse knob. Ensure each press generates a single clear pulse.4. Initialization: Power on the circuit. Ensure all LEDs start in a known state (typically all OFF).5. Core Operation: Use your hand to press the clock button repeatedly at a steady pace. Each press represents one clock pulse.6. Observation: After each clock pulse, observe the change in the LED row.7. Completion: After several pulses, observe the full shifting cycle. Power off the circuit and disconnect the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: All LEDs are OFF (or only the first LED is ON, depending on initial conditions).2. During Operation: Each time the clock button is pressed, the lit LED shifts by one position along the row in a fixed direction.3. Repeated Clocking: With continuous clock pulses, the ON state moves step by step across the LED row, demonstrating sequential data shifting.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA shift register is a sequential digital circuit that stores and shifts binary data under the control of a clock signal. With each rising edge of the clock, the data at the input is loaded into the first stage, and the existing data in each stage shifts to the next output. By connecting LEDs to the outputs, the internal state of the shift register becomes directly visible. The experiment demonstrates the core principle that clock pulses control the timing and order of data movement in digital control systems.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Always power off before modifying wiring.2. Use current-limiting resistors to protect LEDs.3. Ensure the clock button produces clean pulses to avoid false triggering.4. Do not exceed the rated voltage of the shift register IC.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Visual demonstration of a digital shift register controlled by a manual clock. Minimum assumptions: a powered shift register IC, a row of LEDs connected to outputs, a fixed data input, and a hand-operated visible clock button or knob.Expected phased storyline: (1) Static setup showing the shift register and LED row powered on; (2) A hand presses the visible clock button; (3) Immediately after each press, one LED state shifts to the next position; (4) Repeated presses cause sequential movement of the lit LED across the row. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Pre-Charged and Uncharged Capacitors Driving an LED2. Subject: Engineering – Electrical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that a pre-charged capacitor can momentarily drive an LED when connected to a circuit, while an uncharged capacitor cannot, and to visually compare their behaviors using two identical branches.II. Experimental EquipmentDC power supply (for pre-charging), two identical capacitors (left with red sleeve, right with blue sleeve), two identical LEDs, two identical current-limiting resistors, single-pole single-throw switch (one switch controlling both branches), connecting wires, breadboard or mounting panel, camera with fixed focus for time-lapse photography.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Assemble two identical LED–resistor–capacitor branches side by side. Ensure LEDs have the same orientation and resistors have the same resistance.2. Pre-Charging: Connect the left (red-sleeved) capacitor to the DC power supply and charge it to the rated voltage. Disconnect it completely after charging. Leave the right (blue-sleeved) capacitor uncharged.3. Initial Check: Verify both LEDs are off and the switch is open. Fix the camera position and focus; do not adjust during recording.4. Core Operation: Close the single switch so that both branches are connected to their LEDs at the same time.5. Recording: Capture the LED responses using time-lapse or continuous video for several seconds.6. End: Open the switch and safely discharge the capacitor if needed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both LEDs are off before the switch is closed.2. After Switching: The LED in the left branch lights up immediately and then gradually dims and turns off. The LED in the right branch remains off or shows no obvious light.3. Final State: After a short time, both LEDs are off.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleA capacitor stores electrical energy when charged. When the switch is closed, the pre-charged capacitor discharges through the resistor and LED, producing a transient current that lights the LED briefly. The current decreases as the capacitor voltage drops, causing the LED to dim and turn off. An uncharged capacitor has no stored energy, so it cannot drive the LED. This demonstrates capacitor energy storage and discharge behavior.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure correct LED polarity, do not exceed capacitor voltage ratings, and keep both branches electrically identical except for the initial charge state.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Salt Dissolving in Water Enables Electrical ConductionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Electrical Conductivity of Pure Water and Salt Solution2. Subject: Engineering – Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that pure water has very low electrical conductivity, while salt dissolved in water produces ions that enable electrical conduction between electrodes, observed through a bulb lighting experiment.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical clear glass beakers; distilled (pure) water; sodium chloride (table salt); two pairs of identical metal electrodes; two identical simple circuits (battery, connecting wires, small bulb); measuring spoon; stirring rod; camera fixed on tripod (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, clear beakers side by side on a flat surface within the camera frame. Fix the camera focus and do not adjust it during the experiment.2. Filling: Pour equal volumes of pure water into both beakers.3. Solution Setup: Add a measured amount of salt to one beaker only. Stir gently until the salt is completely dissolved, forming a clear salt solution. The other beaker remains pure water.4. Circuit Assembly: Insert identical metal electrodes into each beaker, ensuring equal depth and no contact between electrodes. Connect each electrode pair to an identical battery–bulb circuit.5. Core Operation: Simultaneously switch on both circuits.6. Observation: Keep the setup undisturbed and record the bulb responses for several seconds.7. Completion: Switch off the circuits, remove electrodes, and clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both beakers contain clear, colorless liquids; both bulbs are off before switching on.2. After Switching On: The bulb connected to the salt solution lights up clearly, indicating electrical conduction. The bulb connected to pure water remains off or glows extremely dim.3. Comparison: A clear contrast in bulb brightness is observed between the two circuits.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesPure water contains very few free ions and therefore conducts electricity poorly. When salt (NaCl) dissolves in water, it dissociates into Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. These mobile ions carry electric charge between the electrodes, allowing current to flow through the solution and light the bulb. This demonstrates the relationship between ionic concentration and electrical conductivity in aqueous solutions.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure electrodes are identical and positioned equally; avoid short-circuiting electrodes; use low-voltage batteries for safety; keep camera fixed throughout recording.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Dissolution of salt in water produces ions that enable electrical conduction, contrasted with the near-nonconductive behavior of pure water. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: salt dissociates into ions; electric current in solution requires mobile charge carriers; identical circuits ensure fair comparison.Phased storyline for verification: (1) Static setup phase: two identical clear beakers side by side, equal water levels, electrodes inserted symmetrically, bulbs off. (2) Intervention phase: salt added and dissolved in one beaker only. (3) Activation phase: both circuits switched on simultaneously. (4) Outcome phase: bulb over salt solution lights clearly while bulb over pure water remains dark or very dim. Visibility constraints: camera remains fixed; both bulbs and beakers must be visible in the same frame to allow direct visual comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Reaction Between Magnesium and Dilute Hydrochloric AcidI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Reaction Between Magnesium and Dilute Hydrochloric Acid2. Subject: Engineering – Chemical Engineering (Basic Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the reaction between an active metal (magnesium) and dilute hydrochloric acid, understand the properties of metals reacting with acids, and recognize hydrogen gas generation and salt formation through direct experimental phenomena.II. Experimental Equipment and Reagents1. Test tube (1, clean and dry)2. Test tube rack3. Magnesium strip (silvery white, about 2–3 cm long)4. Dilute hydrochloric acid (colorless, about 5–10 mL)5. Tweezers6. Wooden splint or match (optional, for hydrogen test)7. Safety gogglesIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clean test tube on the test tube rack. Put on safety goggles. Pour a small amount (about 1/4–1/3 of the test tube volume) of colorless dilute hydrochloric acid into the test tube.2. Adding Reactant: Use tweezers to hold a silvery white magnesium strip and slowly place it into the dilute hydrochloric acid in the test tube.3. Reaction Observation: Keep the test tube upright and closely observe the changes occurring in the test tube immediately after magnesium is added.4. Optional Gas Test: After gas evolution becomes obvious, bring a burning wooden splint close to the mouth of the test tube to test the gas (do not insert it deeply).5. Completion: After the reaction weakens, place the test tube back on the rack. Dispose of the solution according to laboratory waste rules and clean the apparatus.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The hydrochloric acid is colorless and transparent; the magnesium strip is solid and silvery white.2. During Reaction: Numerous colorless gas bubbles rapidly form on the surface of the magnesium strip and rise through the solution. The magnesium strip gradually becomes thinner and shorter.3. Gas Test Phenomenon (optional): The burning splint produces a ‘pop’ sound when exposed to the gas, indicating hydrogen.4. Final State: The magnesium strip may partially or completely disappear, leaving a clear solution of magnesium chloride.V. Summary of Experimental Principle1. Core Principle: Magnesium is an active metal that reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, displacing hydrogen from the acid to form magnesium chloride and hydrogen gas.2. Chemical Equation: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂↑3. Principle Explanation: The rapid bubble formation is due to hydrogen gas generation. The disappearance of magnesium indicates its participation in the chemical reaction. This experiment demonstrates the general rule that active metals react with acids to produce salt and hydrogen.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use dilute hydrochloric acid only; concentrated acid is dangerous.2. Handle magnesium with tweezers to avoid contamination.3. Do not point the test tube toward people during the reaction.4. Perform the hydrogen test cautiously and briefly.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Reaction of an active metal (magnesium) with dilute hydrochloric acid producing hydrogen gas and magnesium chloride. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: magnesium is solid and silvery, hydrochloric acid is colorless and dilute, reaction starts upon contact, gas evolution indicates hydrogen formation.Phased storyline: (1) Static setup showing a test tube with colorless dilute hydrochloric acid; (2) magnesium strip is introduced into the acid; (3) immediate formation of colorless bubbles on the magnesium surface, magnesium gradually dissolves; (4) optional verification of hydrogen at the tube mouth. Visibility constraints: bubbles must be clearly visible on magnesium, and the magnesium strip must be seen shrinking to verify causal correctness.
