manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Mohs Hardness Scratch Test Comparing Quartz and FeldsparI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Mohs Hardness Scratch Test Comparing Quartz and Feldspar2. Subject: Natural Science – Geology & Geophysics3. Experiment Objective: To compare the relative hardness of quartz and feldspar using the Mohs scratch test, and to understand the concept that a harder mineral can scratch a softer one.II. Experimental Materials and Equipment1. Quartz specimen (clear or milky white, clean surface)2. Pink feldspar specimen (fresh, flat surface)3. Stable workbench or tabletop4. Bare hand or gloved hand for holding minerals5. Camera fixed on a tripod (focus locked for time-lapse recording)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the quartz and pink feldspar side by side on a clean, stable workbench. Select flat, fresh surfaces on both specimens. Fix the camera position and focus so both minerals are clearly visible.2. Step One – Scratching Feldspar with Quartz: Hold the quartz firmly in hand. Press one sharp edge of the quartz against the surface of the pink feldspar and draw it across the surface with moderate, steady pressure.3. Observation: Stop scratching and examine the feldspar surface under the same camera view.4. Step Two – Scratching Quartz with Feldspar: Hold the pink feldspar firmly. Press its edge against the surface of the quartz and draw it across with similar pressure.5. Observation: Stop scratching and examine the quartz surface.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both quartz and feldspar surfaces appear smooth and unmarked.2. After Scratching Feldspar with Quartz: A visible scratch or white powdery mark appears on the feldspar surface.3. After Scratching Quartz with Feldspar: No visible scratch appears on the quartz surface; at most, feldspar powder may be left on quartz and can be wiped away.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe Mohs hardness scale ranks minerals by their ability to scratch one another. Quartz has a Mohs hardness of 7, while feldspar has a hardness of about 6. A harder mineral can scratch a softer mineral, but not vice versa. Therefore, quartz can scratch feldspar, while feldspar cannot scratch quartz. This experiment demonstrates relative mineral hardness through direct physical interaction.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use fresh, clean mineral surfaces to avoid misjudging scratches.2. Apply similar pressure in both scratching steps for fair comparison.3. Distinguish true scratches from loose powder, which can be wiped away.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Mohs hardness comparison, assuming the basic rule that harder minerals scratch softer ones. Minimum assumptions: quartz (hardness 7) and feldspar (hardness 6) are correctly identified and handled by a human hand on a stable workbench. Expected phased storyline: Phase 1 – static setup with quartz and pink feldspar side by side; Phase 2 – hand uses quartz to scratch feldspar, producing a visible scratch; Phase 3 – hand uses feldspar to scratch quartz, producing no scratch; Phase 4 – clear contrast in results confirms hardness difference. Visibility constraints: mineral colors, scratching motion, and resulting surface marks must remain clearly visible within a fixed camera perspective.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Muddy Sediment Flow in a Clear Laboratory FlumeI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Observation of Muddy Sediment Flow in a Clear Flume under Turbulent and Reduced Flow ConditionsSubject: Natural Science – Paleontology (Sedimentology)Objective: To observe how muddy sediment is transported and suspended by turbulent flowing water in a clear flume, and how sediment behavior changes when the flow rate is reduced, simulating natural river deposition processes relevant to fossil and sediment formation.II. Experimental EquipmentClear laboratory flume (transparent side walls), water circulation system with adjustable pump, fine muddy sediment (silt or clay), water supply, flow control valve, stable support table, camera fixed on tripod (side view), lighting source.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear flume on a stable table. Fill it with clean water and ensure the side walls are transparent. Fix the camera on one side of the flume to capture a full side view of the water column; lock focus for time-lapse recording.2. Sediment Introduction: Evenly add a measured amount of fine muddy sediment into the flume while the pump is off, allowing initial mixing near the bottom.3. High-Flow Operation: Turn on the pump and adjust to a higher flow rate to create visibly turbulent water. Allow the muddy sediment to become fully suspended and transported downstream.4. Flow Reduction: Gradually reduce the pump speed to lower the flow rate. Maintain recording during this process.5. Completion: After sediment movement clearly weakens and partial settling is observed, stop the pump and end recording. Drain and clean the flume.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Water in the flume is clear, with muddy sediment mainly near the bottom.Turbulent Flow Stage: At higher flow rates, water becomes turbulent; muddy sediment is lifted into suspension, forming a cloudy, brownish water column.Reduced Flow Stage: As flow rate decreases, turbulence weakens; suspended sediment concentration decreases, and particles begin to settle toward the bottom, making the upper water clearer.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates the principle of sediment transport in flowing water. Turbulent flow provides sufficient energy to overcome gravity and keep fine sediment suspended. When flow velocity and turbulence decrease, the carrying capacity of water is reduced, causing sediment particles to settle. This process explains natural river deposition and layered sediment formation, which are fundamental to paleontological and geological records.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Sediment transport and deposition in flowing water, emphasizing the relationship between flow velocity, turbulence, and sediment suspension.Minimum Assumptions: A transparent flume, muddy sediment mixed with water, adjustable flow creating turbulence, gravity-driven settling when flow weakens.Phased Storyline: (1) Clear flume with muddy sediment introduced; (2) increased flow produces turbulence and full sediment suspension; (3) flow rate is reduced, turbulence weakens; (4) sediment visibly settles and water clarity increases from top downward. Side-view visibility of the water column is required to verify suspension and settling transitions.

Experiment Title: Sealed Plastic Bag Vinegar–Baking Soda Reaction on a Balance2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the law of conservation of mass through a chemical reaction carried out in a sealed system, and to observe gas production during an acid–base reaction.II. Experimental EquipmentElectronic balance (1), transparent sealable plastic bag (1, intact and airtight), vinegar (acetic acid solution), baking soda (sodium bicarbonate), measuring spoon or small paper cup, small beaker or dropper (optional), camera fixed on a tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Check that the plastic bag has no holes and can be sealed tightly. Place the electronic balance on a stable horizontal surface and zero it.2. Loading Reactants: Pour a measured amount of vinegar into one corner of the plastic bag. Sealing and Weighing: Seal the plastic bag completely, ensuring it is airtight. Place the sealed bag flat on the center of the balance and record the initial mass.4. Core Operation: While the bag remains sealed and on the balance, gently lift or tilt the bag so that the baking soda mixes with the vinegar.5. Observation: Keep the camera focus fixed and record the reaction. Observe the changes inside the bag and the balance reading.6. Conclusion: After the reaction finishes, observe the final state of the bag and the balance reading. Turn off the camera and clean up materials.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The sealed plastic bag lies flat on the balance; vinegar is liquid and clear, baking soda is white solid, and no bubbles are present.2. During Reaction: After mixing, rapid bubbling occurs, and the bag gradually inflates due to gas formation; the balance reading remains essentially unchanged.3. Final State: Bubbling slows or stops, the bag stays inflated, and the balance reading is the same as before the reaction.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the law of conservation of mass in a closed system. Vinegar (acetic acid) reacts with baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) to produce carbon dioxide gas, water, and sodium acetate. Because the reaction occurs in a sealed plastic bag, no matter escapes, so the total mass measured by the balance remains constant even though gas is produced.Core reaction: NaHCO3 + CH3COOH → CH3COONa + H2O + CO2↑VI. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Sodium Alginate Droplets Forming Gel Beads in Calcium Chloride SolutionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Formation of Calcium Alginate Gel Beads2. Subject: Engineering – Biomedical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the gelation behavior of sodium alginate in the presence of calcium ions, understand ionic crosslinking principles used in biomedical applications, and observe bead formation through direct visual phenomena.II. Experimental EquipmentBeaker (250 mL), calcium chloride solution (0.1–0.2 M, clear and colorless), sodium alginate solution (1–2%, viscous and transparent), plastic pipette or dropper, stirring rod or gentle hand swirling, lab bench, gloves and safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the beaker containing calcium chloride solution on a stable lab bench. Ensure the solution is clear and still. Wear safety goggles and gloves.2. Loading the Pipette: Draw sodium alginate solution into the pipette, ensuring no air bubbles to maintain uniform droplet formation.3. Core Operation: Hold the pipette vertically above the beaker and slowly release sodium alginate droplets one by one into the calcium chloride solution.4. Gentle Mixing: While adding droplets, gently swirl the beaker by hand to prevent beads from sticking together and to ensure even exposure to calcium ions.5. Completion: Continue adding droplets until a visible number of gel beads have formed, then stop the operation and allow the beads to settle.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The calcium chloride solution is colorless and transparent; the sodium alginate solution is clear and viscous.2. During Droplet Addition: Each sodium alginate droplet forms a spherical, semi-transparent gel bead immediately upon contacting the calcium chloride solution.3. After Completion: The beaker contains multiple uniform gel beads that sink slowly and retain their shape.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on ionic crosslinking in polymer gels. Sodium alginate is a natural polymer containing negatively charged carboxylate groups. When alginate droplets enter calcium chloride solution, calcium ions replace sodium ions and crosslink adjacent alginate chains, forming a three-dimensional gel network known as calcium alginate. This principle is widely used in biomedical engineering for cell encapsulation, drug delivery, and tissue engineering.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Add droplets slowly to maintain spherical bead shape.2. Avoid vigorous stirring, which may deform the gel beads.3. Dispose of solutions according to laboratory safety guidelines and clean all equipment after use.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Steel Pile Driven into Sand by Drop HammerI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Steel Pile Driven into Sand by Drop Hammer2. Subject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the basic process of pile driving in sandy soil, observe the penetration behavior of a steel pile under repeated impact loading, and understand the principle of energy transfer and soil resistance during pile installation.II. Experimental EquipmentCrane with drop hammer assembly, vertical steel pile, sandy ground or sand-filled test ground, pile positioning frame (or guide), measuring scale or markings on pile, safety helmet and protective equipment, fixed-position camera for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Level the sandy ground and ensure uniform sand conditions. Position the steel pile vertically at the selected location using a guide frame. Fix the camera position and focus for time-lapse photography, ensuring the entire pile and hammer path are in view.2. Equipment Setup: Attach the drop hammer to the crane hook and align it directly above the steel pile head. Check that the hammer can move freely in the vertical direction.3. Core Operation: Use the crane to lift the drop hammer to a specified height and then release it to strike the top of the steel pile. Repeat the lifting and dropping process multiple times in a steady rhythm.4. Observation and Recording: During repeated impacts, observe and record the gradual penetration of the steel pile into the sand and the decreasing penetration per blow over time.5. Completion: Stop hammering after a clear penetration trend is observed. Secure the equipment and stop the camera recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The steel pile stands vertically on the sandy ground with little or no penetration.2. During Hammering: Each hammer drop produces an impact sound, and the pile gradually penetrates deeper into the sand. Early blows cause larger penetration increments, while later blows result in smaller increments due to increased soil resistance.3. Final State: The pile is embedded firmly in the sand, showing significant penetration compared to the initial state.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe experiment demonstrates the pile driving principle in geotechnical engineering. The gravitational potential energy of the lifted hammer is converted into kinetic energy and then impact energy upon striking the pile. This energy overcomes soil resistance, allowing the pile to penetrate the sandy ground. As penetration increases, soil density and friction around the pile increase, leading to greater resistance and reduced penetration per blow. This reflects the balance between driving energy and soil bearing resistance.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure vertical alignment of the pile to avoid bending; maintain a safe distance during hammer drops; confirm camera stability before operation; stop the experiment if abnormal vibrations or misalignment occur.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Linear Perspective Construction of a City StreetI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Constructing a City Street Using Single-Point Linear Perspective2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Renaissance Painting)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the method of linear perspective used in Renaissance painting by constructing a city street scene with a single vanishing point on the horizon, understanding how orthogonal lines create depth and spatial illusion, and documenting the drawing process using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentDrawing paper (A3 or larger), pencil, eraser, ruler or straightedge, drawing board or flat table, reference image of a Renaissance city street (optional), camera or smartphone with tripod, stable light source.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Secure the drawing paper on a flat surface. Set up the camera on a tripod above or slightly in front of the drawing area. Fix the camera focus and framing so the entire paper is visible. Do not change focus or position during recording.2. Establish the Horizon Line: Lightly draw a horizontal line across the paper to represent the viewer’s eye level.3. Set the Vanishing Point: Mark a single point at the center (or slightly off-center) of the horizon line. This is the vanishing point.4. Draw Orthogonal Lines: From the vanishing point, use a ruler to draw multiple straight orthogonal lines extending downward and outward toward the bottom edge of the paper. These represent the receding edges of the street and buildings.5. Construct the Street and Buildings: Add vertical and horizontal lines between orthogonals to define building facades, windows, doors, and street edges, ensuring all depth lines converge to the vanishing point.6. Refinement: Darken final structural lines, erase unnecessary guidelines, and add minimal details while maintaining perspective consistency.7. Recording Completion: Stop the time-lapse recording after the perspective structure is clearly visible.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Blank paper with only the horizon line and a single vanishing point.2. During Construction: As orthogonal lines are added, the flat surface begins to suggest depth; parallel street edges appear to converge toward the vanishing point.3. Final State: The completed drawing creates a convincing illusion of a receding city street, with buildings diminishing in size toward the horizon.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleLinear perspective is a geometric system developed during the Renaissance to represent three-dimensional space on a two-dimensional surface. In single-point perspective, all lines perpendicular to the picture plane (orthogonals) converge at one vanishing point on the horizon line, corresponding to the viewer’s eye level. This convergence creates the visual illusion of depth and distance, forming the mathematical and perceptual basis of realistic spatial representation in Renaissance art.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the camera remains fixed throughout recording; keep orthogonal lines straight and accurately aligned to the vanishing point; avoid adding depth lines that do not converge correctly, as this breaks perspective logic.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Measuring pH of Acidic and Alkaline Soil Using a Handheld pH MeterI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Measurement of Soil pH Using a Handheld pH Meter2. Subject: Engineering – Agricultural Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To learn the correct use of a handheld pH meter, measure and compare the pH values of acidic and alkaline soils, and verify that acidic soil has pH<7 while alkaline soil has pH>7.II. Experimental EquipmentHandheld soil pH meter (with probe), two soil samples (one acidic, one alkaline), sample containers with labels, distilled water, clean cloth or tissue, calibration solution (if required by meter).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two soil samples into separate containers and label them as acidic soil and alkaline soil. Add a small amount of water to each sample and mix until the soil is uniformly moist but not waterlogged.2. Calibration: Turn on the handheld pH meter and calibrate it according to the manufacturer’s instructions using the calibration solution or built-in calibration function.3. Measurement of Acidic Soil: Insert the clean probe vertically into the moist acidic soil. Ensure good contact between probe and soil. Wait until the displayed pH value stabilizes, then record or observe the reading.4. Cleaning: Remove the probe from the acidic soil, rinse with distilled water, and wipe it clean with a cloth or tissue.5. Measurement of Alkaline Soil: Insert the cleaned probe into the moist alkaline soil. Wait for the reading to stabilize and observe the displayed pH value.6. Completion: Turn off the pH meter, clean the probe, and return all equipment to their proper places.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The pH meter displays a numerical value after insertion into soil.2. In acidic soil, the stable reading is less than 7.3. In alkaline soil, the stable reading is greater than 7.4. The two soil samples show different pH values, indicating different acidity and alkalinity.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSoil pH reflects the concentration of hydrogen ions in the soil solution. A pH value below 7 indicates acidic conditions, while a value above 7 indicates alkaline conditions. The pH meter measures the electrical potential difference related to hydrogen ion activity in the moist soil, converting it into a numerical pH value. By calibrating the meter and measuring different soils, their acidity or alkalinity can be accurately compared.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure soil is moist for accurate measurement.2. Always clean the probe between measurements to avoid cross-contamination.3. Handle the pH meter gently to avoid damaging the probe.

Visibility constraints: labels, probe insertion, and numerical pH values on the meter screen must be clearly visible to verify correctness.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Food Dye Diffusion Through Agar Gel with Pre-cut ChannelsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Food Dye Diffusion Through Agar Gel with Pre-cut Channels2. Subject: Engineering – Materials Science & Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate molecular diffusion in a soft solid medium and observe how pre-cut channels influence mass transport pathways using food dye in agar gel.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentClear rectangular agar gel slab (uniform thickness, transparent), pre-cut straight or branching channels visible on the surface, food dye (water-based, high contrast color), dropper or pipette, flat table or lab bench, camera or smartphone with fixed focus and tripod (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear rectangular agar gel slab flat on a stable table. Ensure the pre-cut channels are clearly visible and the gel surface is clean and dry.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera directly above or at a slight angle to fully capture the agar slab. Fix focus, exposure, and framing to avoid changes during recording.3. Dye Application: Using a dropper, gently place one small drop of food dye onto one edge of the agar slab, ensuring contact with the openings of the pre-cut channels.4. Diffusion Stage: Do not disturb the setup. Allow time to pass while recording continuously or via time-lapse.5. Completion: Stop recording after the dye has visibly spread into the gel and along the channels.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The agar gel is colorless and transparent, with clear geometric channels; the dye is concentrated at the edge.2. Early Diffusion: The dye slowly penetrates the agar from the edge, forming a high-to-low concentration gradient.3. Channel-Guided Spread: The dye advances more rapidly along the pre-cut channels than through the bulk gel.4. Later Stage: The color becomes more diffuse and lighter as it spreads farther from the source.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates diffusion in a polymer gel, a key concept in materials science. Food dye molecules move from regions of high concentration to low concentration due to random molecular motion. Agar acts as a porous, water-rich solid that resists but allows diffusion. Pre-cut channels reduce transport resistance, creating preferential pathways that accelerate dye movement, illustrating how microstructural features influence mass transport in materials.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Avoid shaking or tilting the agar slab during diffusion.2. Use a small, consistent dye volume to maintain clear gradients.3. Keep camera settings fixed to ensure valid time-lapse comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Light Dispersion (Prism Light Splitting)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Light Dispersion Using a Prism2. Subject: Natural Science - Physics3. Experiment Objective: To observe that when white sunlight passes through a prism, it is dispersed into a band of seven colors, and to identify the distribution and order of these colors.II. Experimental EquipmentTriangular glass prism (one), sunlight source (direct sunlight near a window, or sunlight reflected by a mirror), white screen or white paper (one sheet), stand or books to support the prism, darkened room or shaded environment (recommended for clearer observation).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Choose a location with strong sunlight. If indoors, darken the room as much as possible. Place a white screen or white paper vertically or flat on a table to receive the light.2. Placement of Prism: Place the triangular prism on a stable surface near the sunlight beam. Adjust its position so that sunlight enters one face of the prism at an angle.3. Core Operation: Slowly rotate or slightly adjust the prism until the refracted light emerging from the prism falls onto the white screen or paper.4. Observation: Observe the light pattern on the screen carefully. When the position is suitable, a clear colored light band will appear.5. Adjustment and Confirmation: Fine-tune the prism angle to make the color band longer and clearer, then fix the prism position and continue observing.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before passing through the prism, the sunlight appears white and does not show separate colors on the screen.2. After Passing Through the Prism: The white light is split into a continuous band of colors on the screen.3. Color Distribution and Order: The color band shows seven colors arranged in order: red, orange, yellow, green, cyan (blue-green), blue, and violet. Red appears on one side with the smallest bending, while violet appears on the opposite side with the largest bending.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleWhite light is composed of light of different colors, each with a different wavelength. When white light enters a prism, it is refracted. Because different wavelengths travel at different speeds in glass, they are refracted by different amounts. This phenomenon is called dispersion. Longer-wavelength red light bends less, while shorter-wavelength violet light bends more, causing white light to spread out into a band of seven colors.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not look directly at strong sunlight to protect your eyes.2. Ensure the prism is placed stably to prevent it from falling or breaking.3. Perform the experiment in a relatively dark environment to improve the visibility of the color band.4. Handle the glass prism carefully to avoid scratches or damage.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Dispersion of white light by a prism due to wavelength-dependent refraction. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: white light contains multiple wavelengths; glass refracts different wavelengths by different angles; a prism geometry causes angular separation. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) White sunlight enters the prism; (2) light refracts at the first surface; (3) different colors separate while exiting the prism; (4) a continuous seven-color band appears on a white screen, ordered from red (least deviation) to violet (greatest deviation). Visibility requirements: prism, incoming light direction, and projected color band must be clearly visible from a fixed viewpoint to verify color order and causal sequence.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Glyphosate Residue Detection (Enzyme Inhibition Test Strip Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Detection of Glyphosate Residues in Food by Enzyme Inhibition Test Strip2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food Hygiene3. Experiment Objective: To learn how to rapidly detect glyphosate residues in food using an enzyme inhibition test strip, master the standard operation of sample immersion, timing, and result comparison, and understand the basic principle of enzyme inhibition detection.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentGlyphosate enzyme inhibition test strips, food extract sample (prepared by soaking or homogenizing food in water and filtering), clean transparent container (e.g., plastic cup or beaker), reference color card provided with the test kit, timer or stopwatch, disposable gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear gloves. Place the prepared food extract into a clean container, ensuring the liquid level is sufficient to immerse the reaction end of the test strip.2. Insertion of Test Strip: Take one test strip and insert it vertically into the food extract, with the reaction end fully immersed. Do not tilt or shake the strip.3. Reaction Waiting: Keep the strip still in the extract for the specified short time (about 5–10 seconds). Use time-lapse photography to emphasize the waiting process.4. Removal: Remove the strip vertically from the container and hold it horizontally in the air without touching the reaction area.5. Result Comparison: After the color stabilizes (within the kit’s specified time), compare the color or band intensity on the test strip with the reference card to determine the glyphosate residue level.6. Completion: Record the result, dispose of the used strip properly, and clean the workspace.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The test strip shows its original baseline color before contact with the sample.2. During Reaction: After immersion and removal, the reaction area on the strip gradually develops a color or band intensity.3. Final Result: The developed color is lighter or darker depending on glyphosate concentration and corresponds to a specific level on the reference card.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis method is based on enzyme inhibition. Glyphosate inhibits specific enzymes immobilized on the test strip. When glyphosate is present in the food extract, enzyme activity is reduced, leading to a change in color development. The degree of color change is inversely or directly related (as specified by the kit) to the glyphosate residue concentration. By comparing the strip color with a standard reference card, the residue level can be rapidly assessed.VI. Precautions1. Insert the test strip vertically and avoid touching the reaction zone.2. Strictly control the immersion and reaction time according to instructions.3. Use a clean container to avoid cross-contamination.4. Do not interpret results after excessive standing time.

Experiment Title: Comparison of Dissolution of Tablet, Capsule, and Liquid Medication in Water2. Subject: Healthcare – Nursing3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare the dissolution and dispersion characteristics of three common medication forms (tablet, capsule, liquid) in water, and to understand how dosage form affects onset of action in nursing practice.II. Experimental EquipmentThree identical clear glass cups, clean drinking water (room temperature), one tablet medication, one capsule medication, one liquid medication (same or similar drug type if possible), dropper or small measuring cup (for liquid), flat surface, camera or smartphone fixed on a tripod.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place three identical clear glasses side by side on a flat surface. Pour equal volumes of clear water into each glass.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera focus and position facing the three glasses to ensure all are visible in the same frame.3. Core Operation:   (1) Drop one tablet gently into the left glass.   (2) Drop one capsule gently into the center glass.   (3) Pour a small, equal-dose amount of liquid medication into the right glass.4. Observation: Keep the setup undisturbed and observe the changes in each glass over time. For demonstration, the process may be accelerated or shown as time-lapse.5. Completion: After clear differences are observed, stop recording and safely dispose of the solutions according to medication safety rules.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: All three glasses contain clear, colorless water.2. Liquid Medication: Immediately disperses and mixes uniformly with water, changing the water color or clarity evenly.3. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesDifferent medication dosage forms have different dissolution and dispersion behaviors in water. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Gas Discharge Tube Glowing Under High VoltageI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Gas Discharge Tube Glowing When High Voltage Is Applied2. Subject: Natural Science – Astrophysics & Astronomy3. Experiment Objective: To observe the light emission phenomenon of a sealed gas discharge tube under high voltage, understand how electric fields excite gas atoms to emit characteristic light, and relate this process to astronomical spectroscopy and emission nebulae.II. Experimental EquipmentSealed glass gas discharge tube (filled with low-pressure inert gas or hydrogen), high-voltage power supply with adjustable voltage control, connecting wires with insulated clamps, tube holder or stand, dark laboratory environment, insulated gloves (recommended for safety).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Darken the laboratory as much as possible to enhance visibility of light emission. Ensure the power supply voltage control is set to the off or minimum position. Secure the gas discharge tube horizontally on the holder.2. Equipment Connection: Connect both electrodes of the sealed glass gas discharge tube firmly to the output terminals of the high-voltage power supply using insulated wires. Confirm all connections are stable and no bare conductors are exposed.3. Core Operation: With one hand kept away from the circuit, use the other hand to slowly turn the voltage control knob from off toward higher voltage. Increase the voltage gradually and continuously.4. Observation: Closely observe the interior of the gas discharge tube as the voltage increases, noting any changes in brightness, color, and uniformity of the glow.5. Completion: Once the glowing phenomenon is clearly observed, stop increasing the voltage. After observation, slowly turn the voltage control back to zero, then switch off the power supply before disconnecting the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: When the power supply is off, the gas discharge tube remains dark and transparent, with no visible light.2. Voltage Increase: As the voltage is increased from zero, a faint glow appears inside the tube.3. Stable Discharge: With sufficient high voltage applied, the tube emits a clear, steady colored glow (color depends on the type of gas), filling most or all of the tube.4. Intensity Change: Further increase in voltage makes the glow brighter, while remaining continuous and stable.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesUnder high voltage, a strong electric field is established across the low-pressure gas inside the sealed tube. Free electrons are accelerated by the electric field and collide with gas atoms, exciting them to higher energy states. When these excited atoms return to lower energy states, they emit photons of specific wavelengths, producing visible light. Different gases emit characteristic colors, which is the same physical principle used in astrophysics to analyze the composition of stars and nebulae through emission spectra.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Always start with the voltage control at zero to prevent sudden discharge.2. Do not touch the electrodes or exposed conductors during operation.3. Increase and decrease voltage slowly to protect equipment and ensure stable observation.4. Perform the experiment under instructor supervision and follow high-voltage safety rules.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: High-voltage gas discharge and light emission in low-pressure gas. Minimum assumptions: a sealed glass tube contains gas at low pressure, connected to a controllable high-voltage source in a dark environment. Expected phased storyline: Phase 1 – Dark lab with inactive tube and voltage at zero; Phase 2 – Hand turns voltage control upward, establishing an electric field; Phase 3 – Electrons excite gas atoms, producing a faint then stable colored glow inside the tube; Phase 4 – Voltage stabilizes and glow remains steady. Visibility constraints: tube interior must be clearly visible against the dark background, and the causal link between hand action and glowing must be visually obvious.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment String Reversal Algorithm VisualizationI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: String Reversal Algorithm Visualization (Back-to-Front Splicing)Subject: Engineering - Software EngineeringExperiment Objective: To understand the basic idea of a string reversal algorithm by visually demonstrating how characters are extracted from back to front and appended to form a new reversed string.II. Experimental Environment and MaterialsComputer or display screen, simple programming or animation environment (text-based visualization), input string Hello.III. Experimental Operation Process1. Initialization: Display the input string Hello on the screen. Set an index variable to the position of the last character in the string.2. Step Execution: Extract the character at the current index (starting from the last character o).3. Appending: Append the extracted character to an initially empty new string used to store the reversed result.4. Display: Show the current state of the new string as the intermediate reversed result.5. Iteration: Move the index one position to the left and repeat the extraction and appending steps.6. Completion: Continue until the index reaches the first character H. Display the final reversed string olleH.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The screen shows the original string Hello and an empty reversed string.2. During the Process: With each step, one character is taken from the back of Hello and added to the new string, which grows from o, to ol, to oll, to olle, and finally to olleH.3. Final State: The reversed string olleH is fully displayed, and the algorithm stops.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the core principle of the string reversal algorithm in software engineering. By using an index that starts at the end of the string and moves backward, each character is sequentially extracted and appended to a new string. The reversal is achieved through orderly traversal and concatenation, reflecting the fundamental idea of iterative algorithms and string manipulation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Visual demonstration of a string reversal algorithm using back-to-front character extraction and splicing. Minimum assumptions: a visible input string Hello, a visible index moving from right to left, and a second string that accumulates characters. Expected phenomena storyline: Phase 1 shows Hello with index at the last character; Phase 2 repeatedly shows character extraction causing the reversed string to grow step by step; Phase 3 ends with the complete reversed string olleH. Visibility constraints: both the current index position and the intermediate reversed string must be clearly visible at each step to verify causality and order.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Relationship between Earthquake Frequency and Building Height AmplitudeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Relationship between Earthquake Frequency and Building Height Amplitude2. Subject: Physics – Natural Science3. Experiment Objective: To simulate how buildings of different heights respond differently to earthquake frequencies and to understand resonance through observation of vibration amplitude changes.II. Experimental EquipmentSmall horizontal vibration table with adjustable frequency; rigid base fixed on the table; three identical plastic balls; three slender, flexible metal rods of different lengths; power controller for vibration table.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fix the base firmly on the vibration table. Attach three metal rods vertically on the base, ensuring they are slender and flexible.2. Assembly: Fix one identical plastic ball to the top of each rod. Ensure the rods have different lengths to represent buildings of different heights.3. Initial State: Turn on the vibration table at a very low frequency, producing gentle horizontal vibration.4. Core Operation: Gradually and continuously increase the vibration frequency while keeping the vibration direction horizontal.5. Observation: Observe and compare the swing amplitude of each plastic ball at different frequencies.6. Completion: After clear amplitude changes are observed, stop increasing the frequency and turn off the vibration table.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. At low frequency, all balls swing slightly with small amplitudes.2. As frequency increases, one ball shows a明显 increase in swing amplitude while the others remain smaller.3. With further frequency increase, the ball with the largest amplitude changes, and another ball reaches maximum swing.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleEach rod–ball system has a natural frequency determined mainly by rod length (height). When the vibration frequency of the base matches a system’s natural frequency, resonance occurs, producing maximum amplitude. Taller structures correspond to lower natural frequencies, while shorter structures correspond to higher natural frequencies. This explains why buildings of different heights respond differently to earthquakes of different frequencies.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: resonance between external vibration frequency and natural frequency of structures, modeled by rods of different lengths. Minimum assumptions: horizontal base vibration, flexible rods, identical masses, gradually increasing frequency.Expected phenomena storyline: Phase 1 (low frequency) – all balls show small, similar oscillations. Phase 2 (matching frequency) – one specific ball exhibits a sharp increase in amplitude due to resonance. Phase 3 (higher frequency) – resonance shifts to another ball with different rod length. Visibility requirement: all three balls must be visible simultaneously to compare amplitudes and identify resonance transitions.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Visualization of the Accumulation AlgorithmI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Step-by-Step Visualization of the Accumulation Algorithm2. Subject: Engineering – Software Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To understand the accumulation (running sum) algorithm by sequentially inputting numeric values into a list and observing how intermediate sums are updated and displayed step by step until the final accumulated result is obtained.II. Experimental Environment and Tools1. A simple software interface or simulation window (text-based or graphical).2. An input list of numeric values: [1, 2, 3, 4].3. A display area showing the current input value and the running sum.III. Experimental Operation Process1. Initialization: Open the simple interface. Prepare the input list [1, 2, 3, 4]. Set the initial running sum to 0 and display it clearly.2. Step 1 (Input 1): Input the first value 1 into the algorithm. Add it to the running sum (0 + 1). Update and display the running sum as 1.3. Step 2 (Input 2): Input the second value 2. Add it to the current running sum (1 + 2). Update and display the running sum as 3.4. Step 3 (Input 3): Input the third value 3. Add it to the running sum (3 + 3). Update and display the running sum as 6.5. Step 4 (Input 4): Input the fourth value 4. Add it to the running sum (6 + 4). Update and display the running sum as 10.6. Completion: Highlight or display the final accumulated result (10) as the output of the algorithm.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The running sum is displayed as 0 before any input is processed.2. During Execution: After each numeric input, the running sum increases incrementally and is updated immediately on the interface.3. Final State: After processing all values in order, the running sum stabilizes at 10, indicating the completion of the accumulation process.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Core Principle: The accumulation algorithm iteratively processes a sequence of values by maintaining a running total.2. Algorithm Logic: Starting from an initial sum (usually 0), each new input value is added to the current sum, producing a new intermediate result.3. Significance: Visualizing intermediate sums helps learners understand loop-based computation, state updating, and the cause–effect relationship between input values and algorithm output.VI. Experimental Notes1. Inputs must be processed strictly in sequence to ensure correctness.2. Each update of the running sum should be clearly displayed to emphasize intermediate states.3. The interface should avoid skipping steps so that the gradual accumulation process is evident.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: visualization of the accumulation (running sum) algorithm. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Reduction of Potassium Dichromate by Anaerobically Germinating Rice Seed ExtractI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Color Change of Potassium Dichromate by Anaerobic Rice Seed Extract2. Subject: Engineering – Agricultural Engineering (Biochemical Processes)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that metabolites produced during anaerobic germination of rice seeds can reduce potassium dichromate, observed as a characteristic color change from orange to grayish green; to master the key operational sequence of dropwise addition and gentle mixing.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (clear glass, 15×150 mm), test tube rack, dropper, anaerobically germinating rice seed extract (filtered, pale yellow to colorless), potassium dichromate solution (orange, dilute), gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, dry test tube on the rack. Wear gloves and goggles.2. Loading Extract: Using a dropper, add approximately 2–3 mL of anaerobically germinating rice seed extract into the test tube.3. Core Operation: Add potassium dichromate solution dropwise into the test tube while gently swirling to mix.4. Reaction Completion: Continue adding and mixing until no further color change is observed.5. Finish: Place the test tube upright for clear observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The rice seed extract is light-colored; potassium dichromate solution is orange.2. During Reaction: Upon dropwise addition and mixing, the orange color gradually fades.3. Final State: The solution turns grayish green, indicating completion of the reaction.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleUnder anaerobic germination, rice seeds produce reducing metabolites such as ethanol via anaerobic respiration. PrecautionsPotassium dichromate is toxic; avoid skin contact and dispose of waste according to regulations. Use only clear glassware to ensure accurate observation.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Observation of Phosphorescent Safety Tape After IlluminationSubject: Healthcare – Pharmacy (Material Properties and Safety Applications)Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the phosphorescent property of safety tape by observing its glow after room lights are switched off, and to understand the principle of energy absorption and delayed light emission.II. Experimental EquipmentPhosphorescent safety tape (commercial safety-grade tape, light green), indoor room with controllable lighting, wall surface for tape placement, fixed camera or smartphone with tripod, room lights (white LED or fluorescent).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Attach a strip of phosphorescent safety tape vertically to a clean wall at eye level. Fix the camera on a tripod facing the wall, ensuring the tape is centered in the frame. Set the camera focus manually and keep it fixed.2. Illumination Stage: Turn on the room lights and illuminate the tape evenly for sufficient time so it is clearly visible under normal lighting conditions.3. Recording Stage: Start video recording while the room lights remain on for a short moment to show the initial state.4. Core Operation: Switch off the room lights while recording continues, keeping the camera stationary and focused.5. Observation Stage: Continue recording to capture the glowing tape in darkness for a short period.6. Completion: Stop recording after the glow is clearly observed.IV. Immediately After Lights Off: The tape emits a visible greenish glow against the dark background.3. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePhosphorescent safety tape contains phosphorescent materials that absorb light energy when illuminated. This delayed emission causes the tape to glow in darkness, which is useful for safety guidance in low-light or emergency conditions.VI. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Rubber Eraser vs Metal Block Sliding Down Identical RampsI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Sliding on Identical RampsSubject: Natural Science – PhysicsObjective: To observe how different materials slide on identical inclined planes and understand the effect of friction.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical ramps (smooth surface), rubber eraser, metal block of similar size, adjustable support to change ramp angle, flat table.III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Place two identical ramps side by side on a table with the same initial small angle. Ensure surfaces are clean and identical.2. Placement: Put the rubber eraser at the top of the left ramp and the metal block at the top of the right ramp, aligned evenly.3. Angle Increase: Slowly and synchronously increase the angle of both ramps to the same height.4. Release: Stop increasing the angle and allow both objects to slide freely.5. Observation: Watch which object starts sliding first and compare their speeds and travel distances.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena- At small angles, both objects may remain at rest.- As the angle increases, the metal block begins to slide first.- The metal block slides faster down the ramp than the rubber eraser.- The rubber eraser slides later and more slowly, sometimes with intermittent motion.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleOn an inclined plane, gravity pulls objects downward while friction resists motion. The rubber eraser has a larger friction force with the ramp than the metal block. As the angle increases, the component of gravity along the ramp increases. The metal block, with lower friction, overcomes friction earlier and accelerates more, demonstrating the role of friction in motion.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Sodium Formaldehydesulfoxylate (Rongalite) Detection (Colorimetric Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Colorimetric Detection of Sodium Formaldehydesulfoxylate (Rongalite)2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food Hygiene3. Experiment Objective: To qualitatively detect the presence of sodium formaldehydesulfoxylate (Rongalite) in a sample through a colorimetric reaction, and to master the basic operation of stepwise reagent addition and observation of color change.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (clean, colorless, transparent), test tube rack, droppers, hydrochloric acid solution (dilute), fuchsin‑sulfurous acid reagent, sample solution (suspected of containing Rongalite), protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack. Using a dropper, add an appropriate amount of the sample solution (about 1–2 mL) into the test tube.2. Acidification: Using a clean dropper, add 2–3 drops of dilute hydrochloric acid into the test tube. Do not shake vigorously.3. Reagent Addition: Using another dropper, add 2–3 drops of fuchsin‑sulfurous acid reagent into the same test tube.4. Mixing: Gently shake the test tube to mix the solution evenly.5. Reaction: Place the test tube still on the rack and allow it to stand for reaction. Observe the color change over time.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The solution in the test tube is colorless or lightly colored and transparent.2. After Adding Hydrochloric Acid: No obvious color change is observed; the solution remains clear.3. After Adding Fuchsin‑Sulfurous Acid and Standing: If Rongalite is present, the solution gradually develops a characteristic color (typically red or purplish‑red). If Rongalite is absent, the solution shows little or no color change.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSodium formaldehydesulfoxylate (Rongalite) is a strong reducing agent. In acidic conditions, it reacts with the fuchsin‑sulfurous acid reagent, reducing the colorless leuco form to restore the colored fuchsin structure. This red or purplish‑red color development serves as the basis of qualitative colorimetric detection. The intensity of the color correlates with the presence of Rongalite, allowing visual identification.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use clean droppers for different reagents to avoid cross‑contamination.2. Add reagents in the correct order: hydrochloric acid first, then fuchsin‑sulfurous acid.3. Gently shake the test tube to avoid splashing.4. Dispose of waste solutions according to laboratory safety regulations.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: qualitative colorimetric detection of sodium formaldehydesulfoxylate based on acidification followed by a redox color reaction with fuchsin‑sulfurous acid. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: Rongalite acts as a reducing agent under acidic conditions, enabling restoration of fuchsin color. Phased storyline: (1) clear sample in test tube; (2) addition of hydrochloric acid with no immediate color change; (3) addition of fuchsin‑sulfurous acid; (4) gentle mixing; (5) standing reaction leading to gradual visible color development. Visibility constraints: close‑up view of transparent glassware and solution color is required to verify each causal transition.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Iodine Reaction with Starch vs CelluloseI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Iodine Reaction with Starch and Cellulose2. Subject: Chemistry – Organic Chemistry / Natural Polymers3. Experiment Objective: To compare the interaction of iodine with starch and cellulose, observe differences in color change, and understand how polymer structure affects molecular binding.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo clear glass beakers (100 mL), starch suspension (1–2% aqueous), cellulose fibers (e.g., cotton or filter paper pieces soaked in water), iodine solution (I2/KI), droppers or pipettes, glass rod, white background, camera fixed on tripod.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, transparent beakers side by side on a white background. Label one ‘Starch’ and the other ‘Cellulose’.2. Sample Addition: Pour equal volumes (about 50 mL) of starch suspension into the first beaker. Add an equal volume of water containing visible cellulose fibers into the second beaker.3. Initial Observation: Observe and record the initial appearance. The starch suspension is milky white; cellulose fibers are colorless/white in clear water.4. Core Operation: Using a dropper, add 2–3 drops of iodine solution into the starch beaker, then add the same amount into the cellulose beaker.5. Observation and Recording: Keep the camera focus fixed and observe the color changes over time (can be time-lapse accelerated).6. Completion: Stop observation once color changes are stable; dispose of solutions according to lab rules and clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before iodine addition: Both beakers appear colorless to white with no dark coloration.2. After iodine addition: The starch suspension rapidly turns blue-black. The cellulose sample remains yellow-brown (iodine color) with no dark complex formation.3. Comparison: A clear contrast in color between the two beakers is observed.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesStarch contains amylose, a helical polymer of glucose that can trap iodine molecules, forming a blue-black starch–iodine complex. Cellulose, although also a glucose polymer, has linear chains with strong hydrogen bonding and no helical cavities, so iodine cannot bind effectively. Therefore, iodine produces a characteristic color with starch but not with cellulose, demonstrating how polymer structure affects molecular interactions.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use dilute iodine to avoid overly dark backgrounds.2. Ensure equal iodine volumes are added to both beakers for fair comparison.3. Keep camera position fixed to clearly record comparative changes.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Iodine selectively binds to starch due to its helical polymer structure, but not to cellulose with linear chains.Minimum mechanistic assumptions: iodine molecules can enter amylose helices forming a colored complex; cellulose lacks suitable binding sites.Expected phased storyline: (1) Two identical clear beakers with different polymer samples are shown side by side; (2) iodine is added to both; (3) starch beaker rapidly darkens to blue-black while cellulose remains yellow-brown; (4) final stable contrast is visible. Camera remains fixed with clear frontal view to verify color differences and causal sequence.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Attraction of Opposite Poles of Bar MagnetsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Attraction of Opposite Poles of Bar Magnets2. Subject: Natural Science - Physics3. Experiment Objective: To observe and verify that opposite magnetic poles attract each other, and to understand the basic law of magnetic interaction.II. Experimental Materials1. Identical bar magnets (2)2. Marker or label stickers (for marking N and S poles)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Take two identical bar magnets. Identify and clearly mark the north (N) pole and south (S) pole on each magnet using a marker or labels.2. Positioning: Hold one magnet in each hand. Orient the magnets so that the N pole of one magnet faces the S pole of the other magnet.3. Core Operation: Slowly bring the N and S poles close together while still holding the magnets firmly with your hands.4. Release: When the poles are very close, release both magnets at the same time.5. Observation: Observe the movement and final state of the magnets after release.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before release: The two magnets are held close together with opposite poles facing each other.2. After release: The magnets move toward each other automatically and stick together, showing a clear attraction between the N and S poles.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleBar magnets have two magnetic poles: north (N) and south (S). According to the law of magnetism, opposite poles attract each other, while like poles repel each other. When the N pole of one magnet is brought close to the S pole of another magnet, a magnetic force of attraction acts between them. After the hands are released, this force causes the magnets to move together and attach to each other.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the magnets are identical to avoid differences in magnetic strength affecting observation.2. Mark the poles clearly to prevent confusion between opposite and like poles.3. Release the magnets gently to avoid external force interference or damage to the magnets.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Airfoil in a Wind Tunnel with Smoke StreamlinesI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Visualization of Airflow Around an Airfoil Using Smoke in a Wind TunnelSubject: Engineering – Aerospace EngineeringExperiment Objective: To visually demonstrate airflow behavior around a fixed airfoil at a slight angle of attack, observe acceleration of airflow and downward deflection of smoke streamlines, and understand the aerodynamic principle of lift generation. The experiment also aims to document the process using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentLow-speed wind tunnel with transparent test section; airfoil model (symmetrical or cambered); airfoil mounting mechanism with adjustable angle of attack; smoke generator or smoke wire; uniform airflow source (fan or tunnel drive); lighting system; camera mounted on tripod with fixed focus and fixed viewpoint.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Install the airfoil model in the center of the wind tunnel test section. Adjust and fix the airfoil at a slight positive angle of attack (approximately 3–5 degrees). Ensure the test section is clean and transparent.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera perpendicular to the test section. Fix the focus, framing, and exposure. Do not adjust the camera during the experiment to enable time-lapse recording.3. Smoke Setup: Place the smoke generator upstream of the airfoil so that thin, parallel smoke streams enter the tunnel uniformly.4. Core Operation: Start the wind tunnel at a low, steady speed. Gradually introduce smoke until clear, continuous streamlines are visible approaching the airfoil.5. Observation and Recording: Allow airflow to stabilize. Record the motion of smoke as it flows over and under the airfoil, focusing on changes in speed and direction as the smoke passes the airfoil.6. Shutdown: Stop smoke generation first, then gradually reduce wind tunnel speed. Turn off equipment and save recorded footage.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Smoke streamlines upstream of the airfoil are straight, parallel, and evenly spaced.During Flow Over Airfoil: As smoke reaches the airfoil, streamlines over the upper surface accelerate and curve smoothly. Downstream of the airfoil, the smoke is deflected downward as a whole.Final State: A stable pattern of downward-bent wake is visible, indicating a net downward momentum imparted to the airflow.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the aerodynamic principle of lift generation. When a fixed airfoil is set at a slight angle of attack in a uniform airflow, it alters the surrounding flow field. The airflow accelerates over the upper surface and is deflected downward overall. According to Newton’s third law and conservation of momentum, the downward deflection of air results in an upward force (lift) acting on the airfoil. Smoke visualization makes these otherwise invisible flow patterns observable.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the airfoil is firmly mounted; maintain steady airflow; avoid disturbing smoke streams; keep camera settings fixed throughout the experiment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Visualization of aerodynamic lift using smoke streamlines around a fixed airfoil in a wind tunnel. Minimum assumptions include steady, low-speed airflow; a rigid airfoil at slight angle of attack; and smoke acting as a passive flow tracer.Phased Storyline: (1) Establishment phase – straight, parallel smoke streams approach a stationary airfoil in a transparent wind tunnel; (2) Interaction phase – airflow accelerates over the airfoil surfaces, and smoke streamlines curve smoothly; (3) Outcome phase – downstream smoke shows a clear downward deflection, visually confirming momentum change and lift generation. The camera viewpoint remains fixed and unobstructed to allow verification of spatial continuity and causal flow behavior.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment "Laser Beam Refraction at the Air–Water Interface in a Clear Tank"I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Laser Beam Refraction at the Air–Water Interface2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics (Optics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and verify the refraction of light at the air–water interface by shining a laser beam from air into water at different angles of incidence; to understand the relationship between incidence angle and refraction angle and the basic law of refraction.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent rectangular water tank (clear glass or acrylic), clean water (filled to at least 3/4 of the tank), low-power visible laser pointer (red or green), adjustable holder or clamp for the laser, protractor or angle scale (optional, for reference), darkened background or room, camera fixed on a tripod (side view), ruler or marker tape (optional), safety goggles (laser safety).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the clear tank on a stable horizontal surface and fill it with clean water until the water surface is flat and calm. Darken the background to improve beam visibility. Fix the camera on a tripod to obtain a clear side view of the tank, ensuring the entire air–water interface is visible. Set the camera focus manually and keep it fixed for time-lapse recording.2. Laser Setup: Mount the laser pointer on an adjustable holder so that the beam travels in air and strikes the water surface at one side of the tank. Ensure the laser beam lies approximately in a vertical plane perpendicular to the tank wall.3. Core Operation: Turn on the laser and adjust its height so the beam enters the water through the side wall above the waterline and reaches the air–water interface from air. Slowly tilt the laser source to change the angle of incidence while keeping the beam aimed at the same region of the interface.4. Observation and Recording: For each tilt angle, observe the path of the laser beam in air and the refracted beam in water. Record a short time-lapse or continuous video from the fixed camera position, clearly showing the change in beam direction at the interface.5. Completion: After observations, turn off the laser, stop recording, empty the tank if required, and store all equipment properly.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The laser beam travels in a straight line through air before reaching the water surface.2. At the Interface: When the beam enters the water, it changes direction abruptly at the air–water boundary.3. Angle Dependence: As the angle of incidence in air increases, the refracted beam in water bends toward the normal, and the angle of refraction changes accordingly.4. Overall Appearance: From the side view, two straight segments of the beam are visible: one in air and one in water, connected at the interface with a clear change in direction.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates the law of refraction of light. When light passes from air into water, its speed decreases due to the higher optical density of water, causing the beam to bend at the interface. The relationship between the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction follows Snell’s law: n1·sinθ1 = n2·sinθ2, where n1 and n2 are the refractive indices of air and water. Because water has a higher refractive index than air, the refracted ray bends toward the normal.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use a low-power laser and never look directly into the beam.2. Ensure the tank walls are clean to avoid scattering that may obscure the beam path.3. Keep the camera focus fixed to maintain consistent visual comparison during time-lapse recording.4. Avoid disturbing the water surface during observation to keep the interface flat.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Refraction of light at an air–water interface. Minimum assumptions: a transparent tank with still water, a visible laser beam traveling from air into water, and a fixed side-view perspective. Phased storyline: (1) Laser travels straight in air toward the water surface; (2) At the flat interface, the beam abruptly changes direction; (3) As the laser source is tilted, the incidence angle changes and the refracted beam in water adjusts accordingly, always bending toward the normal; (4) Throughout, the camera remains fixed, enabling clear comparison of beam paths in air and water.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Gastrin Detection (Immunological Test Strip Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Gastrin Detection by Immunological Test Strip MethodSubject: Healthcare – Digestive PhysiologyObjective: To demonstrate the use of an immunological test strip to qualitatively detect gastrin in a liquid sample, understand the operation of test strips, observe capillary flow and result lines, and summarize the immunochromatographic principle.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentGastrin immunological test strip (labeled, single-use), liquid sample (simulated serum or buffer), dropper or micropipette, clean flat surface, timer or stopwatch.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Remove the gastrin test strip from its packaging and check that the label and sample well are intact. Place the strip horizontally on a clean, flat surface.2. Sample Addition: Use a dropper to draw a measured amount of liquid sample (according to kit instructions). Carefully add the sample dropwise into the sample well of the test strip, avoiding overflow.3. Capillary Flow Reaction: Allow the liquid to migrate naturally along the strip by capillary action. Do not move or tilt the strip during this process.4. Waiting Period: Wait briefly (typically 3–5 minutes; may be accelerated for demonstration) until the reaction area is fully developed.5. Result Display: After completion, display the test strip clearly for result reading, ensuring the reaction zone is visible.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The test strip is dry, with no visible colored lines in the reaction area.During Reaction: The liquid sample flows along the strip from the sample well toward the absorbent end by capillary action.Final State: One colored control line appears to indicate the test is valid. A second test line appears if gastrin is present in the sample; absence of the test line indicates a negative result.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on immunochromatography. The sample migrates along the strip via capillary action and encounters antibodies specific to gastrin that are labeled with a color indicator. If gastrin is present, antigen–antibody complexes form and are captured at the test line, producing a visible colored band. The control line captures excess labeled antibodies regardless of gastrin presence, confirming proper flow and test validity. The presence or absence of the test line reflects the qualitative detection of gastrin.VI. PrecautionsUse the test strip immediately after opening; avoid touching the reaction area. Add the correct sample volume to prevent invalid results. Do not interpret results beyond the specified time window. Dispose of used strips according to biomedical waste guidelines.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Gastric Acid pH Detection (Simulated Test Strip Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Gastric Acid pH Detection Using pH Test Strips (Simulated Method)2. Subject: Healthcare – Digestive Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To understand the acidity of gastric juice by using pH test strips, master the basic operation of pH detection, and learn how to interpret acidity by comparing color changes with a standard pH chart.II. Experimental EquipmentpH test strips (acid range), simulated gastric juice (dilute acidic solution), dropper, clean flat surface (e.g., white tray or paper), standard pH color reference chart, disposable gloves (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, dry pH test strip flat on a clean surface. Ensure the pH color chart is nearby and clearly visible.2. Sampling: Use a dropper to draw a small amount of simulated gastric juice.3. Core Operation: Carefully add one drop of the simulated gastric juice onto the reactive end of the pH test strip. Avoid touching the strip with the dropper tip.4. Waiting: Wait for 1–3 seconds to allow the color on the test strip to fully develop.5. Comparison: Hold the reacted test strip next to the standard pH color chart and compare the color to determine the pH value.6. Conclusion: Record the observed pH range, then dispose of the used strip properly and clean the workspace.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The dry pH test strip has a uniform original color on its reactive area.2. After Adding Simulated Gastric Juice: The reactive area of the strip rapidly changes color.3. Comparison Result: The final color corresponds to an acidic range (low pH) on the standard pH color chart, indicating strong acidity similar to gastric acid.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesGastric juice contains hydrochloric acid, which gives it strong acidity. pH test strips contain acid–base indicators that change color depending on hydrogen ion concentration. When simulated gastric juice contacts the strip, the indicator reacts with hydrogen ions, producing a characteristic color. By comparing this color with a standard pH chart, the acidity (pH value) of the gastric juice can be estimated.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use only simulated gastric juice; do not use real gastric samples.2. Keep the test strip dry before use to avoid inaccurate results.3. Observe the color change promptly, as prolonged exposure may cause fading or diffusion.4. Dispose of used materials according to laboratory hygiene requirements.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Enterobacter aerogenes Detection (Lactose-Citrate Color Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Detection of Enterobacter aerogenes by Lactose Fermentation and Citrate Utilization2. Subject: Healthcare – Pathology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the standard procedure for identifying Enterobacter aerogenes by inoculating bacteria onto lactose fermentation medium, incubating, and transferring growth to citrate medium, while mastering sterile loop use, streaking technique, incubation, and test tube handling.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentLactose fermentation medium test tube (with Durham tube), Simmons citrate agar slant test tube, inoculating loop, alcohol lamp or electric sterilizer, test tube rack, bacterial culture (suspected Enterobacter aerogenes), incubator (35–37°C), marker pen.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place lactose fermentation medium and citrate agar slant in a test tube rack. Label tubes clearly. Disinfect the working area.2. Sterile Loop Handling: Hold the inoculating loop like a pen and sterilize it in the flame until red hot. Allow it to cool briefly without touching any surface.3. Inoculation of Lactose Medium: Use the cooled sterile loop to pick a small amount of bacterial culture. Open the lactose medium tube carefully, flame the tube mouth, and insert the loop to streak or mix the culture into the medium. Flame the tube mouth again and recap.4. Incubation: Place the inoculated lactose medium into the incubator at 35–37°C for 18–24 hours (shown as time-lapse).5. Transfer to Citrate Medium: After incubation, sterilize and cool the loop again. Open the lactose medium tube, collect a small amount of growth, then open the citrate agar slant tube. Lightly streak the slant surface in a zigzag pattern. Flame and recap the tube.6. Second Incubation: Incubate the citrate tube at 35–37°C for 18–24 hours (time-lapse depiction).IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Lactose Medium: Initially red and clear. After incubation, lactose fermentation produces acid and possibly gas, causing the medium to turn yellow, with gas bubbles in the Durham tube.2. Citrate Medium: Initially green. After incubation, citrate utilization results in an alkaline reaction, turning the medium blue.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis method combines two biochemical characteristics of Enterobacter aerogenes. First, lactose fermentation produces acid (and often gas), changing the pH indicator in the lactose medium from red to yellow. Second, Enterobacter aerogenes can utilize citrate as the sole carbon source, producing alkaline metabolites that change Simmons citrate agar from green to blue. The sequential use of these media allows differentiation and confirmation based on metabolic properties.VI. PrecautionsUse aseptic technique throughout; always sterilize the loop before and after contact with cultures. Avoid touching tube rims with the loop. Incubation times are represented in accelerated time-lapse for demonstration purposes only.

Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the dark matte surface and the white surface side by side on a flat table, ensuring they receive equal exposure to the heat source.2. Placement of Ice: Place one identical ice block at the center of each surface at the same time.3. Heat Exposure: Turn on the single overhead heat lamp or position the setup under direct sunlight so both ice blocks receive the same illumination angle and intensity.4. Recording: Fix the camera position and focus; begin time-lapse or continuous recording without moving the camera.5. Observation Period: Allow the ice to melt for a fixed period, observing differences in melting speed and water accumulation.6. Completion: Stop recording once a clear difference in melting is visible; wipe up melted water and clean materials.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both ice blocks are solid, transparent-white, and equal in size.2. During Heating: The ice on the dark matte surface begins to melt faster, producing water more quickly.3. Later Stage: The ice on the white surface melts more slowly and remains larger for a longer time compared to the ice on the dark surface.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates the albedo effect. Dark surfaces have low albedo and absorb more incoming radiation, converting it into heat, which accelerates ice melting. White surfaces have high albedo and reflect more radiation, absorbing less heat and slowing the melting process. This principle helps explain natural phenomena such as faster ice loss on darkened glaciers or land surfaces.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both ice blocks are identical to maintain fairness.2. Use only one heat source to avoid uneven heating.3. Do not touch the ice during the experiment to prevent heat interference.4. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Effect of Diagonal Bracing on Tower Stability Under Wind LoadI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Wind Load Comparison of Tall Model Towers With and Without Diagonal Bracing2. Subject: Engineering - Structural Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how diagonal bracing improves the lateral stability of tall structures under wind load by visually comparing the deformation and motion of two model towers.II. Experimental EquipmentTall model tower A (with diagonal bracing), tall model tower B (without diagonal bracing), flat tabletop, electric fan with constant speed setting, camera or smartphone mounted on a tripod, ruler or grid background (optional for deformation reference).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the tabletop in a stable indoor environment with minimal external airflow. Position the camera on a tripod facing the tabletop and fix the focus.2. Setup: Place the two model towers upright on the tabletop, side by side, with equal spacing from the fan. Ensure tower A has clearly visible diagonal bracing and tower B has only vertical members.3. Fan Positioning: Place the electric fan directly in front of the two towers so that airflow is perpendicular to their height. Set the fan to a steady, constant speed.4. Core Operation: Turn on the fan and allow steady wind to blow toward both towers simultaneously. Record the scene continuously (or in time-lapse) for a short duration.5. Completion: After sufficient observation, turn off the fan and stop recording. Keep the camera position unchanged throughout the experiment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both towers stand vertically upright without visible deformation.2. During Wind Loading: As the fan blows, both towers begin to sway slightly due to lateral wind force.3.
