Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWind acting on a tall structure generates lateral forces that cause bending and sway. Diagonal bracing forms triangular load paths within the structure, increasing lateral stiffness and reducing deformation. This experiment visually demonstrates the structural engineering principle that diagonal bracing enhances stability and resistance to lateral loads.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Phosphorus Detection in Egg Yolk by Molybdenum Blue MethodSubject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess EngineeringObjective: To qualitatively detect phosphorus in egg yolk by forming a blue complex and to understand the basic principle of the molybdenum blue color reaction.II. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on a test tube rack. Ensure the egg yolk extract is homogeneous.2. Sampling: Use a pipette to accurately transfer 2 mL of egg yolk extract into the test tube.3. Experimental EquipmentStandard badminton court with clear markings, badminton racket, shuttlecock (white), two players wearing sports attire, net.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Player A stands near midcourt holding a racket; Player B stands in the opposite court ready to receive.2. Retreat to Backcourt: Player A moves backward quickly to the backcourt as the shuttle is lifted high.3. Jump Smash: Player A jumps vertically, raises the racket arm, and strikes the shuttlecock at the highest point with a downward, forceful motion.4. Shuttle Trajectory: The shuttle travels steeply downward over the net toward the opponent front court.5. Scoring Outcome: The shuttle lands clearly inside Player B front service line; Player B attempts but fails to return.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial: Shuttle is high in the air; Player A positioned in backcourt.During Action: Player A jumps and smashes; shuttle accelerates downward with a steep angle.Result: Shuttle lands inside opponent front service line; opponent reaction is too late, resulting in a direct score.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe principle is based on badminton offensive tactics and biomechanics. A backcourt jump smash increases contact height and racket head speed, producing a steep downward trajectory and high shuttle velocity. This reduces the opponent reaction time and forces the shuttle to land sharply in the front court, making successful return difficult.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure court markings are visible; confirm shuttle lands in-bounds; perform jumps safely to avoid injury.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Badminton backcourt jump smash scoring. Minimum assumptions: standard court geometry, gravity-driven shuttle motion, legal in-bounds landing, human biomechanics of jumping and smashing.Phased storyline: (1) Player retreats to backcourt as shuttle rises; (2) player jumps and strikes shuttle at peak height; (3) shuttle follows steep downward path; (4) shuttle lands inside opponent front service line; (5) opponent fails to return. Visibility constraints: clear side or diagonal view showing court lines, net, shuttle trajectory, and opponent response for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Salt Added to Muddy Clay Water Causes Clumping and SettlingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effect of Salt on the Settling of Muddy Clay Water2. Subject: Natural Science – Marine Science3. Experiment Objective: To observe how adding salt to muddy clay water causes fine clay particles to clump together and settle faster, helping to understand particle aggregation processes in seawater.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo clear glass jars of the same size, muddy clay water (prepared by mixing fine clay with water), table salt, stirring rods or spoons, camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clear glass jars side by side on a stable surface. Pour equal volumes of muddy clay water into each jar.2. Salt Addition: Add a measured amount of salt to the right jar only. Do not add salt to the left jar (control).3. Stirring: Briefly stir both jars gently and equally to distribute contents evenly.4. Standing: Stop stirring and leave both jars undisturbed. Fix the camera focus and record the jars over time.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both jars appear uniformly muddy and opaque after stirring.2. After Standing: In the right jar, clay particles gradually form visible clumps and settle to the bottom, making the water clearer above. In the left jar, particles remain more dispersed and settle more slowly.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesClay particles in freshwater carry similar electrical charges and repel each other, staying suspended. When salt is added, dissolved ions neutralize these charges, allowing particles to aggregate into larger clumps (flocculation). Larger clumps settle faster under gravity. This process explains why sediment settles more quickly in seawater than in freshwater.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse identical jars and equal water volumes; stir both jars in the same way; avoid shaking during settling; ensure camera position and focus remain fixed throughout recording.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Salt ions promote flocculation of fine clay particles, accelerating settling compared with unsalted muddy water. Minimum assumptions: two identical clear jars, equal muddy clay water, salt added only to the right jar, brief stirring, then rest. Phased storyline: (1) identical muddy appearance in both jars; (2) salt addition to right jar followed by stirring; (3) early aggregation visible only in right jar; (4) progressive settling forming sediment at the bottom of the right jar while the left remains turbid. Visibility constraints: jars must be fully in frame, transparent, with fixed camera perspective to verify left–right differences and causal sequence.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Water Rising Through a Transparent Column of Fine SandI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Water Rising Through a Transparent Column of Fine Sand2. Subject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe capillary rise and seepage in fine sand, understand soil–water interaction, and visualize water migration in porous media.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent vertical tube (glass or acrylic, sealed at sides), fine dry sand, shallow tray, clean water, support stand or clamp, ruler or scale (optional), camera fixed for side-view time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the tube is clean and dry. Pour dry fine sand slowly into the tube while gently tapping to achieve uniform packing without compaction.2. Positioning: Fix the tube vertically on a support. Place the tube so that its bottom opening is slightly above the tray base.3. Submergence: Pour water into the tray until the bottom of the sand column is submerged by a few millimeters, avoiding disturbance of the sand.4. Observation Setup: Fix the camera at a side view, lock focus and framing, and begin time-lapse recording.5. Observation: Allow the system to stand undisturbed while water rises through the sand over time.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Sand is uniformly light-colored and dry throughout the tube; water is only in the tray.2. Early Stage: Water enters the sand from the bottom, forming a darker wet zone near the base.3. Development Stage: The wetting front gradually rises upward, with a clear boundary between wet and dry sand.4. Later Stage: The rise slows and eventually stabilizes at a certain height above the water level in the tray.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates capillary action and seepage in fine-grained soils. Fine sand contains small interconnected pores that generate capillary forces. When the base is submerged, surface tension and adhesion between water and sand particles pull water upward against gravity. The rise height depends on pore size, grain characteristics, and water properties, illustrating fundamental principles of soil–water interaction in geotechnical engineering.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use dry, fine, and clean sand to ensure clear capillary effects.2. Avoid shaking or disturbing the setup during observation.3. Ensure the tube remains vertical and the camera position is fixed throughout the experiment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Capillary rise and water migration in fine sand as a porous medium under geotechnical engineering principles. Minimum assumptions: sand is fine, dry, and uniformly packed; tube is vertical and transparent; water contacts sand only from the base.Expected Phased Storyline: (1) Initial dry sand column with water confined to tray; (2) causal transition where base submergence allows water to enter pores; (3) gradual upward movement of a darker wetting front driven by capillary forces; (4) slowing and stabilization of rise height. Visibility constraints: side view must clearly show tube, sand color change, water level in tray, and continuous upward progression over time.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Live-cell fluorescence imaging of glucocorticoid receptor nuclear translocationSubject: Natural Science – Cell & Developmental BiologyObjective: To observe ligand-induced translocation of a fluorescently tagged glucocorticoid receptor (GR-GFP) from cytoplasm to nucleus in living mammalian cells using time-lapse fluorescence microscopy.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentCultured mammalian cells expressing green fluorescent glucocorticoid receptor (GR-GFP); two glass-bottom culture dishes; glucocorticoid hormone solution (e.g., dexamethasone); fluorescence microscope with live-cell imaging capability; temperature/CO2 control chamber (optional); micropipette and sterile tips; imaging software.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Culture GR-GFP–expressing cells in two identical dishes to similar confluence. Place both dishes on the microscope stage side by side. Adjust fluorescence excitation and emission for GFP and fix the camera focus.2. Baseline Imaging: Begin time-lapse fluorescence imaging. Record baseline distribution of GR-GFP in both dishes for several frames; fluorescence should be mainly cytoplasmic.3. Hormone Addition: During continuous imaging, gently add glucocorticoid hormone to the left dish only without disturbing focus. Do not add hormone to the right dish (control).4. Time-lapse Observation: Continue imaging at fixed intervals, maintaining constant focus and field of view.5. Termination: Stop imaging after clear fluorescence redistribution is observed. Save and label image sequences for both dishes.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: In both dishes, green fluorescence is predominantly cytoplasmic with dark nuclei.After Hormone Addition (Left Dish): Fluorescence gradually decreases in cytoplasm and accumulates in nuclei, making nuclei appear bright green.Control Dish (Right): Fluorescence distribution remains largely cytoplasmic with minimal nuclear accumulation.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleGlucocorticoid receptor is a cytoplasmic receptor that binds glucocorticoid hormone. Upon ligand binding, the receptor undergoes a conformational change, dissociates from chaperone proteins, and translocates into the nucleus. The GFP tag allows direct visualization of this cytoplasm-to-nucleus movement in living cells, demonstrating hormone-dependent receptor signaling.VI. PrecautionsMaintain sterile conditions; avoid changing microscope focus during imaging; add hormone gently to prevent mechanical artifacts; keep imaging conditions consistent between dishes.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Ligand-induced nuclear translocation of glucocorticoid receptor visualized by live-cell fluorescence microscopy. Minimum assumptions: GR is GFP-tagged, hormone binding triggers nuclear import, control cells remain unchanged.Phased storyline: (1) Stable microscope view with two side-by-side dishes and cytoplasmic green fluorescence in both; (2) Hormone added to left dish only; (3) Over time, left dish shows progressive nuclear brightening and cytoplasmic dimming; (4) Right dish remains stable as control. Visibility constraints: fixed focus, constant field of view, clear distinction between cytoplasm and nucleus to verify causal transition.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Mimosa pudica Leaf Folding After Touch StimulusI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Mimosa pudica Leaf Folding After Touch Stimulus2. Subject: Natural Science – Cell & Developmental Biology3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the rapid movement response of Mimosa pudica leaves to mechanical stimulation and relate the phenomenon to plant cell physiological processes.II. Experimental MaterialsPotted Mimosa pudica (healthy, well-watered), human finger (as touch stimulus), stable table, adequate natural or indoor light.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the potted Mimosa pudica on a stable surface under good lighting. Allow the plant to remain undisturbed for several minutes so the leaves are fully open.2. Observation Before Stimulus: Observe the compound leaves, noting that each leaflet is spread flat and open.3. Core Operation: Using a human finger, gently touch a single leaflet on one compound leaf. Avoid shaking the pot or touching other parts of the plant.4. Observation After Stimulus: Keep the camera or eyes focused closely on the touched leaflet and the same leaf for several seconds.5. End of Experiment: Stop touching and continue observing until the movement response is complete.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Leaflets are open, flat, and symmetrically arranged along the petiole.2. After Touch: The touched leaflet rapidly folds inward; neighboring leaflets on the same leaf may also fold, and the petiole may droop slightly.3. Later State (optional): After several minutes, the leaflets slowly reopen.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMimosa pudica responds to mechanical stimulation through changes in turgor pressure in specialized motor cells (pulvini) at the base of leaflets and petioles. Touch triggers an electrical and chemical signal, causing potassium and water to move out of these cells, reducing turgor pressure and leading to rapid leaf folding. This demonstrates plant sensitivity and cell-level regulation of movement.VI. Precautions1. Touch gently to avoid damaging the plant.2. Do not repeatedly stimulate the same leaf in a short time, as the response may weaken.3. Ensure the plant is healthy and not dehydrated before the experiment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Mechanical stimulus-induced rapid movement in Mimosa pudica, based on turgor pressure changes in pulvini; assumes basic plant physiology and touch sensitivity.Phased storyline: (1) Stable close-up of a healthy potted Mimosa pudica with fully open compound leaves; (2) a human finger gently approaches and touches one clearly visible leaflet; (3) immediately after touch, the contacted leaflet folds inward, followed by adjacent leaflets and slight petiole drooping; (4) camera remains steady to verify causal transition from touch to folding. Visibility constraints: leaflet structure, finger contact point, and subsequent folding motion must remain clearly in frame.

Label each vertex with its coordinates.3. Mark Symmetry Axis: Highlight the x-axis (y=0) using a red dashed line to indicate the axis of symmetry.4. Perform Symmetry Transformation: Reflect each vertex of triangle ABC across the x-axis to obtain A"(1,-2), B"(3,-2), and C"(2,-1). Draw the reflected triangle A"B"C" in blue and label each vertex.5. Connect Corresponding Points: Use green dashed lines to connect A to A", B to B", and C to C", emphasizing equal perpendicular distances to the x-axis.6. Annotation: Add yellow text stating symmetric about the x-axis to reinforce the concept.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Capillary Rise of Water in a Paper Towel Compared to OilI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Capillary Rise of Water in a Paper Towel Compared to Oil2. Subject: Natural Science - Biochemistry & Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To compare the capillary rise behavior of water and cooking oil in identical paper towel strips, observe differences in liquid movement, and understand the role of intermolecular forces and polarity.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical paper towel strips, two transparent containers or beakers, blue-colored water, yellow cooking oil, ruler or marker (optional), flat surface, camera or smartphone fixed on a tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two transparent containers side by side on a flat surface. Pour equal volumes of blue water into the left container and yellow cooking oil into the right container.2. Setup: Cut two identical paper towel strips. Align them vertically and ensure they are the same length and width.3. Operation: Simultaneously dip the lower ends (about 1–2 cm) of each paper towel strip into the corresponding liquid, keeping the strips upright and not touching each other.4. Recording: Fix the camera focus and angle so both strips are fully visible. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.5. Observation Period: Allow the liquids to move up the paper towels for a short, accelerated observation period suitable for video capture.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both paper towels are dry above the liquid level.2. During Experiment: Blue water rises quickly and continuously up the left paper towel. Yellow oil rises more slowly and to a lower height on the right paper towel.3. Final State: A clear height difference is observed, with water reaching significantly higher than oil.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCapillary rise occurs due to the interaction between liquid molecules and the solid fibers of the paper towel. Water is a polar molecule and forms strong hydrogen bonds with the cellulose fibers, resulting in strong adhesion and cohesion, causing higher capillary rise. Cooking oil is nonpolar, has weaker intermolecular interactions with cellulose, and therefore rises more slowly and to a lesser height. This experiment demonstrates how molecular polarity and intermolecular forces affect capillary action.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Wood Surface Before and After Progressive SandingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of Wood Surface Changes After Progressive Sanding2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Archaeology (Material Analysis and Craft Techniques)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and document how progressive sanding with different grit sandpapers alters the surface texture of wood, and to understand the principle of surface modification through abrasion commonly used in archaeological artifact preparation and analysis.II. Experimental EquipmentWooden board (flat, untreated), workbench, clamp or vise, coarse-grit sandpaper (e.g., 60–80 grit), medium-grit sandpaper (e.g., 120–150 grit), fine-grit sandpaper (e.g., 220–320 grit), camera fixed on tripod, adequate lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the wooden board flat on the workbench and secure it firmly with a clamp to prevent movement. Fix the camera position and focus so the board surface remains centered throughout recording.2. Initial Observation: Record the untreated wood surface, noting visible roughness, tool marks, or grain irregularities.3. Coarse Sanding: Sand the surface evenly by hand using coarse-grit sandpaper, moving along the wood grain. Remove visible roughness and major surface irregularities.4. Medium Sanding: Switch to medium-grit sandpaper and sand the same area to reduce the deep scratches left by the coarse grit.5. Fine Sanding: Switch to fine-grit sandpaper and sand gently to further smooth the surface and refine texture.6. Final Observation: Record the final surface state after fine sanding, ensuring a clear before-and-after comparison.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before sanding: The wood surface appears rough with visible grain unevenness or tool marks.2. After coarse sanding: Large irregularities are removed, but deep scratches from coarse grit are visible.3. After medium sanding: Scratches become finer and less noticeable; the surface appears more uniform.4. After fine sanding: The surface appears smooth and even, with minimal visible scratches and enhanced grain clarity.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesProgressive sanding works on the principle of mechanical abrasion. Coarse grit sandpaper removes material quickly, leveling the surface. Medium grit reduces the depth of scratches left by coarse grit. Fine grit produces a smoother finish by removing small surface imperfections. This controlled abrasion process is essential in archaeological conservation and analysis, where surface preparation affects observation, documentation, and interpretation of wooden artifacts.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the board is firmly clamped to avoid movement; sand along the grain to prevent unnecessary scratches; maintain consistent pressure during each sanding stage.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Progressive sanding as a mechanical abrasion process that systematically modifies wood surface texture from rough to smooth. Minimum assumptions include a fixed wooden board, hand-applied sanding force, and sequential grit changes.Expected Phenomena Storyline: Phase 1 – Initial state: rough, uneven wood surface visible. Phase 2 – Coarse sanding: rapid material removal and visible deep scratches. Phase 3 – Medium sanding: reduction of scratch depth and increased uniformity. Phase 4 – Fine sanding: smooth, refined surface with clear grain. Visibility constraints require a stable camera perspective focused on the same surface area to verify causal transitions between sanding stages.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Mass–Spring System Oscillating After Being Stretched and ReleasedI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Oscillation of a Mass–Spring System After Stretching and Release2. Subject: Engineering – Systems Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the oscillatory motion of a mass–spring system when a hanging weight is pulled down from rest and released, and to relate the observed motion to system dynamics principles.II. Experimental EquipmentCeiling-mounted vertical spring, weight (mass) securely attached to the spring, stable ceiling support, hand for applying downward force, camera or phone fixed on a tripod with focus locked for time-lapse photography.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the spring is firmly mounted to the ceiling and the weight hangs freely at rest. Fix the camera position and lock focus so the entire vertical motion is in frame.2. Initial State: Allow the system to come to rest so the weight is stationary at its equilibrium position.3. Stretching: Use a hand to gently pull the weight straight downward along the vertical line of the spring, stretching the spring without sideways motion.4. Release: Hold briefly to ensure zero initial velocity, then release the weight smoothly without adding extra force.5. Recording: Let the camera record the motion as the weight oscillates up and down.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The weight is stationary, hanging vertically at equilibrium.2. After Release: The weight moves upward toward equilibrium, passes it, and continues into repeated vertical oscillations.3. Ongoing Motion: The oscillation is approximately periodic, and the amplitude may gradually decrease due to damping (air resistance and internal friction).V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the dynamics of a mass–spring system. When the spring is stretched and released, the restoring force described by Hooke’s law (F = −kx) pulls the mass back toward equilibrium. The mass overshoots due to inertia, resulting in oscillatory motion. Energy alternates between elastic potential energy in the spring and kinetic energy of the mass, with gradual energy loss due to damping.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: a vertical mass–spring system undergoing oscillatory motion after being stretched and released from rest. Minimum assumptions: a ceiling-fixed spring, a freely hanging mass, vertical motion dominated by gravity and spring restoring force, and a fixed camera viewpoint.Phased storyline: (1) static equilibrium with the mass hanging still; (2) hand pulls the mass straight downward, increasing spring extension; (3) brief pause indicating release from rest; (4) release causes upward acceleration; (5) visible vertical oscillations about equilibrium with smooth, continuous motion. Visibility constraints: the full spring and mass must remain in frame, vertical alignment must be clear, and no camera movement should obscure the causal sequence.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Effervescent Tablet Dissolving in Cold vs Hot WaterI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Bubble Rate Comparison of Effervescent Tablets in Cold and Hot Water2. Subject: Engineering - Chemical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the effect of temperature on reaction rate by comparing the dissolution and gas release rate of identical effervescent tablets in cold water and hot water through direct visual observation.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical clear glass cups; ice water (with visible ice cubes); hot water (near boiling, producing visible steam); two identical effervescent tablets; heat-resistant surface; camera or smartphone fixed on a tripod (front view); timer (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two identical clear glasses side by side on a stable surface. Pour equal volumes of ice water into the left glass and hot water into the right glass, ensuring ice cubes and steam are clearly visible.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera directly in front of the glasses, ensuring both are fully in frame. Lock focus and exposure to keep visual conditions constant for time-lapse recording.3. Core Operation: Hold one effervescent tablet above each glass. Drop both tablets into the water simultaneously.4. Observation: Record the entire process as the tablets sink, dissolve, and release bubbles. Continue recording until bubbling significantly decreases in both glasses.5. Completion: Stop recording, allow the water to cool, and safely dispose of the solution. Clean and store the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both glasses contain clear water; the cold glass shows ice cubes, while the hot glass emits visible steam.2. Immediately After Dropping Tablets: Both tablets begin to effervesce. The tablet in hot water releases bubbles rapidly and vigorously, while the tablet in cold water produces bubbles more slowly.3. During Dissolution: The hot-water tablet dissolves faster and finishes effervescing earlier; the cold-water tablet continues bubbling at a lower rate for a longer time.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleEffervescent tablets react in water to release carbon dioxide gas. Increasing temperature raises molecular kinetic energy, increasing collision frequency and reaction rate. Therefore, in hot water, the chemical reaction and gas release occur faster than in cold water, resulting in a higher bubble generation rate.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Handle hot water carefully to avoid burns.2. Use identical glasses, water volumes, and tablets to ensure a fair comparison.3. Maintain a fixed camera position and focus to ensure reliable visual comparison.4. Do not touch the glasses during the reaction to avoid disturbing the observation.

Minimum assumptions: identical tablets and containers, equal water volume, and clearly distinct temperatures.Phased Storyline: (1) Static setup with two identical glasses, one icy and one steaming, viewed from the front; (2) simultaneous tablet drop establishing a common start point; (3) rapid, vigorous bubbling in hot water versus slower bubbling in cold water; (4) earlier completion of reaction in hot water. Visibility constraints: both glasses must remain fully visible, with clear cues of temperature (ice and steam) and uninterrupted front-view perspective for causal verification.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Time-lapse Growth of Sodium Chloride Crystals from Evaporating Salt SolutionI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Time-lapse Growth of Sodium Chloride Crystals from Evaporating Salt SolutionSubject: Engineering – Materials Science & EngineeringExperiment Objective: To observe and understand the crystallization behavior of sodium chloride as water evaporates from a shallow salt solution, and to relate crystal morphology to the crystallization principle.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass dish (shallow), sodium chloride (table salt or analytical grade), distilled water, stirring rod or spoon, flat and stable surface, optional camera or time-lapse recording device.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clean, dry clear glass dish on a flat surface. Add a small amount of sodium chloride to the dish.2. Solution Making: Pour distilled water into the dish and stir gently until most of the salt dissolves, forming a clear, shallow salt solution. Ensure the liquid layer is thin.3. Evaporation Setup: Leave the dish uncovered at room temperature in a vibration-free environment. Avoid direct airflow that may disturb crystal growth.4. Observation / Recording: Allow the water to evaporate naturally. Observe continuously or record using time-lapse photography to capture crystal formation.5. Completion: When most water has evaporated and visible crystals have formed, stop the observation and document the final crystal patterns.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The solution is clear and transparent, with no visible solid crystals.During Evaporation: As water evaporates, the solution level gradually decreases. Small cubic sodium chloride crystals begin to appear, often nucleating at the edges or bottom of the dish.Final State: Well-defined, colorless, cubic crystals remain distributed across the dish after most water has evaporated.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAs water evaporates, the concentration of sodium chloride in the solution increases until it reaches supersaturation. At this point, sodium and chloride ions arrange into a regular cubic lattice, forming sodium chloride crystals. The crystal shape reflects the internal ionic structure and minimization of surface energy during growth.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse a shallow solution to ensure observable crystal growth. Avoid shaking or moving the dish during evaporation. Ensure the dish is clean to prevent impurity-induced nucleation.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Edge-Triggered D Flip-Flop Driving an LED2. Subject: Engineering – Electrical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the working principle of an edge-triggered D flip-flop by observing how an LED output responds to clock pulses from a pulse generator and changes in the D input.II. Experimental EquipmentEdge-triggered D flip-flop IC (e.g., 74HC74), breadboard, DC power supply (5 V), pulse generator (square wave output), LED with current-limiting resistor, toggle switch for D input, connecting wires, lab bench.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the breadboard on the lab bench. Insert the D flip-flop IC correctly. Connect Vcc and GND to the DC power supply. Connect the LED with a resistor to the Q output.2. Clock Connection: Connect the pulse generator output to the clock (CLK) input of the D flip-flop. Set the generator to a low-frequency square wave.3. D Input Setup: Connect the toggle switch to the D input so it can be manually set to logic high or low.4. Core Operation: Turn on the power supply and pulse generator. Flip the D toggle switch by hand to set the desired input state. Observe the LED. Then slowly turn the frequency knob of the pulse generator to increase the clock frequency.5. Completion: After observation, turn off the pulse generator and power supply, and disconnect the circuit.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The LED remains steady until a clock edge occurs.2. During Operation: Each active clock edge causes the LED to update its state according to the D input at that moment.3. Frequency Adjustment: As the clock frequency increases, the LED switches on and off more rapidly, reflecting faster clock edges.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesAn edge-triggered D flip-flop samples the D input only at a specific clock edge (rising or falling). The sampled value is stored and presented at the Q output until the next active edge. The LED visually represents the stored logic state. Increasing the clock frequency increases how often the output updates, but does not change the fundamental edge-triggered behavior.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Demonstration of Mineral Cleavage by Breaking a CrystalI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Mineral Cleavage Demonstrated by Breaking a Crystal Along Flat Planes2. Subject: Natural Science – Earth Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the property of mineral cleavage by observing how a single crystalline mineral breaks along smooth, flat planes when struck once with a small rock hammer, and to understand the structural cause of cleavage in crystalline minerals.II. Experimental EquipmentSingle crystalline mineral with clear cleavage (such as halite or calcite, 1 piece), solid flat surface (stone slab or concrete floor), small rock hammer, safety goggles, gloves (optional), camera or smartphone with fixed focus for time-lapse photography.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Put on safety goggles. Place the solid surface on a stable ground. Ensure the camera is positioned above or to the side of the surface and fix the focus and angle for continuous recording.2. Placement of Sample: Place one single crystalline mineral flat on the solid surface, ensuring it is stable and does not roll.3. Core Operation: Hold the small rock hammer firmly and strike the mineral once with moderate force from above.4. Separation: After the strike, put down the hammer and use your hands to gently separate the broken pieces of the mineral.5. Completion: Keep the broken pieces in place briefly for camera recording, then stop recording and clean the area.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The mineral is a single intact crystal with visible flat faces.2. After Striking: The mineral breaks into several pieces immediately after being struck.3. Broken Surfaces: The newly exposed surfaces are smooth and flat, forming regular planes rather than irregular fragments.4. Handling: When separated by hand, the pieces show consistent flat cleavage surfaces.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesMineral cleavage is caused by the internal atomic structure of a crystal. In crystalline minerals, atoms are arranged in a regular lattice with planes of weaker bonding. This experiment demonstrates cleavage rather than fracture, which would produce irregular surfaces.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Always wear safety goggles to prevent eye injury from flying fragments.2. Strike the mineral only once to clearly demonstrate cleavage.3. Keep hands away from the mineral during striking.4. Use a mineral known to show clear cleavage for best results.

Experiment Title: Demonstration of Delayed Dermatographic Urticaria2. Subject: Healthcare – Skin Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate and observe delayed dermatographic urticaria by applying mechanical stimulation to the skin, and to understand the physiological basis of delayed wheal formation.II. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Detection of Legionella in Water Samples by Fluorescence Colorimetric MethodSubject: Healthcare – Microbiology and ImmunologyExperiment Objective: To demonstrate the basic procedure for detecting Legionella in water samples using a fluorescence colorimetric reagent, and to understand the principle of fluorescence-based microbial detection.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Iron(III)–Thiocyanate Equilibrium Showing the Same Final Red ColorI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Iron(III)–Thiocyanate Equilibrium Showing the Same Final Red Color from Different Starting Conditions2. Subject: Chemistry – Physical and Inorganic Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate chemical equilibrium by showing that different initial concentrations of iron(III) ions and thiocyanate ions can lead to the same equilibrium state and color; to understand the concept of dynamic equilibrium and equilibrium composition.II. Experimental Equipment and Reagents1. Clear glass beakers (2, identical size)2. Iron(III) salt solution (e.g., Fe(NO3)3, dilute aqueous solution)3. Potassium thiocyanate solution (KSCN, dilute aqueous solution)4. Glass stirring rods (2) or gentle swirling by hand5. Lab bench, room-temperature environment6. Camera fixed on tripod (for time-lapse recording)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, clear beakers side by side on a lab bench. Label the left beaker as A and the right beaker as B.2. Solution Setup:   (1) Beaker A (left): Add a measured volume of iron(III) solution, then add an excess amount of thiocyanate solution.   (2) Beaker B (right): Add a measured volume of thiocyanate solution, then add an excess amount of iron(III) solution.3. Mixing: Gently swirl each beaker for several seconds to ensure uniform mixing of the solutions.4. Standing: Place both beakers undisturbed at room temperature and allow them to stand.5. Observation Recording: Fix the camera focus and record the process, observing the color changes over time until the solutions appear stable.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before mixing, both solutions are pale yellow or colorless and transparent.2. After Mixing: Upon swirling, both beakers quickly develop a red coloration due to complex formation.3. After Standing: After a short time, the color in both beakers stabilizes to a similar deep red, even though the initial reactant in excess is different.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on the reversible equilibrium reaction:Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq)The FeSCN²⁺ complex has a characteristic red color. According to the law of chemical equilibrium, the final equilibrium state depends on temperature and equilibrium constant, not on the initial concentrations alone. Although the two systems start with different excess reactants, both adjust through the forward and reverse reactions until the same equilibrium ratio of species is reached, resulting in the same final red color.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use dilute solutions to ensure clear observation of color changes.2. Ensure beakers are identical and clean to avoid visual bias.3. Swirl gently to avoid splashing and ensure uniform mixing.4. Dispose of iron-containing waste according to laboratory regulations.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Cantilever Beam with Tip Load Bending DemonstrationSubject: Engineering – Structural EngineeringObjective: To observe the deformation of a cantilever beam under a gradually increasing tip load, understand smooth curvature and rotation of cross-sections, and relate observed behavior to basic beam bending theory.II. Experimental EquipmentStriped thin plastic ruler (uniform thickness), rigid clamp or vise, flat table, small calibrated weights (or coins), string or hook for attaching weights, camera or smartphone with tripod, ruler or scale (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clamp securely on the edge of a table. Insert one end of the plastic ruler into the clamp and tighten firmly so that the ruler extends horizontally outward, forming a cantilever. Ensure the ruler is level and not pre-bent.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera perpendicular to the side of the ruler. Fix the focus and framing so the entire ruler is visible. Do not move the camera during the experiment.3. Initial State Recording: Record or photograph the undeformed ruler with no load applied at the free end.4. Loading Process: Gently attach a small weight to the free tip of the ruler. Wait briefly for the ruler to reach a stable shape, then record the deformation. Add additional small weights one by one at the same location, recording after each addition.5. Completion: After reaching a clear bending state, stop loading. Carefully remove the weights and unclamp the ruler.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The ruler remains straight and horizontal when no load is applied.2. With Small Load: The free end deflects downward slightly, and the ruler begins to curve smoothly.3. With Increasing Load: The downward deflection increases progressively; the curvature becomes more pronounced, with the largest curvature near the fixed end. Cross-sections rotate gradually without sharp kinks.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleA cantilever beam fixed at one end and loaded at the free tip experiences bending due to the applied moment. According to elementary beam theory, the bending moment is maximum at the fixed end and zero at the free end, producing a smooth curvature along the beam. The deformation increases with load magnitude, and beam cross-sections rotate while remaining approximately plane, demonstrating elastic bending behavior.

manual: Sucrase Activity Detection (Sucrose Hydrolysis Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Detection of Sucrase Activity by Sucrose HydrolysisSubject: Healthcare – Digestive PhysiologyObjective: To demonstrate the digestive function of sucrase by comparing the hydrolysis of sucrose by active and heat-inactivated sucrase, using Benedict reagent to detect reducing sugars.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tubes (2), test tube rack, dropper or pipette, water bath (37°C), beaker, heat source (hot plate or alcohol lamp), sucrose solution, active sucrase solution, heat-inactivated sucrase solution, Benedict reagent, marker or labels.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean test tubes on the rack and label them Tube A (active sucrase) and Tube B (inactivated sucrase, control).2. Substrate Addition: Add an equal volume of sucrose solution to both test tubes.3. Enzyme Addition: Add active sucrase solution to Tube A; add heat-inactivated sucrase solution to Tube B.4. Incubation: Place both tubes into a warm water bath maintained at 37°C and incubate for a short period (time-lapse or accelerated demonstration).5. Detection: Remove the tubes from the water bath. Add an equal volume of Benedict reagent to each tube and mix gently.6. Heating: Heat both tubes gently until the solution color stabilizes, then place them back on the rack for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both tubes contain colorless or light-blue solutions after Benedict reagent addition.After Heating: Tube A shows a distinct color change (green, yellow, or orange-red precipitate), indicating the presence of reducing sugars. Tube B shows little or no color change and remains blue.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSucrase is a digestive enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of sucrose into glucose and fructose, both of which are reducing sugars. Benedict reagent reacts with reducing sugars under heating conditions to produce a color change. Active sucrase hydrolyzes sucrose, resulting in a positive Benedict test, while heat-inactivated sucrase lacks enzymatic activity and serves as a negative control.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure equal volumes of solutions in both tubes; maintain the water bath at approximately 37°C; heat gently to avoid boiling or splashing; label tubes clearly to avoid confusion.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Cooling Humid Air vs Dry Air in Clear Chambers Causing Earlier Condensation2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that humid air reaches saturation and condenses earlier than dry air under the same cooling conditions, and to understand the role of water vapor content in atmospheric condensation phenomena such as cloud and fog formation.II. Experimental Equipment1. Two identical transparent sealed chambers (same volume and material)2. Red band or label (for the left chamber)3. Blue band or label (for the right chamber)4. Steam source (electric kettle or steam generator)5. Cooling source (ice packs, cold plate, or refrigerated surface)6. Thermometer or temperature sensor (optional, for reference)7. Camera with fixed focus and tripod (for time-lapse photography)8. Timer or clockIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   (1) Place two identical clear sealed chambers side by side on a flat surface; label the left chamber with a red band and the right chamber with a blue band.   (2) Ensure both chambers are initially clean, dry, and at the same room temperature.   (3) Set up the camera on a tripod facing both chambers; adjust framing so both chambers are fully visible and fix the focus. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.2. Humidity Setup:   (1) Open the red-banded left chamber briefly and inject visible steam into it until the inner air appears humid but not filled with liquid water droplets.   (2) Quickly seal the red chamber to prevent vapor loss.   (3) Keep the blue-banded right chamber sealed with dry air inside and do not inject steam.3. Cooling Operation:   (1) Place both sealed chambers simultaneously onto the same cooling source, or surround them evenly with ice packs to ensure equal cooling conditions.   (2) Do not move or disturb the chambers during cooling.   (3) Continue recording as the temperature of both chambers decreases.4. Observation and Completion:   (1) Observe the inner walls of both chambers during cooling.   (2) When clear condensation phenomena appear, continue recording briefly for comparison.   (3) Stop recording, remove the cooling source, and end the experiment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both chambers are transparent and clear; no condensation is visible on the inner walls.2. During Cooling:   (1) In the red-banded (humid) chamber, tiny water droplets or mist appear on the inner wall earlier.   (2) The droplets gradually increase in number and may merge into visible water films.   (3) In the blue-banded (dry) chamber, the inner wall remains clear for a longer time, with condensation appearing later or being much weaker.3. Final Comparison: Under the same cooling conditions, condensation occurs earlier and more obviously in the humid (red) chamber than in the dry (blue) chamber.V. Summary of Experimental Principle1. Core Principle:   Air contains water vapor. When air is cooled to its dew point temperature, water vapor condenses into liquid droplets.2. Principle Analysis:   The red chamber contains humid air with a higher water vapor content, so it reaches saturation sooner during cooling and condenses earlier. The blue chamber contains dry air with lower water vapor content, requiring further cooling to reach saturation. This demonstrates that higher humidity leads to earlier condensation under identical cooling conditions.3. Atmospheric Significance:   This principle explains natural phenomena such as why clouds, fog, and dew form more readily in humid environments.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both chambers are identical and cooled simultaneously to maintain fair comparison.2. Avoid introducing liquid water droplets directly when injecting steam; only humid air is required.3. Keep the camera focus fixed to ensure valid time-lapse comparison.4. Handle hot steam and cold sources carefully to avoid burns or frostbite.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Humid air condenses earlier than dry air when cooled due to higher water vapor content reaching saturation sooner. Minimum assumptions: two identical sealed chambers, different humidity levels, identical cooling conditions. Expected storyline: Phase 1 – both clear chambers shown side by side, labeled red (left) and blue (right). Phase 2 – steam added only to red chamber while blue remains dry. Phase 3 – both chambers cooled simultaneously. Phase 4 – condensation appears first and more strongly in the red chamber, while the blue chamber lags or shows weaker condensation. Visibility constraints: inner chamber walls must be clearly visible throughout to verify timing and intensity differences.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Rotating a Wire Loop Between Magnet Poles (Electromagnetic Induction)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Rotating a Rectangular Wire Loop Between the Poles of a Horseshoe Magnet2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics (Electromagnetism)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate electromagnetic induction by observing induced current when a rectangular wire loop rotates steadily between the north and south poles of a fixed horseshoe magnet, and to understand the relationship between changing magnetic flux and induced current.II. Experimental EquipmentHorseshoe magnet (fixed, clearly marked N and S poles), rectangular wire loop (conductive copper wire, insulated except at terminals), rotation shaft or hand-driven handle, connecting wires, analog galvanometer (center-zero preferred), stable stand or clamp, camera or mobile device fixed on a tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fix the horseshoe magnet on the stand so that the north and south poles face each other with a clear air gap. Place the rectangular wire loop between the poles so it can rotate freely about its central axis. Ensure all equipment is stable.2. Circuit Connection: Connect the two ends of the wire loop to the terminals of the analog galvanometer using connecting wires, forming a closed circuit. Check that the galvanometer pointer rests at zero when the loop is stationary.3. Camera Setup: Fix the camera on a tripod facing the magnet–coil–galvanometer system. Adjust focus so that the wire loop, magnet poles, and galvanometer pointer are all clearly visible. Do not change focus during recording.4. Core Operation: Rotate the wire loop steadily at a uniform speed using the handle or shaft, keeping the rotation axis perpendicular to the magnetic field between the poles.5. Observation: Observe the deflection of the galvanometer pointer as the loop rotates. Continue rotating for several cycles to confirm repeatability.6. Completion: Stop the rotation and observe the galvanometer pointer returning to zero. Turn off recording and disconnect the circuit.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: When the wire loop is stationary, the galvanometer pointer stays at zero.2. During Rotation: As the wire loop rotates between the magnet poles, the galvanometer pointer deflects alternately to the left and right, indicating the presence of an induced current whose direction changes periodically.3. After Stopping: When rotation stops, the galvanometer pointer returns to zero, showing that induced current only exists when magnetic flux changes.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on Faraday’s law of electromagnetic induction. When the rectangular wire loop rotates in the magnetic field between the north and south poles of the horseshoe magnet, the magnetic flux through the loop changes continuously. A changing magnetic flux induces an electromotive force in the loop, producing an induced current. The direction of the induced current changes as the direction of flux change reverses, which is reflected by the alternating deflection of the galvanometer pointer. When there is no change in magnetic flux, no induced current is generated.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure firm electrical connections to avoid false readings.2. Rotate the loop steadily; irregular motion may cause unclear galvanometer deflections.3. Avoid touching the magnet poles together, which may reduce magnet strength.4. Keep the camera fixed to ensure clear time-lapse observation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: electromagnetic induction caused by changing magnetic flux. Minimum assumptions: a fixed magnetic field between N and S poles, a conductive rectangular loop, and a closed circuit with an analog galvanometer. The loop must rotate steadily to ensure continuous flux change.Expected phased storyline: (1) Static setup phase: magnet fixed, loop stationary, galvanometer at zero. (2) Action phase: loop begins steady rotation within the magnetic field. (3) Phenomenon phase: galvanometer pointer deflects alternately as rotation continues, indicating induced current with changing direction. (4) End phase: rotation stops and the pointer returns to zero. Visibility constraints: camera must clearly show the magnet poles, rotating loop, and galvanometer pointer simultaneously to verify causal relationships.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Comparison of Bulb Brightness Using Copper Wire and Iron WireI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Bulb Brightness Using Copper Wire and Iron Wire of the Same Length2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics3. Experiment Objective: To verify that, under identical conditions, a bulb connected with a copper wire is brighter than one connected with an iron wire, and to understand the effect of conductor resistance on current and brightness.II. Experimental EquipmentBattery (1 dry cell or low-voltage power supply), small bulb with holder, switch, copper wire (fixed length), iron wire (same length as copper wire), connecting leads, insulating base.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the battery, switch, and bulb on the insulating base. Ensure the power supply voltage is the same throughout the experiment.2. Circuit Setup with Copper Wire: Connect the battery, switch, bulb, and copper wire in series to form a complete circuit. Ensure all connections are firm and the wiring order is correct.3. Operation: Close the switch and observe the brightness of the bulb. Keep the circuit closed only briefly to avoid overheating.4. Replacement with Iron Wire: Open the switch. Remove the copper wire and replace it with the iron wire of the same length, keeping all other components and connections unchanged.5. Second Observation: Close the switch again and observe the brightness of the bulb.6. Comparison: Compare the brightness of the bulb in the two cases under identical conditions.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. When the copper wire is connected and the switch is closed, the bulb lights up brightly.2. When the iron wire of the same length is connected under the same conditions, the bulb lights up but is noticeably dimmer.3. The brightness difference is obvious and stable during observation.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleDifferent materials have different electrical resistances. Copper has a lower resistivity than iron. For wires of the same length and thickness, the copper wire has smaller resistance, allowing a larger current to flow through the circuit. A larger current causes the bulb to emit more light, making it brighter. The iron wire has higher resistance, resulting in a smaller current and a dimmer bulb.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Substitution Reaction of BromoethaneSubject: Natural Science – Chemistry (Organic Chemistry)Experiment Objective: To verify that bromoethane undergoes a nucleophilic substitution reaction with aqueous sodium hydroxide to produce ethanol and bromide ions, and to confirm the presence of bromide ions by reaction with silver nitrate after acidification.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsEquipment: Test tube, test tube rack, test tube holder, alcohol lamp or hot water bath, dropper, beaker, thermometer (optional).Reagents: Bromoethane (colorless liquid), sodium hydroxide aqueous solution, dilute nitric acid, silver nitrate solution.Safety: Wear goggles; bromoethane is volatile and flammable, heating should be done in a water bath.III. Experimental Procedure1. Add about 2 mL of sodium hydroxide aqueous solution into a clean test tube, then add 1 mL of bromoethane.2. Remove the test tube and allow it to cool to room temperature.4. Add a few drops of dilute nitric acid to the cooled solution to acidify it, removing excess hydroxide ions.5. Summary of Experimental PrincipleBromoethane reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide under heating via a nucleophilic substitution reaction, where the bromine atom is replaced by a hydroxyl group, forming ethanol and bromide ions.Core reaction: C2H5Br + NaOH(aq) → C2H5OH + NaBr.After cooling, nitric acid is added to neutralize excess hydroxide ions, preventing interference. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Simulation Experiment of Liquefiable Sand Reinforcement with Stone ColumnsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Simulation Experiment of Liquefiable Sand Reinforcement with Stone Columns2. Subject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To simulate sand liquefaction under vibration and demonstrate the reinforcement effect of stone columns by visually comparing deformation behaviors of reinforced and unreinforced saturated loose sand.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent container A (1), transparent container B (1), loose sand, water supply, stone column model (gravel-filled cylindrical column), vibration table, fixing clamps, measuring scale (optional), camera for focused and time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place containers A and B side by side. Fill both with loose sand. Slowly add water until the sand is fully saturated and water level is just above the sand surface.2. Reinforcement Setup: Insert a stone column vertically into the center of container A, ensuring firm contact with the sand. Container B remains without reinforcement.3. Fixing: Secure both containers firmly onto the vibration table to prevent sliding during vibration.4. Vibration Loading: Start the vibration table and apply uniform vibration for a short, accelerated duration suitable for demonstration.5. Observation and Recording: Use a focused camera to record the process in time-lapse mode, observing sand deformation, settlement, and lateral movement in both containers.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both containers show saturated loose sand with no visible deformation; the stone column in container A is stable.2. During Vibration: In container B, sand exhibits significant settlement, surface lowering, and lateral deformation, indicating liquefaction-like behavior. In container A, deformation is noticeably smaller and more localized around the stone column.3. Final State: After vibration stops, container B shows larger overall deformation, while container A maintains better structural integrity with reduced settlement.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleUnder vibration, saturated loose sand tends to develop excess pore water pressure, reducing effective stress and leading to liquefaction and large deformation. Stone columns act as reinforcement by increasing stiffness, improving drainage, and redistributing stress, thereby reducing pore pressure buildup and limiting deformation. This experiment visually demonstrates the effectiveness of stone columns in liquefiable sand reinforcement.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Protein Precipitation by Salt AdditionI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Salt-Induced Protein Precipitation in Cell-Free Microbial CultureSubject: Natural Science – MicrobiologyObjective: To demonstrate that increasing ionic strength with concentrated salt causes dissolved proteins to precipitate, forming visible solids that settle from solution.II. Materials and EquipmentClear glass beaker (250 mL); cell-free microbial culture (clarified supernatant, transparent); concentrated salt solution (e.g., saturated ammonium sulfate or sodium chloride); glass stirring rod or magnetic stirrer; pipette or dropper; lab bench; camera fixed for time-lapse recording; safety gloves and goggles.III. Salt Addition: While stirring, slowly add the concentrated salt solution dropwise along the inner wall of the beaker to avoid turbulence.4. Mixing Completion: Continue gentle stirring for several seconds to evenly distribute the salt.5. Resting Stage: Stop stirring completely. Leave the beaker undisturbed on the bench. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Benedict’s Test on Glucose Solution Heated in a Water BathI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Benedict’s Test on Glucose Solution (Reducing Sugar Reaction)2. Subject: Healthcare – Medicine (Biochemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To detect the presence of reducing sugar (glucose) by observing the color change of Benedict’s reagent after heating in a water bath, and to understand the principle of redox reactions between reducing sugars and copper(II) ions.II. Experimental EquipmentTest tubes (2), test tube rack, glucose solution, distilled water, Benedict’s reagent (blue), dropper or pipette, beaker for water bath, hot plate or heating source, thermometer (optional), safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean test tubes on a rack. Add an equal volume (about 2 mL) of glucose solution to the first test tube and the same volume of distilled water to the second test tube as a control.2. Reagent Addition: Using a dropper, add an equal volume (about 2 mL) of Benedict’s reagent to each test tube. Gently shake to mix. Both solutions should appear blue initially.3. Heating: Place both test tubes into a beaker containing hot water (water bath). Heat them together for several minutes, ensuring the water level is above the liquid level inside the test tubes. Maintain gentle heating.4. Observation: Keep the test tubes in the water bath and observe changes in color and precipitate formation. The camera focus should remain fixed for time-lapse recording.5. Completion: After sufficient heating, remove the test tubes carefully and place them back on the rack for final observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both test tubes contain clear blue solutions.2. During Heating: The glucose-containing tube gradually changes color from blue to green, yellow, orange, or brick-red, with a visible precipitate forming. The water control tube remains blue with no precipitate.3. Final State: A colored precipitate is present only in the glucose tube, while the control shows no significant change.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleBenedict’s test is based on a redox reaction. Glucose is a reducing sugar that can reduce Cu²⁺ ions in Benedict’s reagent to Cu⁺ ions when heated in alkaline conditions. The Cu⁺ ions form insoluble copper(I) oxide (Cu₂O), which appears as a colored precipitate ranging from green to brick-red depending on glucose concentration. Distilled water lacks reducing sugars and therefore does not cause any color change.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure equal volumes of solutions and reagent for accurate comparison.2. Heating must be done in a water bath, not directly over a flame.3. Handle hot glassware carefully to avoid burns.4. Dispose of chemical waste according to laboratory safety guidelines.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Golf Driver Tee-Off Demonstration2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Sport (Golf)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the standard process and principles of using a driver club to tee off from the tee box, observe the flight of the golf ball traveling approximately 250 yards, and understand how correct technique and physical principles enable the ball to land in the center of the fairway.II. Experimental Equipment1. Driver golf club (standard 1-wood driver).2. Golf ball (regulation size and color: white).3. Tee (plastic or wooden, appropriate height for driver).4. Tee box area (flat, marked starting area).5. Golf fairway (open field with visible center line or target area).6. Optional: Golf glove, golf shoes.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the golf ball on the tee in the tee box, ensuring the ball sits slightly above the clubface height. The player stands with feet shoulder-width apart, body aligned parallel to the target fairway center.2. Grip and Stance: The player grips the driver with both hands using a neutral grip. Knees are slightly bent, spine tilted slightly away from the target, and eyes focused on the ball.3. Backswing: The player rotates the shoulders and hips smoothly, bringing the driver back in a wide arc while maintaining balance and head stability.4. Downswing and Impact: The player shifts weight from the back foot to the front foot, accelerates the club downward, and strikes the ball squarely with the center of the clubface.5. Follow-Through: After impact, the club continues forward and upward, with the player’s body facing the target and weight mostly on the front foot.6. Completion: The player holds the finish position briefly and observes the ball’s flight and landing position.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The golf ball is stationary on the tee at the tee box.2. At Impact: A clear striking sound is heard as the driver contacts the ball, and the ball rapidly accelerates upward and forward.3. Ball Flight: The ball follows a high, arcing trajectory, traveling approximately 250 yards downrange.4. Landing Result: The ball lands and rolls slightly, stopping near the center of the fairway.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Mechanics Principle: The driver’s large clubhead and long shaft generate high clubhead speed, transferring kinetic energy to the ball at impact.2. Projectile Motion: After impact, the golf ball behaves as a projectile influenced by initial velocity, launch angle, gravity, and air resistance.3. Skill and Control: Proper grip, stance, swing path, and timing ensure efficient energy transfer and directional control, allowing the ball to travel long distance and land accurately in the fairway center.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the tee box area is clear of people before swinging.2. Maintain balance and controlled motion to prevent injury.3. Use appropriate equipment suited to the player’s skill level.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Golf driver tee-off demonstrating how correct swing mechanics and physical principles produce a long, accurate drive. Minimum assumptions: a regulation driver, a teed golf ball, a clear tee box, and an open fairway.Phased storyline: (1) Setup phase – ball on tee, player aligned toward fairway center; (2) Action phase – backswing, downswing, and solid impact creating a clear cause for ball acceleration; (3) Flight phase – high, arcing projectile motion consistent with a 250-yard drive; (4) Result phase – ball lands and settles in the center of the fairway. Visibility should allow clear observation of stance, impact moment, continuous ball flight, and final landing position.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Observation of Sandy Soil Sedimentation in WaterI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Sedimentation of Sandy Soil in Clear WaterSubject: Engineering – Agricultural EngineeringExperiment Objective: To observe the sedimentation behavior of sandy soil in water and verify that, after standing, sand settles at the bottom while clear water remains above, forming a clear stratification boundary.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent container (glass beaker or plastic cup), clear water, sandy soil (dry and loose), stirring rod (glass or plastic).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the transparent container on a stable surface and fill it with clear water to about two-thirds of its volume.2. Adding Soil: Gently add an appropriate amount of sandy soil into the container.3. Stirring: Use the stirring rod to stir the mixture evenly until the sandy soil is fully suspended in the water.4. Standing: Stop stirring and leave the container undisturbed for about 10 seconds.5. Observation: Observe the changes in the mixture during standing.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Immediately after stirring, the water becomes turbid due to suspended sand particles.2. After standing for a short time, sandy soil gradually settles to the bottom of the container.3. A clear layer of water appears on the top, with a distinct boundary between the clear water and the sand layer.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the physical process of sedimentation. Sandy soil particles are relatively large and dense, so when stirring stops, gravity causes them to settle quickly at the bottom of the container. Water remains above, forming a clear stratified structure. This principle is important in agricultural engineering for understanding soil–water separation and sediment behavior.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Physical sedimentation of sandy soil in water under gravity, assuming normal gravity, transparent observation conditions, and no chemical reactions. Minimum assumptions include a clear liquid, insoluble sandy particles, and a short standing time. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) Initial state with clear water in a transparent container; (2) Sand addition and stirring cause uniform turbidity; (3) Stirring stops, removing kinetic support; (4) During standing, sand settles downward due to gravity; (5) Final state shows clear water on top and a sand layer at the bottom with a visible boundary. The camera should maintain a stable perspective focused on the container to clearly verify each phase and the causal transition from stirring to sedimentation.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Wagon-Wheel Aliasing in a Rotating Bicycle WheelI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Rotating Spoked Bicycle Wheel Filmed at Low vs High Frame Rate (Wagon-Wheel Aliasing)2. Subject: Natural Science – Physics (Optics and Motion Perception)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the wagon-wheel aliasing phenomenon by filming a steadily rotating bicycle wheel with evenly spaced spokes at different camera frame rates, and to understand how discrete sampling in time affects the perceived direction and speed of rotation.II. Experimental Equipment1. Bicycle with an evenly spoked wheel (front wheel preferred, 24–36 evenly spaced spokes).2. Bicycle stand or method to lift the wheel so it can rotate freely.3. Camera or smartphone capable of recording video at adjustable frame rates (e.g., 10–15 fps and 60 fps or higher).4. Tripod or fixed mount to keep the camera position stable.5. Uniform background and adequate lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   (1) Mount the bicycle securely so the selected wheel can rotate freely without moving the bicycle frame.   (2) Place the camera on a tripod directly facing the wheel from the side, ensuring the entire wheel is visible.   (3) Manually adjust and fix the camera focus on the plane of the wheel; disable autofocus to keep focus constant.2. Low Frame Rate Recording:   (1) Set the camera to a low frame rate (e.g., 10–15 frames per second).   (2) Rotate the wheel steadily at a constant speed by hand or with a simple motor.   (3) Record a short video (3–5 seconds) while maintaining constant wheel speed and camera position.3. High Frame Rate Recording:   (1) Without changing the wheel speed, camera position, or focus, adjust the camera to a higher frame rate (e.g., 60 fps or above).   (2) Record another short video of the rotating wheel for the same duration.4. Completion:   (1) Stop the wheel safely.   (2) Save and label both videos clearly as low frame rate and high frame rate recordings.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Low Frame Rate Video:   (1) The wheel may appear to rotate slowly, stop, or even rotate backward, despite actually rotating forward.   (2) The spokes may seem to jump between positions rather than move smoothly.2. High Frame Rate Video:   (1) The wheel rotation appears smooth and continuous.   (2) The direction of rotation is correctly perceived, matching the real motion of the wheel.3. Comparison:   (1) The apparent difference in motion arises even though the wheel speed and camera position are identical.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. This experiment demonstrates temporal aliasing, commonly known as the wagon-wheel effect.2. A camera records motion by sampling images at discrete time intervals (frame rate).3. When the frame rate is too low compared with the rotational speed of evenly spaced spokes, successive frames capture similar spoke positions, leading the brain to misinterpret the motion.4. At higher frame rates, the sampling interval is shorter, so the true continuous motion and correct rotation direction are accurately represented.5. This phenomenon illustrates the relationship between sampling frequency, motion speed, and perceived motion in physics and signal processing.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: temporal aliasing (wagon-wheel effect) arising from discrete time sampling of periodic motion. Minimum assumptions: a rigid bicycle wheel with evenly spaced spokes rotates steadily; the camera samples motion at fixed, known frame rates with a fixed viewpoint and focus. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) establish a clear side view of a steadily rotating spoked wheel; (2) at low frame rate, successive samples capture similar spoke positions, causing apparent slowing, stopping, or reversal; (3) without changing wheel speed or viewpoint, increase frame rate; (4) higher sampling resolves intermediate positions, revealing smooth, correctly directed rotation. Verification requires a stable camera perspective, visible spokes, and a clear before–after comparison tied causally to frame rate change.

manual: Instructions for the Art Experiment Eye-Level Perspective Using a Horizon LineI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Eye-Level Perspective Construction Using a Horizon Line2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Visual Arts)3. Experiment Objective: To understand the concept of the horizon line as eye level, recognize that all vanishing points lie on the horizon line, and learn how one-point and two-point perspective are constructed by drawing objects whose edges converge toward vanishing points.II. Experimental MaterialsWhite drawing paper (1 sheet), pencil, ruler, eraser, marker or darker pen (optional for final lines).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the paper flat on the table. Imagine the observer standing upright and looking straight ahead.2. Drawing the Horizon Line: Use a ruler to draw a straight horizontal line across the paper. Label it Horizon Line. Explain that this line represents the observer’s eye level.3. One-Point Perspective Construction:   a. Mark a single point at the center of the horizon line and label it Vanishing Point.   b. Draw the front face of a simple box below the horizon line.   c. Use the ruler to draw straight lines from the corners of the box toward the vanishing point.   d. Close the box by drawing vertical and horizontal lines, forming a three-dimensional box.   e. Draw a straight road by sketching two lines from the bottom of the page converging toward the same vanishing point.4. Two-Point Perspective Construction:   a. Add a second vanishing point on the horizon line, far from the first one.   b. Draw a vertical edge of a box below the horizon line.   c. Draw the left edges of the box converging toward the left vanishing point and the right edges converging toward the right vanishing point.   d. Complete the box form.5. Finishing: Darken correct lines and erase construction lines if necessary.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The paper is blank except for a horizontal horizon line.2. One-Point Perspective: All depth lines of the box and road converge toward the single vanishing point on the horizon line, creating a sense of depth.3. Two-Point Perspective: The box appears rotated, with its left and right edges converging toward two different vanishing points on the same horizon line.4. Overall Effect: Objects appear smaller as they recede toward the horizon, clearly demonstrating eye-level perspective.V. When parallel edges of objects recede into space, they visually converge toward a vanishing point.
