manual: Instructions for the Experiment "DAC Feeding RC Filter Driving LED with Gradual Rise/Fall"I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: DAC Feeding RC Filter Driving LED with Gradual Rise/Fall2. Subject: Engineering – Mechatronics & Robotics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how a microcontroller digital-to-analog converter (DAC) outputs a changing voltage signal, how an RC low-pass filter smooths the signal, and how this filtered analog voltage drives an LED to show gradual brightness rise and fall. The experiment also aims to visually record the process using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentMicrocontroller development board with DAC output (e.g., Arduino with DAC or STM32 board), RC low-pass filter components (resistor 1–10 kΩ, capacitor 10–100 µF), LED (any visible color), current-limiting resistor (220–1 kΩ), breadboard, jumper wires, USB cable, computer with programming environment, camera or smartphone with tripod for time-lapse recording, stable workbench power supply (if required).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the microcontroller board, breadboard, and components neatly on the workbench. Fix the camera on a tripod facing the setup, adjust framing to include the LED and circuit, and lock the focus to avoid refocusing during recording.2. Circuit Assembly: Connect the DAC output pin of the microcontroller to the resistor of the RC filter. Connect the capacitor from the resistor output to ground, forming an RC low-pass filter. Connect the filtered output to the LED in series with a current-limiting resistor, then to ground.3. Program Upload: Write and upload a program that continuously updates the DAC output value in a loop (for example, linearly increasing from minimum to maximum, then decreasing), with a short delay between steps.4. Core Operation: Power the microcontroller via USB. Start the program so the DAC outputs a slowly changing voltage. Begin time-lapse recording with the camera while ensuring the setup remains undisturbed.5. Completion: Allow the system to run for several cycles of brightness change. Stop the recording, then power down the circuit and disconnect components.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: When powered on, the LED is either off or very dim, depending on the initial DAC value.2. During Operation: As the DAC output voltage increases, the RC filter smooths the step changes, and the LED brightness gradually increases rather than changing abruptly.3. Reverse Process: When the DAC value decreases, the RC filter causes the LED brightness to gradually fade, showing a smooth fall instead of an instant off state.4. Overall Effect: Over time, the LED shows a continuous breathing-like effect of smooth rise and fall in brightness.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on digital-to-analog conversion and analog signal filtering. The microcontroller DAC converts digital values into corresponding analog voltages. Because the DAC output updates in steps, an RC low-pass filter is used to smooth these steps by charging and discharging the capacitor gradually. The filtered voltage drives the LED, and since LED brightness depends on current and voltage, the gradual voltage change results in a smooth brightness transition. The experiment visually demonstrates signal smoothing and basic analog behavior in mechatronic systems.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the LED has a proper current-limiting resistor to prevent damage.2. Check all wiring before powering the circuit to avoid short circuits.3. Keep the camera fixed and focused throughout the recording to ensure consistent visual comparison.4. Do not touch the circuit during operation to avoid disturbing the time-lapse recording.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Soap Film Illuminated by White Light Showing Shifting Color BandsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Soap Film Illuminated by White Light Showing Shifting Color Bands2. Subject: Physics – Optics (Thin-Film Interference)3. Experiment Objective: To observe interference color bands produced by a soap film under white light, understand the relationship between film thickness and observed color, and recognize how gravity-driven drainage and frame tilting affect the interference pattern.II. Experimental EquipmentRectangular wire frame, soap solution (water with detergent or glycerin), shallow tray or beaker for soap solution, steady white light source (lamp or LED), dark or neutral background, support stand or hand grip for holding the frame.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Pour the soap solution into the tray. Ensure the white light source is steady and positioned to illuminate the frame uniformly from the front or side. Use a dark background to enhance color visibility.2. Forming the Soap Film: Dip the rectangular wire frame fully into the soap solution, then slowly lift it out to form a uniform soap film spanning the frame.3. Vertical Placement: Hold or mount the frame vertically so that gravity causes the liquid in the film to drain downward.4. Illumination: Illuminate the soap film continuously with the steady white light. Avoid changing the light position or intensity during observation.5. Gentle Tilting: Slowly and gently tilt the frame by a small angle while keeping it vertical overall, and continue observing the film as it drains.6. Observation and Completion: Observe the changes in color bands over time. After observation, allow the film to break naturally or rinse the frame with water and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Immediately after forming, the soap film appears mostly transparent with faint or irregular colors.2. During Drainage: As the film drains under gravity, distinct horizontal or curved color bands appear and gradually shift position, often moving downward.3. During Tilting: Gentle tilting causes the color bands to deform or shift direction slightly, reflecting changes in local film thickness.4. Final Stage: Very thin regions may appear dark or black before the film breaks.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe observed colors arise from thin-film interference. When white light reflects from the front and back surfaces of the soap film, the two reflected waves interfere. The path difference depends on the local thickness of the film. Different thicknesses enhance or cancel different wavelengths, producing shifting color bands. As gravity causes the film to drain and thin unevenly, and as tilting redistributes the liquid, the interference conditions change, leading to dynamic color patterns.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use steady white light; colored or flickering light will affect observations.2. Avoid rapid movements or strong air currents that may rupture the film.3. Handle the wire frame gently to maintain a uniform film.4. Clean the frame after use to ensure consistent results in future experiments.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Fluorescence Microscopy of Live GFP-Expressing CellsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Fluorescence Microscopy of Live GFP-Expressing Cells with Excitation Light Switching2. Subject: Engineering – Biomedical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe live cells expressing green fluorescent protein (GFP) under a fluorescence microscope, understand how blue excitation light controls GFP fluorescence, and compare fluorescence images with transmitted-light images of the same field.II. Experimental EquipmentInverted or upright fluorescence microscope; blue excitation light source (≈470–490 nm); GFP filter set (excitation, dichroic mirror, emission); transmitted-light illumination (bright-field or phase-contrast); live GFP-expressing cells cultured on a glass-bottom dish or slide; objective lens (20×–40×); camera and imaging software; cell culture medium; stage incubator (optional, for temperature/CO₂ control).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Turn on the microscope, camera, and computer; allow light sources to stabilize. Place the live GFP-expressing cell sample on the microscope stage and secure it.2. Transmitted-Light Imaging: Select transmitted-light mode. Focus on the cells to obtain a clear image of cell morphology. Adjust focus and field of view; record or observe the image.3. Fluorescence Imaging (Excitation ON): Switch to the GFP fluorescence channel. Turn on the blue excitation light. Adjust focus and exposure to avoid overexposure. Observe green fluorescence from GFP-expressing cells.4. Excitation OFF: Turn off the blue excitation light while keeping the same field of view. Observe that the green fluorescence signal disappears or becomes very dim.5. Alternating Observation: Alternate between transmitted-light mode and fluorescence mode (excitation ON/OFF) several times to confirm that fluorescence depends on excitation light and that the same cells are observed.6. End of Experiment: Turn off excitation light, remove the sample, save images, and shut down the microscope according to standard procedures.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Transmitted-Light Mode: Cells appear colorless or gray with visible morphology and boundaries; no fluorescence is observed.2. Fluorescence Mode (Excitation ON): Cells expressing GFP emit bright green fluorescence in the same locations as observed under transmitted light.3. Excitation OFF: Green fluorescence rapidly disappears, while the transmitted-light appearance of cells remains unchanged.4. Repeated Switching: Fluorescence repeatedly appears and disappears in sync with the excitation light being turned on and off.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesGFP is a fluorescent protein that absorbs blue light and emits green light. When blue excitation light illuminates live GFP-expressing cells, GFP molecules are excited and emit green fluorescence. When the excitation light is turned off, emission stops immediately. Transmitted-light microscopy relies on light passing through cells to reveal morphology and does not depend on fluorescence. Alternating between these modes demonstrates the excitation–emission principle of fluorescence microscopy and confirms that observed fluorescence originates from GFP within live cells.VI. Experimental PrecautionsAvoid prolonged excitation to reduce photobleaching and phototoxicity; keep cells in appropriate culture conditions; do not change the field of view when switching modes; use appropriate exposure settings to prevent saturation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Fluorescence microscopy of live GFP-expressing cells demonstrating excitation-dependent emission. Minimum assumptions: presence of live cells expressing GFP, a fluorescence microscope with blue excitation and transmitted-light modes, and a stable field of view.Expected phased storyline: (1) Begin with transmitted-light imaging showing non-fluorescent cell morphology; (2) switch blue excitation ON, causing immediate green fluorescence in the same cells; (3) switch excitation OFF, leading to disappearance of fluorescence; (4) alternate once more to confirm causality. Key causal transition is the direct dependence of green fluorescence on blue excitation light. Visibility constraints: same microscopic field, consistent focus, and clear contrast between fluorescence and non-fluorescence states.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Paper Brush Blending for Uniform Sketch ShadowsSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Drawing Techniques)Objective: To demonstrate and verify that controlled paper-brush blending produces a uniform soft gray tone in shaded sketch areas without visible hatching, while maintaining sharp contrast with unblended areas.II. MaterialsCompleted graphite sketch with hatched shadow areas; paper brush (tortillon or stump); clean workspace; soft lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the completed sketch flat on the table. Identify a shaded area to be blended and an adjacent area to remain unblended.2. Tool Handling: Hold the paper brush lightly, ensuring the tip is clean and dry.3. Core Operation: Gently move the paper brush over the shaded area using small circular or linear motions with even pressure. Blend only within the target shadow region.4. Boundary Control: Stop the brush movement just before reaching the adjacent unblended area to preserve a clear edge.5. Completion: Lift the paper brush cleanly and crisply away from the paper without dragging.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena- Before blending: Shaded area shows visible hatching lines and uneven texture.- During blending: Hatching gradually softens as graphite redistributes evenly.- After blending: The blended area appears as a uniform soft gray tone with no obvious hatching traces and a sharp contrast against the unblended area.V. Experimental Principle SummaryPaper-brush blending works by mechanically redistributing graphite particles across the paper surface. Even pressure spreads pigment uniformly into the paper texture, reducing line visibility. Controlled stopping and clean lifting prevent graphite transfer into adjacent areas, preserving contrast and clarity between blended and unblended regions.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Controlled blending in graphite drawing using a paper brush to achieve uniform tonal transitions. Minimum assumptions: a completed sketch with hatched shadows, a paper brush, and deliberate hand control.Phased Storyline: (1) Initial state shows hatched shadow area; (2) artist applies paper brush with even pressure, causing visible softening of graphite; (3) brush stops before adjacent area, preserving a sharp boundary; (4) brush lifts cleanly, revealing a uniform soft gray blended area contrasted with the unblended region. Visibility must clearly show hand, brush contact, boundary stopping, and final tonal result.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Yogurt Fermentation Effect Detection (pH Colorimetric Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Yogurt Fermentation Effect Detection (pH Colorimetric Method)2. Subject: Engineering – Food and Bioprocess Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To detect and compare the fermentation degree of milk at different stages by observing pH changes using a colorimetric indicator, and to understand the relationship between lactic acid fermentation and pH variation.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tubes (3), test tube rack, graduated dropper or pipette, bromocresol green indicator solution, unfermented milk, fermenting milk, fermented milk, protective gloves (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place three clean test tubes on a test tube rack and label them as unfermented milk, fermenting milk, and fermented milk.2. Sample Addition: Using a pipette, add 2 mL of unfermented milk into the first test tube, 2 mL of fermenting milk into the second, and 2 mL of fermented milk into the third.3. Indicator Addition: Add exactly two drops of bromocresol green indicator into each test tube.4. Mixing and Observation: Gently shake each test tube to mix and immediately observe the color change.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Unfermented milk: The solution appears blue-green, indicating near-neutral pH.2. Fermenting milk: The solution turns green, indicating a moderate decrease in pH.3. Fermented milk: The solution turns yellow, indicating a明显 acidic environment.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleDuring yogurt fermentation, lactic acid bacteria convert lactose into lactic acid, causing the pH of milk to decrease. Bromocresol green is a pH indicator that changes color from blue-green in neutral conditions to yellow in acidic conditions. By comparing the color of the indicator in milk samples at different fermentation stages, the degree of fermentation and corresponding pH changes can be visually detected.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Yogurt fermentation leads to progressive acidification of milk due to lactic acid production, which can be detected by a pH-sensitive color indicator.Minimum mechanistic assumptions: Milk samples represent three fermentation stages; bromocresol green reliably changes color with pH; acid production increases with fermentation time.Phased storyline: (1) Three labeled test tubes with different milk samples are presented; (2) equal volumes of milk are confirmed; (3) bromocresol green is added dropwise; (4) distinct color changes appear across tubes, transitioning from blue-green to yellow as acidity increases. Visibility constraints: test tubes and liquid colors must be clearly visible in the same frame for direct comparison.

Preparation: Place intestinal model A and model B side by side on a flat tray; ensure labels are clearly visible.2. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Calcium Imaging of a Cultured Neuron with Soma StimulationI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Calcium Imaging of Neuronal Activity Initiating in the SomaSubject: Natural Science – NeuroscienceObjective: To observe, under a fluorescence microscope, calcium activity in a live cultured neuron loaded with a calcium-sensitive dye, and to verify that neuronal activity initiates at the soma and spreads into neurites following brief microelectrode stimulation.II. Experimental EquipmentFluorescence microscope with time-lapse imaging function; live cultured neurons on glass-bottom dish; calcium-sensitive fluorescent dye (e.g., Fluo-4 AM); extracellular recording/stimulation microelectrode; micromanipulator; electrical stimulator; physiological saline solution; computer with imaging software.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Maintain cultured neurons in physiological saline. Load neurons with calcium-sensitive dye according to protocol, then rinse to remove excess dye.2. Microscope Setup: Place the culture dish on the fluorescence microscope stage. Focus on a single healthy neuron with clearly identifiable soma and neurites. Set continuous imaging mode.3. Baseline Imaging: Record baseline fluorescence for several seconds to establish resting calcium levels.4. Stimulation: Using a micromanipulator, position the microelectrode near the soma. Deliver a brief electrical stimulus to the soma while continuing fluorescence imaging.5. Continued Imaging: Continue recording for several seconds after stimulation to capture calcium signal propagation.6. Experiment Title: Gallstone Simulation Detection (Bile Cholesterol Detection)2. Subject: Healthcare – Digestive Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To simulate the detection of cholesterol in bile, observe visual changes after adding a cholesterol detection reagent, and understand the relationship between cholesterol concentration in bile and gallstone formation.II. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, dry test tube upright on the test tube rack. Wear gloves and goggles.2. Sample Addition: Use a dropper to add simulated bile solution into the test tube until it reaches about one-third of the tube volume. Observe and confirm that the solution is clear and uniform.3. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Dissolution of Crystalline Sugar vs. Amorphous Sugar Glass in WaterI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Dissolution Rates of Crystalline Sugar and Amorphous Sugar Glass in Water2. Subject: Healthcare – Pharmacy (Physical Pharmacy)3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare and understand the difference in dissolution behavior between crystalline sugar and amorphous sugar glass in water, and to relate the observed phenomena to solid-state properties such as crystallinity and free energy.II. Experimental Materials and Equipment1. Clear glass beakers (2 identical beakers, 250 mL)2. Room‑temperature distilled water (200 mL per beaker)3. Crystalline sugar (granulated sucrose, equal mass)4. Amorphous sugar glass (sugar glass shards, equal mass)5. Glass stirring rods (2 identical rods)6. Camera fixed on a tripod for time‑lapse recordingIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear beakers side by side on a flat surface. Pour equal volumes of room‑temperature water into each beaker. Ensure the water is clear and still.2. Addition of Samples: Simultaneously add crystalline sugar into the left beaker and sugar glass shards into the right beaker, ensuring equal mass for both solids.3. Stirring Operation: Using identical stirring rods, gently stir each beaker at the same speed and for the same duration to ensure equal mechanical conditions.4. Recording: Fix the camera focus and angle, and record the dissolution process using time‑lapse photography without changing the viewpoint.5. Completion: Stop stirring once most of the sugar glass has dissolved and the crystalline sugar is still partially visible. End recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both beakers contain clear, colorless water; crystalline sugar appears as regular granules, while sugar glass appears as irregular transparent shards.2. During Dissolution: Sugar glass in the right beaker dissolves rapidly, with shards shrinking and disappearing quickly. Crystalline sugar in the left beaker dissolves more slowly, with granules remaining visible for a longer time.3. Final State: The right beaker becomes uniformly clear earlier, while the left beaker still shows undissolved sugar or requires more time to reach clarity.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCrystalline sugar has an ordered lattice structure with lower free energy, requiring more energy for molecules to escape into solution. Amorphous sugar glass lacks long‑range order and has higher free energy, making its molecules more readily interact with water. Therefore, under identical conditions, amorphous sugar glass dissolves faster than crystalline sugar. This experiment demonstrates the influence of solid‑state form on dissolution behavior, a key concept in physical pharmacy.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure equal masses of sugar samples and equal water volumes.2. Maintain identical stirring speed and duration for both beakers.3. Avoid changing camera position or focus during recording.4. Handle glassware carefully to prevent breakage.

Dye Uptake: Place the corn seedlings upright in the container, ensuring only the roots are immersed in the red dye. Keep the stems and leaves above the solution.3. Waiting Period: Allow the seedlings to stand for about 5 seconds to enable rapid dye uptake through the roots (time may be visually accelerated).4. Sampling: Remove one seedling from the container and gently blot excess dye from the stem surface with a paper towel.5. Cross Cutting: Using a blade, cut the stem horizontally at a position above the root–stem junction.6. Display: Place the stem cross-section on a white background and observe the internal tissue structure.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before immersion, the corn stem cross-section is pale, and vascular tissues are not colored.2. After Dye Uptake: In the cross-section, several discrete red-stained circular or oval areas are visible, corresponding to xylem vessels.3. Tissue Contrast: The phloem and surrounding tissues remain colorless or lightly colored, forming a clear contrast with the red xylem.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleWater absorbed by corn roots is transported upward mainly through xylem vessels driven by transpiration pull and capillary action. When roots are immersed in red dye solution, the dye moves with the water through the xylem. Cutting the stem reveals red-stained xylem vessels, while phloem remains colorless, demonstrating the functional difference between xylem (water transport) and phloem (organic nutrient transport).VI. Precautions1. Ensure roots are intact and fully immersed; damaged roots affect dye uptake.2. Cut the stem cleanly and horizontally to clearly show vascular tissue.3. Handle blades carefully to avoid injury.

Experiment Title: Chocolate Softening and Melting Under Gentle Heating2. Subject: Engineering - Energy Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe heat transfer and phase change by placing a single piece of chocolate on a gently heated metal pan, recording the softening and liquefaction process continuously for several minutes.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Relief Printing (Woodcut)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Relief Printing Using a Woodcut BlockSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Printmaking)Objective: To understand and demonstrate the relief printing technique by inking the raised parts of a wooden block and transferring the pattern onto paper through pressure, observing the final relief pattern when the paper is lifted.II. Experimental MaterialsWooden printing block with carved recesses and raised pattern lines, printing ink, brayer or roller, flat inking surface, clean printing paper, flat table surface, optional spoon or baren for pressing.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the wooden block on a flat surface with the raised pattern facing upward. Prepare a small amount of ink on the inking surface.2. Inking the Block: Use the roller to evenly spread ink, then roll ink across the surface of the wooden block. Ensure ink adheres only to the raised lines (relief pattern) and not the carved recesses.3. Placing the Paper: Carefully place a sheet of paper on top of the inked block, aligning it without sliding.4. Applying Pressure: Gently but firmly press the paper against the block using hands or a spoon/baren to ensure ink transfer from raised lines.5. Revealing the Print: Slowly lift the paper from one edge to reveal the printed relief pattern.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The wooden block shows visible raised pattern lines and natural wood grain texture.During Printing: Ink is visible only on raised areas of the block; the paper remains blank before lifting.Final Result: After lifting the paper, a clear printed pattern appears, with raised-line shapes transferred as dark ink lines, showing crisp edges and subtle wood grain texture.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleRelief printing is based on the principle that only raised surfaces of a matrix receive ink and transfer it to paper under pressure. Carved recesses remain uninked and therefore do not print. When paper is pressed onto the inked raised lines and then lifted, the ink transfers, producing a relief pattern that mirrors the raised design of the wooden block.VI. PrecautionsApply ink evenly to avoid blotting; do not slide the paper when placing it; lift the paper slowly to prevent smearing.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Relief printing (woodcut) as an artistic printmaking process where ink on raised wooden surfaces is transferred to paper through pressure.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: The wooden block has physically raised lines; ink adheres preferentially to these raised areas; contact and pressure are required for ink transfer; lifting paper reveals the result.Phased Storyline: (1) Display of carved woodblock with raised pattern and wood grain; (2) Even inking of raised lines; (3) Paper placed and pressed; (4) Paper lifted to reveal the relief pattern. Visibility Requirements: Close-up view of block surface and clear reveal moment to verify raised-line printing and causal sequence.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Color Change of Universal pH Indicator with Acid and BaseI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Color Change of Universal pH Indicator with Acid and Base2. Subject: Natural Science – Biochemistry & Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To observe how a universal pH indicator changes color in response to acidic and basic solutions, and to understand the relationship between pH and indicator color.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass beaker, distilled water, universal pH indicator solution, dropper, clear acidic solution (e.g., dilute hydrochloric acid or vinegar), clear basic solution (e.g., dilute sodium hydroxide or baking soda solution), lab bench, camera fixed on a tripod.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, clear glass beaker on the lab bench. Add an appropriate amount of distilled water to the beaker.2. Indicator Addition: Add several drops of universal pH indicator to the water and gently swirl until the solution is uniformly colored (initially green, indicating near-neutral pH).3. Acid Addition: Using a dropper, slowly add a few drops of clear acidic solution into the beaker while keeping the camera focus fixed. Allow the solution to mix naturally.4. Base Addition: After observing the acid-induced color change, use a clean dropper to add a few drops of clear basic solution to the same beaker and observe the subsequent color change.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The indicator solution appears green, indicating approximately neutral pH.2. After Acid Addition: The solution gradually changes from green to yellow, orange, or red, indicating a decrease in pH.3. After Base Addition: The solution shifts from acidic colors back through green toward blue or purple, indicating an increase in pH.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesUniversal pH indicators are mixtures of dyes that exhibit different colors at different hydrogen ion concentrations. Adding an acid increases the concentration of H⁺ ions, lowering pH and shifting the indicator color toward red or yellow. Adding a base reduces H⁺ concentration (or increases OH⁻ concentration), raising pH and shifting the color toward blue or purple. The observed color changes visually represent the pH changes in the solution.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Universal pH indicators change color in response to pH variations caused by acids and bases. Minimum assumptions: acids lower pH, bases raise pH, and indicator colors correspond reliably to pH ranges. Expected phased storyline: (1) Neutral indicator solution in a clear beaker appears green; (2) addition of acidic drops causes a gradual shift toward warm colors (yellow/red) as pH decreases; (3) subsequent addition of basic drops reverses the change, moving toward cool colors (blue/purple) as pH increases. Visibility constraints: the beaker must remain in clear view, color transitions must be observable in sequence, and actions (droplet addition) must temporally precede the corresponding color changes.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Projection Distortion Map DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visualization of Projection Distortion Using Mercator and Transverse Mercator Projections2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Geography3. Experiment Objective: To understand how different map projections introduce spatial distortion by visually comparing distortion distribution maps of Mercator and Transverse Mercator projections using a color scale and error labels.II. Experimental Equipment and SoftwareComputer with GIS or cartographic visualization software (e.g., ArcGIS/QGIS or web-based projection tool), global vector map dataset, projection distortion analysis module, screen recording or time-lapse capture tool.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Open the GIS software and load a global map dataset. Ensure the projection distortion visualization function is enabled.2. Mercator Projection Display: Set the map projection to Mercator. Activate the projection distortion map layer. Display distortion using a color scale where red indicates high distortion and blue indicates low distortion. Turn on numeric or symbolic error labels. Adjust the color scale legend to be clearly visible.3. Observation and Recording: Focus the view on the entire world map. Begin screen recording or time-lapse capture. Observe distortion distribution, especially toward high latitudes.4. Projection Switching: Smoothly transition the projection setting from Mercator to Transverse Mercator. Keep the distortion map, color scale, and error labels active during the switch.5. Transverse Mercator Observation: After the switch, adjust the legend if necessary. Observe how distortion redistributes along the central meridian rather than the poles.6. Completion: Stop recording. Save the resulting visualization or video.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Under Mercator projection, distortion values increase toward the poles, shown as red areas at high latitudes, while equatorial regions remain blue or low distortion.2. Under Transverse Mercator projection, maximum distortion appears away from the chosen central meridian, while areas near it show lower distortion.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesMap projections transform the spherical Earth onto a plane, inevitably causing distortion in area, shape, distance, or direction. The Mercator projection preserves angles but greatly distorts area at high latitudes. The Transverse Mercator rotates the projection cylinder, concentrating accuracy along a central meridian and shifting distortion elsewhere. Distortion maps quantify these errors and visualize them through color scales and labels, allowing direct comparison of projection properties.VI. Experimental NotesEnsure consistent color scale standards between projections; focus on relative distortion patterns rather than exact numeric values; time-lapse is used only to condense the switching process.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Hot-Water Recrystallization of Impure Copper Sulfate CrystalsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Hot-Water Recrystallization of Impure Copper Sulfate Crystals2. Subject: Healthcare – Pharmacy (Pharmaceutical Chemistry Basics)3. Experiment Objective: To purify impure copper sulfate by hot-water recrystallization, observe dissolution, filtration, and crystallization phenomena, and understand the solubility-based purification principle.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsImpure copper sulfate crystals (blue), beaker (250 mL), clean beaker (250 mL), glass rod, hot plate, filter funnel, filter paper, ring stand, thermometer (optional), distilled water, heat-resistant gloves, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear safety goggles. Place impure copper sulfate crystals into a beaker and add a small amount of distilled water.2. Heating and Dissolution: Place the beaker on a hot plate. Heat gently while stirring with a glass rod until the copper sulfate crystals completely dissolve, forming a clear blue solution. Add minimal hot water if needed.3. Hot Filtration: While the solution is still hot, assemble the funnel and filter paper. Filter the hot solution into a clean beaker to remove insoluble impurities.4. Cooling and Crystallization: Place the filtered blue solution undisturbed on the bench and allow it to cool slowly to room temperature. Fix the camera focus and record by time-lapse.5. Completion: Blue copper sulfate crystals gradually form. Decant the remaining solution if needed and collect crystals.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial: Impure copper sulfate appears as blue crystals with visible impurities.2. Heating: Crystals dissolve in hot water, producing a transparent blue solution.3. Filtration: Insoluble impurities remain on filter paper; filtrate is clear blue.4. Cooling: Blue, well-formed copper sulfate crystals appear and grow as temperature decreases.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCopper sulfate has higher solubility in hot water than in cold water. Heating increases solubility, allowing dissolution; insoluble impurities are removed by hot filtration. Upon cooling, solubility decreases and pure copper sulfate recrystallizes from solution, achieving purification.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use minimal water to ensure effective crystallization.2. Perform filtration while hot to prevent premature crystallization.3. Avoid disturbance during cooling to obtain larger crystals.4. Handle hot equipment carefully and dispose of waste properly.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: DNA Gel Electrophoresis of Fresh vs Degraded DNAI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Fresh and Degraded DNA by Agarose Gel Electrophoresis2. Subject: Engineering - Biomedical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how DNA integrity affects electrophoretic patterns by visually comparing clear bands from fresh DNA with smeared bands from degraded DNA, and to understand the basic principles of DNA gel electrophoresis.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsAgarose gel (prepared with appropriate concentration, e.g., 1 percent), electrophoresis chamber and power supply, DNA loading dye, fresh DNA sample (in one colored microcentrifuge tube), degraded DNA sample (in a different colored microcentrifuge tube), DNA ladder, micropipettes and tips, UV transilluminator or gel documentation system, protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the solidified agarose gel into the electrophoresis chamber and add running buffer until the gel is just submerged. Put on gloves and goggles.2. Sample Handling: Identify the differently colored tubes containing fresh DNA and degraded DNA. Mix each DNA sample with loading dye if not pre-mixed.3. Loading the Gel: Using a micropipette, load the DNA ladder into the first lane. Load fresh DNA into one designated lane and degraded DNA into a separate lane, ensuring no cross-contamination and steady pipetting.4. Running Electrophoresis: Close the chamber, connect it to the power supply, and run the gel at a constant voltage until the dye front has migrated an appropriate distance.5. Visualization: Turn off the power, carefully remove the gel, and place it on the UV transilluminator. Fix the camera focus and record images or time-lapse photography under UV illumination.6. Summary of Experimental PrincipleDNA gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments based on size under an electric field. DNA molecules migrate through the agarose matrix toward the positive electrode. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Finding the Median of Eight Ordered NumbersI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Finding the Median of Eight Ordered NumbersSubject: Natural Science - Statistics & Data ScienceObjective: To demonstrate that for eight ordered numeric data points, the median is the average of the 4th and 5th values and lies exactly between them on a number line.II. Experimental MaterialsBoard or paper, marker or pen, ruler (optional for number line).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Draw a horizontal workspace on a board or paper. Ensure it is clean and visible.2. Data Arrangement: Write eight numeric values in ascending order from left to right (for example: 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10, 12, 15).3. Identifying Central Values: Point to and clearly mark the 4th and 5th values in the ordered list.4. Core Operation: Compute the average of the 4th and 5th values using basic arithmetic: (4th value + 5th value) ÷ 2.5. Median Marking: Draw a simple number line below the data. Mark the computed average at the correct position between the 4th and 5th values and label it as Median.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Eight numbers appear in strict ascending order.2. During Operation: The 4th and 5th numbers are highlighted; a numerical average is calculated.3. Final Result: The marked median appears exactly between the 4th and 5th values on the number line.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleFor an even number of data points, there is no single middle value. The median is defined as the arithmetic mean of the two central values. Therefore, for eight ordered numbers, the median equals the average of the 4th and 5th values and is located midway between them on a number line.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Visualization of Acoustic Performance Comparison of Architectural MaterialsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visualization of Acoustic Performance Comparison of Sponge and Glass2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Architecture & Urban Planning3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare the acoustic performance of sound-absorbing and reflective architectural materials by using sound wave ripples (wave graphics) to represent sound propagation, helping learners understand how different materials influence sound behavior in space.II. Experimental EquipmentSound source icon or point source (virtual), ripple-style sound wave graphics, sponge material block (sound-absorbing, matte texture), glass material panel (sound-reflective, smooth and transparent), flat background plane, display or animation software.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the sound source at the center-left of the scene. Position the sponge block in front of the sound source on one side and the glass panel at the same distance on the other side for comparison.2. Sound Emission: Activate the sound source so that concentric ripple waves propagate outward uniformly.3. Interaction with Sponge: Observe the waves as they reach the sponge. Waves gradually decrease in amplitude and fade after entering the sponge region.4. Interaction with Glass: Reset the scene. Allow waves to propagate toward the glass panel. Observe strong reflection, with waves bouncing back and maintaining clear ripple patterns.5. Comparison Display: Present both interactions side by side or sequentially for clear comparison.IV. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Observation of Soybean Seed StructureI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of Internal Structure of Soybean Seed2. Subject: Engineering – Agricultural Engineering (Plant Structure Basics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the internal structure of a soybean seed by dissecting it, verify that the mature soybean seed has no endosperm, and confirm that two cotyledons enclose the hypocotyl and radicle, filling the interior of the seed coat.II. Experimental Materials and Tools1. Dry soybean seeds (1–2 grains)2. Tweezers (one pair)3. Clean working surface or white paper4. Optional: Hand lens for clearer observationIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a dry soybean seed on a clean surface. Hold the seed gently between fingers to stabilize it.2. Peeling the Seed Coat: Use tweezers to carefully pinch and peel off the seed coat (testa) from the surface of the soybean, removing it completely without damaging the inner structures.3. Separating the Seed: After removing the seed coat, gently separate the seed along the natural split between the two cotyledons.4. Opening and Observation: Open the two cotyledons to expose the internal structures. Observe the embryo located between the cotyledons, including the hypocotyl and radicle.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. After the seed coat is removed, no endosperm is observed inside the soybean seed.2. The interior is almost entirely filled by two large, thick cotyledons.3. The hypocotyl and radicle are enclosed between the two cotyledons and are clearly visible when the cotyledons are opened.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSoybean is a dicotyledonous plant. In mature dicot seeds like soybean, the endosperm is absorbed during seed development. Nutrients are stored in the two cotyledons, which occupy most of the seed interior. The embryo consists of the radicle, hypocotyl, and plumule, and these embryonic structures are wrapped and protected by the cotyledons within the seed coat. By physically dissecting the seed, the structural characteristics of dicot seeds can be directly verified.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Effect of Pickling on Food Acidity (Kimchi Pickling)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effect of Pickling on Food Acidity (Kimchi Pickling)2. Experiment Objective: To observe how pickling and fermentation affect food acidity by measuring pH changes during cabbage fermentation, and to understand the role of salt and lactic acid fermentation in food preservation.II. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wash the glass jar and allow it to dry. Prepare fresh cabbage by cutting it into small pieces.2. Salting and Mixing: Place the cabbage into the clean glass jar. Pressing: Press the cabbage firmly using a hand or tool until liquid is released and begins to cover the cabbage.4. Sealing and Fermentation: Ensure the cabbage is submerged in its liquid. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Phagocytosis of Colored Plastic Beads by Macrophage-like Cells2. Subject: Natural Science - Microbiology3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the process of phagocytosis by macrophage-like cells. Using time-lapse microscopy, students will visualize how cultured macrophage-like cells engulf red and green plastic beads added to the surrounding culture medium, and relate the observed phenomena to the biological function of phagocytosis in innate immunity.II. Experimental Materials and Equipment1. Cultured macrophage-like cells (e.g., RAW 264.7 or similar) grown in a sterile culture dish2. Cell culture medium (appropriate for the cell line)3. Red plastic microspheres (≈1–3 μm diameter)4. Green plastic microspheres (≈1–3 μm diameter)5. Inverted light microscope equipped with a camera6. Time-lapse imaging software7. Micropipette and sterile pipette tips8. CO₂ incubator or temperature-controlled microscope stage (optional)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the culture dish containing adherent macrophage-like cells on the microscope stage. Ensure that cells are evenly distributed and healthy, with visible cell boundaries.2. Microscope Setup: Adjust the microscope to an appropriate magnification (e.g., 20× or 40×). Focus clearly on the cell layer and then fix the focus of the camera so it remains unchanged throughout the experiment.3. Addition of Beads: Using a micropipette, gently add a small volume of red and green plastic bead suspension into the culture medium surrounding the cells. Avoid disturbing the cells by adding the suspension slowly along the edge of the dish.4. Time-lapse Recording: Immediately start time-lapse photography. Capture images at fixed intervals (e.g., every 10–30 seconds) for a short, accelerated duration suitable for demonstration.5. Observation Period: Allow the recording to continue as beads settle and interact with the cells. Do not refocus or move the dish during imaging.6. End of Experiment: Stop the time-lapse recording. Save the image sequence or video for analysis and discussion.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Macrophage-like cells appear spread out and adherent on the dish surface. Red and green beads are initially free-floating in the surrounding medium.2. During the Process: Beads gradually come into contact with the cell surface. Some beads attach to the cell membrane. The cell membrane extends around the beads, forming visible pseudopodia.3. Final State: Red and green beads are observed inside the cells, appearing as colored dots within the cytoplasm. Over time, the number of internalized beads increases, while fewer beads remain outside the cells.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePhagocytosis is a key function of macrophages in the innate immune system. Macrophage-like cells recognize, bind, and engulf foreign particles through active rearrangement of the cytoskeleton. In this experiment, inert colored plastic beads simulate foreign particles. The cells extend pseudopodia to surround the beads, enclosing them in membrane-bound vesicles called phagosomes. Time-lapse microscopy allows continuous observation of this dynamic process, visually demonstrating the cellular mechanism and biological significance of phagocytosis.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Add beads gently to avoid detaching cells.2. Keep the microscope focus fixed to ensure accurate time-lapse observation.3. Maintain sterile conditions if live cells are to be reused.4. Limit observation time to prevent cell stress due to environmental changes.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Phagocytosis by macrophage-like cells as observed under a microscope. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: macrophage-like cells are adherent, capable of extending pseudopodia, and can internalize inert particles; plastic beads act as foreign bodies; microscopy provides a fixed field of view. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) Initial phase—cells adhered, beads free in medium; (2) Contact phase—beads settle and touch cell membranes; (3) Engulfment phase—cell membrane extends around beads; (4) Internalization phase—beads appear inside cytoplasm. Visibility constraints: fixed microscope focus, consistent field of view, clear color distinction between red and green beads to verify engulfment over time.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Cyanogenic Glycoside Detection (Picric Acid Test Strip Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Detection of Cyanogenic Glycosides in Plant Samples by Picric Acid Test Strip Method2. Subject: Healthcare – Pharmaceutical Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the qualitative detection of cyanogenic glycosides in plant material by releasing hydrogen cyanide gas and observing the color change of a picric acid test strip.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsSealed conical flask with stopper, crushed fresh plant sample (suspected to contain cyanogenic glycosides), distilled water, picric acid test strip (dry, yellow), thread or clip for suspension, gentle heat source (warm water bath or low flame), forceps.III. Experimental Procedure1. Sample Placement: Place a small amount of crushed plant sample into the bottom of a clean, dry flask.2. Addition of Water: Add a small volume of distilled water to moisten the sample; do not fill more than one-third of the flask.3. Test Strip Suspension: Suspend a picric acid test strip inside the flask above the liquid level using a thread or clip, ensuring it does not touch the liquid or walls.4. Sealing: Seal the flask tightly with a stopper to prevent gas escape.5. Gentle Warming: Gently warm the flask using a warm water bath or low heat for several seconds.6. Inspection: After waiting several seconds, remove the stopper and take out the test strip with forceps for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The picric acid test strip is dry and yellow.2. After Warming: If cyanogenic glycosides are present, the strip gradually changes from yellow to orange-brown or brick-red.3. Negative Result: If no cyanogenic glycosides are present, the strip remains yellow with no visible change.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCyanogenic glycosides in plant tissues decompose in the presence of water and heat to release hydrogen cyanide (HCN) gas. The liberated HCN reacts with picric acid on the test strip to form isopurpuric acid derivatives, causing a characteristic color change from yellow to brick-red or brown. This color change provides a qualitative indication of cyanogenic glycosides.VI. PrecautionsCarry out the experiment in a well-ventilated area; avoid direct contact with picric acid strips; use gentle heating only; dispose of used strips safely.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: qualitative detection of cyanogenic glycosides via gas-phase reaction with picric acid. Minimum assumptions: crushed plant releases HCN upon warming with water; picric acid strip responds with a visible color change. Phased storyline: (1) setup—crushed plant and water in sealed flask with suspended yellow strip; (2) action—gentle warming initiates gas release; (3) effect—strip color changes while suspended; (4) verification—strip removed and inspected. Visibility constraints: strip must remain above liquid and clearly visible; heating and sealing must precede color change; time-lapse may compress waiting without altering order.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Salivary Amylase Activity Detection by Starch–Iodine MethodSubject: Healthcare – Digestive PhysiologyExperiment Objective: To demonstrate that salivary amylase can digest starch by comparing the iodine reaction of starch solution treated with saliva and with distilled water.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsTest tubes (2), test tube rack, droppers, starch solution, fresh saliva, distilled water, iodine solution, warm water bath or incubator (about 37°C).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean test tubes on a rack. Use a dropper to add equal volumes of starch solution into each test tube.2. Treatment: Add fresh saliva to one test tube using a dropper. Add an equal volume of distilled water to the other test tube as a control.3. Incubation: Place both test tubes in a warm environment at approximately body temperature for a short time to allow enzymatic reaction.4. Detection: Remove the test tubes and add iodine solution dropwise into each tube using a clean dropper.5. Observation: Gently swirl and observe the color change in each test tube.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitially, both tubes contain colorless starch solution. After iodine addition, the control tube with distilled water turns blue-black, indicating the presence of starch. The saliva-treated tube shows little to no blue-black color and remains yellow-brown, indicating starch has been digested.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSaliva contains the enzyme amylase, which breaks down starch into smaller sugars. Iodine reacts with intact starch to produce a blue-black color. In the control tube, starch remains undigested and turns blue-black with iodine. In the saliva tube, amylase digests starch during incubation, so iodine does not produce the blue-black color. This color difference demonstrates salivary amylase activity.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Sequential Search Algorithm Execution Process DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Sequential Search Algorithm Execution Process Demonstration2. Subject: Engineering - Computer Science - Data Structures and Algorithms3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the execution process of a sequential (linear) search algorithm, helping learners understand how elements are compared one by one in an array until a target value is found or the array ends.II. Experimental Materials and Environment1. A 2D animation environment or visualization software.2. A horizontal array of numbered boxes representing data elements, e.g. [5, 1, 2, 4, 3].3. A visible pointer or indicator to represent the current index being examined.4. A clearly displayed target value, e.g. 4.III. Experimental Procedure1. Initialization: Display the array as a row of equally sized boxes arranged horizontally, each labeled with its value. Show the target value separately.2. Pointer Setup: Place a highlighted pointer above or below the first element of the array.3. Sequential Comparison: Move the pointer step by step from left to right. At each position, highlight the current box and visually indicate a comparison with the target value.4. Detection: When the pointer reaches the element whose value equals the target, stop the movement and emphasize the matched box.5. Termination: Display a success indication (e.g. color change or text) showing that the target has been found and the search ends.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The array is static, the pointer is positioned at the first element, and no elements are highlighted.2. During Search: The pointer moves one position at a time from left to right, and each visited element is highlighted briefly to show comparison.3. Upon Finding Target: When the pointer reaches the value 4, the movement stops and that box remains highlighted, indicating a successful search.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe sequential search algorithm works by examining each element of a data collection in order. Starting from the first element, it compares the current element with the target value. If they match, the search stops successfully; otherwise, the algorithm moves to the next element. This process continues until the target is found or all elements have been checked. The demonstration visualizes this principle through ordered pointer movement and comparison highlights.VI. Notes1. The pointer must move strictly from left to right without skipping elements.2. Only one element should be compared at a time.3. The visualization should remain simple and clear to emphasize the core logic of sequential search.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Sequential (linear) search in computer science, assuming a fixed-size array, a single target value, and a pointer that checks elements in order. Expected phenomena: Phase 1 shows a static horizontal array and target; Phase 2 shows a highlighted pointer moving left to right, comparing one element at a time; Phase 3 shows termination when the target value is found, with clear visual emphasis. The viewpoint should remain fixed, all elements visible simultaneously, and causal transitions (compare → move or stop) must be visually explicit for verification.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: PIR Motion Sensor Turning a Lamp On When a Person Enters a RoomI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: PIR Motion Sensor Controls a Lamp Based on Human MotionSubject: Engineering - Mechatronics & RoboticsExperiment Objective: To demonstrate how a PIR motion sensor detects human movement and controls an electrical load (table lamp), and to understand the basic working principle of motion-based automatic lighting systems.II. Experimental Equipment1. PIR motion sensor module (with adjustable sensitivity and delay, if available)2. Table lamp with bulb (functional)3. Power supply (according to sensor and lamp requirements)4. Connecting wires or control relay module5. Door and room environment with dim lighting6. Mounting accessories for fixing the PIR sensor near the doorIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the experiment in a dim room. Fix the PIR motion sensor near the door at about chest height, facing the entrance area. Connect the PIR sensor output to the control input of the lamp or relay so that detected motion turns the lamp on.2. Initial State Check: Ensure the room is dim, the door is closed, and the lamp is off. Confirm that the PIR sensor is powered and in standby mode.3. Entry Operation: Open the door and walk into the room. Pause briefly near the door, then stand still for a moment within the sensor’s detection range.4. Exit Operation: After observing the lamp behavior, walk out of the room and close the door, leaving the sensor’s detection area.5. Completion: Allow sufficient time for the PIR sensor delay to expire and observe the final lamp state.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: In the dim room with no human motion, the lamp remains off.2. Upon Entry: When the person opens the door and enters the room, the PIR sensor detects motion, and the table lamp turns on automatically.3. Standing Still: While the person pauses and stands still, the lamp remains on for the preset delay time.4. After Leaving: When the person leaves the room and no motion is detected, the lamp turns off automatically after a short delay.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleA PIR (Passive Infrared) motion sensor detects changes in infrared radiation emitted by warm objects such as the human body. When a person enters the sensor’s detection zone, the change in infrared energy generates an electrical signal. This signal is processed by the control circuit, which switches the lamp on. When no further motion is detected, the signal ceases, and after a preset delay, the lamp is switched off. This experiment demonstrates a typical mechatronic system integrating sensing, signal processing, and actuation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Automatic lighting control using a PIR motion sensor detecting human infrared radiation to switch a lamp on and off. Phase 2 (Trigger): Door opens and person enters; motion occurs within sensor field, causing lamp to turn on. Phase 3 (Hold): Person pauses and stands still; lamp remains on due to sensor delay. Phase 4 (Release): Person leaves the room; no motion detected; after delay, lamp turns off. Visibility constraints: the sensor, lamp state (on/off), and human motion must be clearly visible in a continuous perspective for causal verification.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Microcontroller Button Input Triggering an LED Output in Real Time2. Subject: Engineering – Mechatronics & Robotics3. Experiment Objective: To understand how a microcontroller reads a digital input from a pushbutton and controls a digital output (LED) in real time; to observe the direct causal relationship between human interaction and electronic system response.II. Experimental EquipmentMicrocontroller board (powered via USB or external supply), breadboard, pushbutton switch, LED (red recommended), current-limiting resistor (220–330 ohms), jumper wires, USB power cable, stable tabletop.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the microcontroller and breadboard on a tabletop. Ensure power is off. Insert the pushbutton across the breadboard gap and place the LED with correct polarity.2. Wiring: Connect one side of the pushbutton to a digital input pin and the other side to ground or Vcc (with pull-up or pull-down configuration). Connect the LED in series with a resistor to a digital output pin and ground.3. Power and Program: Upload a simple program so that when the button is pressed, the LED turns on, and when released, the LED turns off. Power the microcontroller.4. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Ionic Interaction Screening in Milk Colloid After Salt AdditionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Milk Colloid Clumping After Salt Addition2. Subject: Biology – Natural Science (Colloids and Ionic Interactions)3. Experiment Objective: To observe how added salt screens ionic interactions in a colloidal system, causing milk proteins to aggregate; to compare treated and untreated samples through visual observation.II. Experimental MaterialsTransparent glass cups (2 identical), fresh milk (same volume for each glass), table salt (sodium chloride), teaspoon, stirring rod or spoon, flat surface, camera or mobile phone (fixed focus for time-lapse).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical transparent glasses side by side on a flat surface. Pour equal volumes of milk into each glass. Label the left glass as Control and the right glass as Experimental.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera position and focus so that both glasses are fully visible in the frame. Do not adjust focus during recording.3. Core Operation: Add one level spoonful of table salt into the right (Experimental) glass only. Stir gently for 5–10 seconds until the salt is dispersed. Do not touch or stir the left (Control) glass.4. Observation Stage: Keep both glasses undisturbed and in view. Observe changes over a short period (can be accelerated by time-lapse).5. Completion: Stop recording after clear differences are observed between the two glasses.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both glasses contain uniform, opaque white milk with no visible clumps.2. After Salt Addition: In the right glass, small white clumps or floccules gradually appear, and the milk becomes uneven. The left glass remains uniformly opaque.3. Comparison Result: The experimental glass shows aggregation, while the control glass shows no visible change.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMilk is a colloidal system where protein particles are stabilized by surface charges. When salt (NaCl) is added, ions screen these charges, reducing electrostatic repulsion between particles. As a result, the colloidal stability decreases, and milk proteins aggregate into visible clumps. This demonstrates ionic interaction screening leading to colloid destabilization.VI. PrecautionsUse identical containers and equal milk volumes for fair comparison. Stir only the experimental glass. Avoid shaking the control glass. Clean all materials after the experiment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Ionic interaction screening in colloids, demonstrated by salt-induced aggregation of milk proteins. Minimum assumptions: milk is a stable colloid; added salt provides ions that reduce electrostatic repulsion between colloidal particles.Expected phased storyline: (1) Baseline phase – two identical glasses of uniform milk shown side by side. (2) Intervention phase – salt is added and stirred only in the right glass. (3) Reaction phase – over time, visible clumping/flocculation appears in the right glass while the left glass remains unchanged. Visibility constraints: both glasses must remain in the same frame with stable perspective to allow direct comparison and causal verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Protein Denaturation by Heat (Egg White)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Protein Denaturation by Heat Using Egg White2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food Hygiene3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate heat-induced protein denaturation by observing the changes in egg white when heated in a hot water bath, and to understand how heat alters protein structure and properties.II. Experimental EquipmentTest tube (1), test tube rack, beaker (1), thermometer, hot water bath or heat source, liquid egg white (fresh, filtered), water, test tube holder or clamp.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the test tube on the rack. Add liquid egg white to about one third of the test tube volume. Ensure the egg white is clear and fluid.2. Water Bath Setup: Pour water into the beaker to about two thirds full. Insert the thermometer into the water to monitor temperature.3. Heating Operation: Place the beaker on a heat source and heat gently to form a hot water bath (do not boil vigorously). Place the test tube containing egg white into the hot water bath.4. Core Operation: While heating, gently shake the test tube to ensure even heating of the egg white. Maintain controlled heating and observe continuously.5. Completion: When obvious changes are observed in the egg white, remove the test tube from the water bath and place it back on the rack.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The egg white is colorless to slightly transparent and fluid.2. During Heating: As temperature rises, the egg white gradually becomes cloudy, then turns white and opaque.3. Final State: The egg white loses fluidity and becomes coagulated or gel-like, forming a solid or semi-solid mass.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleEgg white is rich in protein, mainly albumin. When heated, the protein molecules absorb thermal energy, causing the disruption of their natural folded structure (denaturation). The unfolded proteins aggregate and coagulate, leading to loss of transparency and fluidity. This process is irreversible under normal conditions and demonstrates heat denaturation of protein, a key concept in nutrition and food hygiene.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Heat denaturation of protein in food, demonstrated using egg white. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: egg white contains proteins that unfold and aggregate when heated; indirect heating via a water bath provides controlled temperature increase. Phase 2 (heating) shows gradual temperature increase and gentle shaking, with egg white turning from transparent to cloudy. Phase 3 (denaturation outcome) shows the egg white becoming white, opaque, and coagulated. Visibility constraints: camera focuses on test tube, beaker, thermometer, and heating steps only; causal transition from heating to coagulation must be visually continuous and clear.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Skin Erythema Reaction (Friction)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Skin Erythema Reaction Induced by Friction2. Subject: Healthcare – Skin Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the skin erythema reaction caused by mechanical friction, and to relate visible skin changes to underlying physiological mechanisms such as capillary dilation.II. Experimental MaterialsClean human forearm (one subject), smooth cotton pad, neutral lighting environment, camera or recording device (for close-up and time-lapse observation).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the forearm skin is clean, dry, and free from existing redness or irritation. Position the forearm comfortably and keep it exposed.2. Initial Observation: Observe and record the normal skin color and condition before stimulation.3. Friction Stimulation: Use a smooth cotton pad to rub the same area of the forearm skin back and forth with moderate pressure for several seconds (approximately 5–10 seconds).4. Stop Stimulation: Remove the cotton pad and stop all contact with the skin.5. Observation Phase: Keep the skin exposed and continue observing the rubbed area for visible changes, focusing on color changes over time.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The forearm skin appears normal in color, without redness.2. After Rubbing: Shortly after friction stops, the rubbed area gradually becomes red compared to surrounding skin.3. Localization: The erythema is mainly confined to the area that was rubbed and does not spread widely.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMechanical friction stimulates sensory receptors and small blood vessels in the skin. This stimulation causes local vasodilation of capillaries, increasing blood flow to the area. The increased blood volume near the skin surface produces visible redness, known as the skin erythema reaction. This response is a normal physiological reaction indicating intact microcirculation and neural regulation of the skin.VI. PrecautionsAvoid excessive pressure to prevent skin injury. Do not perform on damaged or inflamed skin. Individual skin sensitivity may cause variations in redness intensity.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: B Lymphocyte Detection by Surface Antibody Staining MethodI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Detection of B Lymphocytes by Surface Antibody StainingSubject: Healthcare – Basic ImmunologyExperiment Objective: To detect and identify B lymphocytes by staining cell-surface markers with fluorescently labeled antibodies and observing them using a fluorescence microscope or flow cytometer.II. Experimental PrincipleB lymphocytes express specific surface antigens (such as CD19 or CD20). Fluorescently labeled monoclonal antibodies specifically bind these surface antigens. After incubation and washing to remove unbound antibodies, labeled B lymphocytes emit fluorescence under excitation light, allowing their identification and analysis.III. Experimental Materials and ApparatusPrepared single-cell suspension (e.g., peripheral blood mononuclear cells), fluorescently labeled anti-B-cell surface antibody, phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), centrifuge tubes, micropipettes and tips, centrifuge, fluorescence microscope or flow cytometer, protective gloves.IV. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a measured volume of prepared cell suspension into a centrifuge tube.2. Antibody Staining: Add an appropriate amount of fluorescently labeled antibody to the cell suspension.3. Mixing: Gently mix by tapping or slow pipetting to ensure even contact between cells and antibody.4. Incubation: Incubate the mixture at room temperature or 4°C for the specified time, protected from light.5. Washing: Add PBS, centrifuge gently, discard supernatant, and resuspend cells to remove unbound antibody.6. Observation: Place stained cells on a slide for fluorescence microscopy or load into a flow cytometer for analysis.V. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaBefore staining, cells show no specific fluorescence. After staining and washing, B lymphocytes display distinct fluorescence on their surface, while unstained or non-B cells show minimal background signal.VI. manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Latitudinal Radiation Distribution on EarthI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Latitudinal Radiation Distribution from Equator to Poles2. Subject: Geography – Physical Geography3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how solar radiation is distributed unevenly across Earth by latitude, understand that the equator receives the highest solar radiation while the poles receive the lowest, and recognize the zonal pattern of radiation distribution.II. Experimental EquipmentDigital globe model or globe animation software, display screen, control device (mouse or touch screen).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Turn on the display and load the globe model showing Earth with latitude lines marked (0°, 30°, 60°, 90°).2. Initial Display: Present the globe in a static view, ensuring latitude labels and a color legend for radiation values are visible.3. Core Operation: Start the rotation of the globe from west to east. Activate the radiation overlay so that colors appear by latitude.4. Observation Operation: Adjust the view to center on the equator, then slowly rotate toward the Northern and Southern Hemispheres, ensuring all latitudes are shown.5. Completion: Pause the rotation with the full globe visible, showing the complete latitudinal radiation distribution.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The equatorial region (0°) appears in red, indicating the highest solar radiation (>300 W/m²).2. Moving away from the equator toward mid-latitudes, colors gradually change from red to yellow and green, indicating decreasing radiation.3. Polar regions (90°N and 90°S) appear in blue, indicating the lowest radiation (<100 W/m²).4. The radiation distribution forms clear horizontal (zonal) bands parallel to latitude lines.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Solar radiation received at Earth’s surface varies with latitude due to the angle of solar incidence.2. Therefore, global solar radiation shows a zonal pattern: highest at the equator and lowest at the poles.VI. Experimental Notes1. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Thermostable Catalase Producing Oxygen Bubbles After Heat ExposureI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Thermostable Catalase and Regular Catalase After Heating2. Subject: Natural Science - Biochemistry & Molecular Biology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that thermostable catalase retains enzymatic activity after heat exposure, while regular catalase loses activity, by observing oxygen bubble production after adding hydrogen peroxide.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo clear glass beakers (100 mL), thermostable catalase solution (dyed red), regular catalase solution (dyed blue), hot water bath (70–80 °C), thermometer, hydrogen peroxide solution (3%), dropper or pipette, beaker tongs, stopwatch, camera on tripod.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clear beakers side by side on the bench. Add equal volumes of red thermostable catalase to one beaker and blue regular catalase to the other.2. Heating: Using tongs, place both beakers simultaneously into the hot water bath. Heat for the same duration (about 5 minutes) to ensure equal heat exposure.3. Removal: Remove both beakers from the water bath and place them back side by side. Allow brief stabilization without cooling completely.4. Core Operation: Fix the camera focus. Using droppers, add equal volumes of hydrogen peroxide to both beakers at the same time.5. Observation: Observe and record bubble formation in each beaker for a short period.6. Cleanup: Dispose of solutions properly and clean all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both solutions are colored (red and blue) and show no bubbles after heating alone.2. After Adding Hydrogen Peroxide: The red thermostable catalase solution rapidly produces many oxygen bubbles. The blue regular catalase solution produces few or no bubbles.3. Comparison: Bubbling in the red beaker is明显 stronger and more sustained than in the blue beaker.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCatalase catalyzes the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. High temperatures denature most enzymes by disrupting their protein structure. Regular catalase loses activity after heating, while thermostable catalase maintains its structure and function. Therefore, after heat exposure, thermostable catalase continues to produce oxygen bubbles when hydrogen peroxide is added, whereas regular catalase shows reduced or no activity.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Urine Phosphate Detection (Molybdenum Blue Colorimetric Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Urine Phosphate Detection by Molybdenum Blue Colorimetric Method2. Subject: Healthcare – Renal Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To qualitatively detect phosphate in urine by observing the formation of molybdenum blue, and to understand the chemical basis of phosphate excretion assessment in renal physiology.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (15×150 mm), test tube rack, dropper or pipette, water bath (80–90 °C), beaker (for water bath), urine sample, acidic ammonium molybdate reagent, reducing agent (such as stannous chloride or ascorbic acid solution), test tube holder.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, dry test tube in a test tube rack. Use a dropper to add approximately 2 mL of urine sample into the test tube.2. Addition of Molybdate Reagent: Add 1 mL of acidic ammonium molybdate reagent to the urine sample. Gently mix by lightly shaking the test tube to ensure uniform mixing.3. Addition of Reducing Agent: Add several drops (about 0.5 mL) of the reducing agent into the test tube. Mix gently again.4. Heating: Hold the test tube with a test tube holder and place it in a hot water bath for 1–2 minutes. Do not boil. Remove and place the test tube back on the rack.5. Reaction: Allow the solution to stand briefly for color development.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The urine sample is pale yellow and transparent.2. After Reagent Addition: The solution remains light-colored or slightly cloudy.3. After Heating and Standing: A blue to deep blue color gradually appears, with intensity related to phosphate concentration.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIn acidic conditions, phosphate ions in urine react with ammonium molybdate to form phosphomolybdic acid. Upon heating and in the presence of a reducing agent, the molybdenum complex is reduced to form molybdenum blue. The appearance of a blue color indicates the presence of phosphate. This reaction forms the chemical basis for assessing phosphate excretion in renal physiology.VI. Precautions1. Add reagents strictly in order: molybdate reagent first, reducing agent second.2. Heat gently in a water bath to avoid splashing or decomposition.3. Handle urine samples and reagents with care and dispose of waste according to laboratory safety rules.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstration of urine phosphate detection using the molybdenum blue colorimetric method under renal physiology context. Minimum assumptions: presence of urine in a test tube, correct reagents, acidic environment, reduction and heating steps.Phased storyline: (1) Static close-up of test tube containing urine; (2) Addition of acidic ammonium molybdate and gentle mixing; (3) Addition of reducing agent; (4) Brief heating in water bath; (5) Gradual appearance of blue coloration. Key causal transition is from reagent addition plus heating to blue color formation. Visibility constraints: clear focus on test tube contents, reagent order, and color change; background kept simple to highlight core experimental steps.
