manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Liposome-Encapsulated Dye Versus Free Dye Diffusion in WaterI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Diffusion Between Liposome-Encapsulated Dye and Free Dye in WaterSubject: Healthcare – PharmacyExperiment Objective: To visually compare the diffusion behavior of liposome-encapsulated blue dye and free blue dye in still water, and to understand how liposomal encapsulation affects molecular diffusion and drug release behavior.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass beakers (2 identical beakers, 250 mL each); distilled water (room temperature); liposome-encapsulated blue dye solution; free blue dye solution (same dye concentration as encapsulated form); droppers or micropipettes (2); flat laboratory bench; camera or smartphone with tripod for time-lapse photography.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear glass beakers side by side on a stable, level bench. Add equal volumes of still distilled water to each beaker, ensuring no visible convection or bubbles.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera directly in front of the beakers, ensuring both beakers are fully in frame. Fix the focus and exposure, and set the camera to time-lapse or continuous recording mode.3. Dye Addition: Using separate droppers, simultaneously add an equal volume of liposome-encapsulated blue dye to the center of the left beaker and free blue dye to the center of the right beaker. Avoid stirring or disturbing the water.4. Observation Period: Allow the system to stand undisturbed while recording. Observe the diffusion patterns over time.5. Completion: Stop recording after clear differences in diffusion behavior are observed. Dispose of solutions according to laboratory guidelines and clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both beakers contain clear, colorless, still water.Early Stage: In the right beaker, the free blue dye begins to spread rapidly, forming expanding blue gradients. In the left beaker, the liposome-encapsulated dye remains more localized, spreading slowly.Later Stage: The free dye becomes more uniformly distributed throughout the water, while the liposome-encapsulated dye shows delayed and limited diffusion, with color remaining concentrated near the point of addition.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesFree dye molecules diffuse rapidly in water due to random thermal motion and lack of physical barriers. In contrast, liposome-encapsulated dye is enclosed within phospholipid vesicles, which increases effective particle size and restricts immediate diffusion. This demonstrates how liposomes can slow diffusion and release, a key principle in drug delivery systems for controlled and targeted therapy.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure both beakers and water volumes are identical; add dyes simultaneously; avoid vibrations or airflow; do not stir the water; maintain consistent lighting and camera focus throughout recording.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate how liposomal encapsulation alters diffusion behavior compared to free dye, illustrating controlled drug delivery principles in pharmacy. Minimum assumptions include still water, identical containers, equal dye amounts, and clear left–right differentiation.Phased Storyline: (1) Static setup with two identical clear beakers of still water side by side; (2) simultaneous addition of liposome-encapsulated blue dye to the left and free blue dye to the right; (3) early diffusion where free dye spreads rapidly while encapsulated dye remains localized; (4) later phase showing uniform distribution of free dye and delayed, limited spread of liposome dye. Visibility constraints: both beakers must remain in frame, camera focus fixed, and color gradients clearly observable to verify diffusion differences.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Urine Phosphorus Detection (Colorimetric Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Urine Phosphorus Detection by Colorimetric Method2. Subject: Healthcare – Renal Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To detect and estimate the phosphorus content in urine using a colorimetric reaction, understand the principle of phosphate excretion by the kidney, and master basic colorimetric analytical techniques.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tubes (including standard tubes), test tube rack, dropper or pipette, water bath, thermometer, color chart or colorimeter, urine sample, acidic reagent (such as sulfuric acid solution), ammonium molybdate reagent, distilled water, protective gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Sample Preparation: Collect a fresh urine sample and transfer an appropriate volume (about 2–3 mL) into a clean test tube.2. Acidification: Add a fixed volume of acidic reagent to the urine sample to create an acidic environment; mix gently.3. Reagent Addition: Add ammonium molybdate reagent to the test tube using a dropper.4. Mixing: Gently shake or swirl the test tube to ensure thorough mixing without splashing.5. Heating: Place the test tube in a water bath and heat briefly (about 1–2 minutes) to accelerate the reaction.6. Cooling: Remove the test tube and allow it to cool to room temperature.7. Comparison: Compare the color intensity of the solution with standard tubes using a color chart or measure absorbance with a colorimeter.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Urine sample appears pale yellow and transparent.2. After Reagent Addition: The solution gradually develops a yellow coloration.3. After Heating and Cooling: The yellow color becomes more stable and intensified; deeper yellow indicates higher phosphorus concentration.4. Comparison: Color intensity corresponds to that of one of the standard tubes.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIn acidic conditions, inorganic phosphate in urine reacts with ammonium molybdate to form a yellow phosphomolybdate complex. The intensity of the yellow color is proportional to the concentration of phosphorus in the urine. By comparing the sample color with standards or measuring absorbance, the phosphorus content can be estimated, reflecting renal phosphate excretion function.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure accurate reagent volumes for reliable color comparison.2. Avoid overheating during the water bath step.3. Use fresh urine samples to prevent chemical changes.4. Dispose of urine and reagents according to laboratory safety regulations.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Colorimetric detection of urinary phosphate based on phosphomolybdate formation under acidic conditions. Minimum assumptions: presence of urine phosphate, acidic environment, ammonium molybdate reagent, and visible color change proportional to concentration. Phased storyline: (1) clear urine sample in test tube; (2) acid added, no major visual change; (3) ammonium molybdate added, solution begins to yellow; (4) brief heating accelerates reaction; (5) cooling stabilizes color; (6) side-by-side comparison with standard tubes shows relative color intensity. Visibility constraints: close-up focus on test tube, clear view of color change and comparison; time-lapse can compress heating and cooling while preserving order.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Iodine Diffusing into a Starch Agar Gel BlockI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Iodine Diffusing into a Starch Agar Gel BlockSubject: Healthcare – Medicine (Basic Biomedical Concepts)Experiment Objective: To observe molecular diffusion in a gel medium and the characteristic color reaction between iodine and starch through visual time-lapse recording.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentClear starch agar gel cube (approximately 2–3 cm per side), shallow transparent dish (Petri dish or glass dish), iodine solution (dilute Lugol’s iodine), dropper or beaker, camera or smartphone with fixed focus capability, stable bench surface.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear starch agar gel cube at the center of a clean transparent dish on a stable surface. Ensure the cube is intact, colorless, and free of bubbles.2. Adding Iodine: Using a dropper or by gently pouring from a beaker, slowly add iodine solution into the dish so that it surrounds all sides of the gel cube without disturbing or moving it.3. Observation Setup: Do not stir or touch the gel. Fix the camera focus and position directly above or at the side of the dish for clear viewing.4. Reaction Period: Leave the setup undisturbed and record or observe over time (time-lapse recommended).IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The starch agar gel cube is clear and colorless; the surrounding iodine solution is yellow-brown.During Diffusion: A blue-black coloration appears on the outer surface of the gel cube where iodine contacts starch.Progression: The colored region gradually moves inward from the surface toward the center, forming a visible diffusion front.Final State: After sufficient time, much or all of the gel cube becomes blue-black, with the deepest color near the surface if time is limited.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates diffusion and a starch–iodine reaction. Iodine molecules move from a region of higher concentration (the surrounding solution) into the lower concentration region within the starch agar gel. When iodine encounters starch, it forms a blue-black complex, making the diffusion process visible. The gradual inward movement of color reflects the rate and direction of diffusion in a semi-solid medium.VI. Experimental PrecautionsPour iodine gently to avoid moving the gel cube. Do not cut or squeeze the gel during the experiment. Avoid skin contact with iodine and clean spills promptly.

Visibility Constraints: the cube edges and surfaces must remain visible, color contrast between clear gel and blue-black complex must be sufficient, and the viewpoint must remain fixed to verify continuous inward diffusion.

Basic InformationExperiment Title: Limewater Test with Ambient AirSubject: Natural Science – Atmospheric ScienceObjective: To demonstrate that ambient air contains carbon dioxide by bubbling air into calcium hydroxide solution and observing turbidity formation.II. Equipment and MaterialsClear glass container (beaker or jar), clear calcium hydroxide solution (limewater), small air pump, flexible plastic tube, stand or clamp (optional), camera fixed for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Pour clear, colorless calcium hydroxide solution into the glass container to about half its volume. Ensure no initial turbidity.2. Setup: Connect one end of the tube to the small air pump. Submerge the other end of the tube slightly below the surface of the limewater without touching the container wall.3. Recording: Fix the camera focus and position to cover the entire container. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.4. Operation: Turn on the pump so that ambient air is steadily bubbled into the limewater.5. Observation: Allow bubbling to continue until visible changes appear in the solution.6. Completion: Turn off the pump, stop recording, and dispose of the solution properly.IV. Observation of PhenomenaInitial state: Limewater is clear and transparent.During bubbling: Small air bubbles rise through the solution.After continued bubbling: The solution gradually becomes milky and turbid due to formation of a white precipitate.V. Experimental PrincipleAmbient air contains carbon dioxide. When CO2 is bubbled into calcium hydroxide solution, it reacts to form insoluble calcium carbonate, which appears as a white precipitate causing turbidity.Reaction: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3↓ + H2O.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstrate the presence of carbon dioxide in ambient air through the limewater test, assuming only that air contains CO2 and that CO2 reacts with calcium hydroxide to form a visible precipitate.Mechanistic assumptions: Air from the pump represents ambient air; bubbling increases gas–liquid contact; calcium carbonate formation causes turbidity.Phased storyline: (1) Static setup with clear limewater in a transparent container; (2) pump activates and air bubbles pass through the solution; (3) over time, the clear solution gradually turns milky. The camera remains fixed to ensure visibility of gradual change, with no need to verify real-time duration, only correct order and causality.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Comparison of Iron-Core and Air-Core Electromagnets Lifting Metal ObjectsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Iron-Core vs Air-Core Electromagnet Lifting Steel Washers2. Subject: Engineering - Energy Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To compare the magnetic strength of an iron-core electromagnet and an air-core electromagnet under the same power conditions, and to understand the role of a ferromagnetic core in enhancing magnetic fields.II. Experimental EquipmentDC power supply (shared), two identical wire coils, soft iron rod (core), power switch, connecting wires, steel washers (multiple), non-magnetic tabletop, camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two coils side by side on the tabletop. Insert the iron rod into one coil to form an iron-core electromagnet; leave the other coil empty as an air-core electromagnet. Place an equal number of steel washers directly beneath each coil.2. Circuit Setup: Connect both coils in parallel to the same DC power supply through a common switch, ensuring equal voltage and current conditions.3. Camera Setup: Fix the camera position and focus, ensuring both coils and washers are clearly visible.4. Core Operation: Switch on the power supply simultaneously to both coils and maintain power briefly.5. Power-Off Operation: Switch off the power supply simultaneously to both coils.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: With power off, all steel washers rest on the tabletop.2. Power On: When the switch is turned on, both coils become electromagnets. The iron-core electromagnet attracts and lifts more washers (or lifts them more firmly) than the air-core electromagnet.3. Power Off: When the switch is turned off, magnetic attraction disappears and the washers fall back onto the tabletop.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesAn electric current through a coil produces a magnetic field. Inserting an iron core greatly increases the magnetic field strength because the iron becomes magnetized and concentrates magnetic flux. Therefore, under the same electrical conditions, an iron-core electromagnet can lift heavier or more metal objects than an air-core electromagnet.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: The experiment demonstrates how a ferromagnetic core enhances the magnetic field of an electromagnet under identical electrical input.Minimum assumptions: Two visually distinct coils (one with iron core, one without), a shared power source, and steel washers that respond to magnetic fields.Phased storyline: (1) Initial static state with power off and washers at rest; (2) power switched on causing both coils to attract washers, with visibly stronger attraction by the iron-core coil; (3) power switched off causing loss of magnetism and washers dropping. Visibility constraints: fixed camera angle showing both coils and washers simultaneously to allow direct comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Coin at the Bottom of a Cup Becomes Visible as Water Is Poured InI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Coin at the Bottom of a Cup Becomes Visible as Water Is Poured In2. Subject: Healthcare – Optometry / Vision Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the refraction of light at the air–water interface and understand how changes in light path affect human visual perception.II. Experimental EquipmentOpaque cup (non-transparent), coin (1), table, clear water, water container for pouring, fixed table-height camera (focus locked).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the opaque cup on a table. Put a coin flat at the bottom of the cup. Position the camera at table height so that the coin is not visible from the camera view. Fix camera position and focus.2. Initial Observation: Record the initial state. Ensure the coin at the bottom of the cup cannot be seen due to the straight-line propagation of light.3. Core Operation: Slowly and steadily pour clear water into the cup while keeping the camera completely stationary.4. Observation Process: Continue pouring until the coin gradually becomes visible in the camera frame.5. End: Stop pouring once the coin is clearly visible. Keep recording briefly to confirm the stable visibility state.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The coin at the bottom of the opaque cup is not visible from the fixed camera position.2. During Pouring: As the water level rises, the coin gradually appears in the camera view.3. Final State: When sufficient water is added, the coin becomes clearly visible without any change in camera position.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates light refraction. In air, light travels in straight lines, so light from the coin cannot reach the observer’s eyes. When water is added, light rays from the coin refract at the water–air interface, bending toward the observer. This change in light path allows the image of the coin to reach the eye (or camera), making the coin visible. This principle explains how refraction affects visual perception in optometry and vision science.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Refraction of light alters the path of rays from an object, changing its visibility without moving the observer.Minimum mechanistic assumptions: Light travels in straight lines in uniform media; light bends at the boundary between water and air; observer and camera remain fixed.Phased storyline: (1) Initial phase – opaque cup on table, coin invisible from fixed viewpoint; (2) Transition phase – water level rises, refraction begins at the water surface; (3) Outcome phase – refracted light reaches the camera, coin becomes visible. Visibility must change solely due to water addition, with no camera or object movement.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Time-lapse Microscopy of Eukaryotic Cell Mitosis Showing Nuclear Envelope Breakdown2. Subject: Healthcare – Medicine (Cell Biology)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the dynamic process of mitosis in cultured eukaryotic cells using time-lapse fluorescence microscopy, with emphasis on nuclear envelope breakdown (NEBD), chromosome condensation, segregation, and reformation of daughter nuclei.II. Experimental Equipment and Materials1. Cultured eukaryotic cells (e.g., HeLa or other adherent mammalian cells) grown on glass-bottom culture dishes2. Cell culture medium suitable for live-cell imaging3. Fluorescent DNA stain (e.g., Hoechst or H2B-GFP–expressing cells)4. CO₂-controlled live-cell imaging chamber5. Inverted fluorescence microscope equipped with time-lapse imaging system6. Computer with imaging acquisition software7. Personal protective equipment (lab coat, gloves)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   a. Culture cells on glass-bottom dishes until they reach appropriate density (50–70% confluence).   b. Label nuclear DNA using a fluorescent DNA dye or genetically encoded fluorescent histone.   c. Replace medium with fresh, pre-warmed imaging medium.2. Microscope Setup:   a. Turn on the fluorescence microscope and set temperature and CO₂ to physiological conditions (37°C, 5% CO₂).   b. Select appropriate fluorescence channel for DNA visualization.   c. Identify a field of view containing healthy cells likely to enter mitosis.3. Time-lapse Imaging:   a. Set time-lapse parameters (e.g., one image every 2–5 minutes).   b. Start continuous imaging, ensuring the same cells remain in focus throughout acquisition.   c. Continue imaging until cells complete division into two daughter cells.4. Ending the Experiment:   a. Stop image acquisition after mitosis is complete.   b. Save and label image sequences for analysis.   c. Properly shut down the microscope and dispose of biological materials according to safety guidelines.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State (Interphase): DNA appears as a diffuse fluorescent signal within an intact, round nucleus.2. Prophase: Chromatin gradually condenses into distinct chromosomes; the nuclear envelope remains visible initially.3. Nuclear Envelope Breakdown (Prometaphase): The nuclear envelope disassembles, observed as loss of clear nuclear boundary; condensed chromosomes disperse into the cytoplasm.4. Metaphase to Anaphase: Chromosomes align at the metaphase plate, then separate and move toward opposite poles.5. Telophase and Cytokinesis: Chromosomes decondense; new nuclear envelopes reform around daughter genomes, producing two distinct nuclei.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on the principle of live-cell time-lapse fluorescence microscopy. Fluorescent labeling of DNA allows continuous visualization of chromosomal dynamics during mitosis. Nuclear envelope breakdown is a key regulatory event that permits spindle microtubules to interact with chromosomes. Time-lapse imaging enables the same cells to be observed throughout division, revealing the temporal sequence and causal relationships of mitotic events.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Minimize phototoxicity by using low-intensity illumination.2. Maintain stable temperature and CO₂ levels to preserve cell viability.3. Avoid mechanical disturbance of the culture dish during imaging.4. Ensure proper biological safety and waste disposal procedures are followed.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Mitotic progression of cultured eukaryotic cells visualized by time-lapse fluorescence microscopy, with emphasis on nuclear envelope breakdown. Minimum assumptions: cells are alive, DNA is fluorescently labeled, and imaging repeatedly captures the same field. Phased storyline: (1) Interphase nucleus with diffuse fluorescence; (2) chromosome condensation; (3) loss of nuclear boundary indicating NEBD; (4) chromosome alignment and separation; (5) reformation of two nuclei. Key causal transitions include NEBD enabling chromosome–spindle interaction and chromosome segregation leading to two daughter nuclei. Visibility requirements: stable microscopic field, clear fluorescent DNA signal, and continuous tracking of the same cells.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Plotly t-SNE Dimensionality Reduction Interactive DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Plotly t-SNE Dimensionality Reduction Interactive DemonstrationSubject: Engineering – Scientific ComputingExperiment Objective: To understand the concept and application of t-SNE for dimensionality reduction, and to learn how to use Python with numpy, sklearn, and plotly to visualize high-dimensional data as an interactive 2D scatter plot.II. Experimental Environment and Tools1. Hardware: Personal computer with internet access.2. Software: Python 3.x, web browser.3. Python Libraries: numpy, scikit-learn (sklearn), plotly.III. Experimental Procedure1. Environment Preparation: Open a Python development environment (such as Jupyter Notebook or a Python script editor) and ensure that numpy, sklearn, and plotly are installed.2. Code Import: In the editor, import numpy for data generation, sklearn.manifold.TSNE for dimensionality reduction, and plotly.express for visualization.3. Data Generation: Use numpy to generate a set of high-dimensional data points with 10 features, and optionally assign labels to simulate different clusters.4. Dimensionality Reduction: Apply the t-SNE algorithm to reduce the 10-dimensional data to 2 dimensions.5. Visualization: Use plotly to create an interactive 2D scatter plot, mapping different clusters to red, orange, and yellow colors, and enabling hover information to display the original data index.6. Execution: Run the Python code. The interactive scatter plot will automatically open in the web browser.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The screen displays Python code with proper imports and data generation steps.2. After Execution: A browser window opens showing a 2D scatter plot.3. Visual Features: Data points form distinguishable clusters in red, orange, and yellow; a legend appears on the right side.4. Interaction: Users can zoom and pan the plot, and hovering over points displays the index of the original high-dimensional data.V. Summary of Experimental Principlest-SNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) is a nonlinear dimensionality reduction technique that preserves local similarities in high-dimensional data when mapping it to a low-dimensional space. By converting pairwise distances into probability distributions and minimizing divergence between them, t-SNE reveals cluster structures that are difficult to observe directly in high-dimensional space. Plotly enables interactive visualization, enhancing interpretability through color, hover information, and dynamic navigation.VI. Experimental Notes1. t-SNE results may vary slightly between runs due to randomness.2. This demonstration focuses on visualization and intuition rather than quantitative evaluation.3. Interactive operations such as zoom and hover are essential for observing detailed data relationships.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstrating t-SNE dimensionality reduction and interactive visualization in scientific computing. Minimum assumptions include a computer screen, Python environment, and a basic understanding that running code produces a visual output.Phased storyline: (1) Display Python code importing numpy, sklearn, and plotly and generating 10D data; (2) Execute code to apply t-SNE and reduce data to 2D; (3) Browser opens with an interactive scatter plot; (4) Colored clusters appear with legend on the right; (5) User interactions such as zooming, panning, and hovering reveal data indices. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Quadriceps Group Extending the Knee During a Seated Leg RaiseI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Quadriceps Muscle Action in Seated Knee Extension2. Subject: Healthcare – Physiotherapy3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate and observe the role of the quadriceps muscle group in extending the knee during a seated leg raise, and to understand the biomechanical principle of knee extension against gravity.II. Experimental Equipment and ConditionsBench or chair with flat surface; adult participant; comfortable clothing allowing thigh exposure; stable camera fixed at side view (for time-lapse or continuous recording); adequate lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Seat the adult participant upright on the bench with hips and knees flexed at approximately 90 degrees. Expose the thigh of the working leg. Allow one lower leg to hang freely off the bench edge. Keep the trunk upright and hands resting on the bench.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera at a side view perpendicular to the sagittal plane of the participant, ensuring the hip, knee, and lower leg are fully visible. Do not change focus during recording.3. Core Operation: Instruct the participant to slowly extend the knee by lifting the lower leg upward until the knee is nearly straight, keeping the thigh stationary on the bench.4. Controlled Return: Slowly lower the lower leg back to the starting hanging position, maintaining control throughout the movement.5. Repetition: Repeat the extend–lower cycle several times at a slow, even pace.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The lower leg hangs vertically with the knee flexed, and the thigh remains stable on the bench.2. During Extension: The lower leg rotates upward around the knee joint as the knee extends; the thigh remains still, indicating isolated knee movement.3. During Lowering: The lower leg descends smoothly back to the hanging position, showing controlled eccentric action.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe quadriceps femoris muscle group is the primary extensor of the knee joint. During the seated leg raise, concentric contraction of the quadriceps produces knee extension against gravity. During lowering, eccentric contraction controls knee flexion. The experiment visually demonstrates muscle-driven joint movement and basic principles of lower-limb biomechanics used in physiotherapy assessment and training.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure stable seating and posture; avoid swinging the leg or using momentum; maintain slow, controlled movement; stop if discomfort or pain occurs.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Benzo(a)pyrene Detection (Fluorescence Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Detection of Benzo(a)pyrene in Water by Fluorescence Spectrophotometry2. Subject: Natural Science – Environmental Science3. Experiment Objective: To detect and qualitatively analyze benzo(a)pyrene in a water sample extract using fluorescence spectrophotometry; to master the correct use of a quartz cuvette and understand the fluorescence detection principle under UV excitation (365 nm).II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsFluorescence spectrophotometer, quartz cuvette (1 cm path length), micropipette or graduated pipette, benzo(a)pyrene water sample extract, lint-free tissue, gloves and safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Turn on the fluorescence spectrophotometer and allow it to warm up. Set the excitation wavelength to 365 nm. Wear gloves and safety goggles.2. Sample Loading: Use a pipette to accurately measure 1 mL of the water sample extract. Slowly transfer the extract into a clean quartz cuvette, avoiding bubbles.3. Cuvette Handling: Wipe the outside of the cuvette with lint-free tissue to remove fingerprints or droplets. Ensure the clear sides are aligned with the optical path.4. Measurement: Place the quartz cuvette into the sample holder of the fluorescence spectrophotometer. Close the lid to prevent ambient light interference.5. Excitation and Detection: Start the measurement. The sample is irradiated with 365 nm excitation light, and the emitted fluorescence signal is recorded.6. Completion: After measurement, remove the cuvette, dispose of the sample according to waste regulations, and clean the cuvette.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The water sample extract in the quartz cuvette appears clear or slightly colored, with no visible luminescence under normal light.2. During Excitation: Under 365 nm excitation, the sample emits visible fluorescence (typically blue-violet), observable via the instrument display.3. Result: The presence and relative intensity of fluorescence indicate the presence and approximate concentration of benzo(a)pyrene in the sample.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleBenzo(a)pyrene is a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon with strong fluorescent properties. When irradiated with ultraviolet light at an appropriate excitation wavelength (365 nm), its molecules absorb energy and transition to an excited state. As they return to the ground state, they emit light at a longer wavelength (fluorescence). The fluorescence intensity is proportional to the amount of benzo(a)pyrene present, enabling qualitative or quantitative analysis.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use only quartz cuvettes, as glass absorbs UV light.2. Avoid bubbles and contamination, which can affect fluorescence intensity.3. Protect the sample from prolonged light exposure to prevent photodegradation.4. Follow laboratory safety and waste disposal regulations.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstration of Cloud Condensation Nuclei Using Humid Air and Incense Smoke2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the role of cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) in cloud formation by comparing condensation in humid air with and without aerosol particles (incense smoke).II. Experimental Equipment1. Clear sealed chambers (2 identical transparent chambers)2. Source of humid air (humidifier or warm water vapor)3. Incense stick or incense smoke source4. Cooling method (ice packs, cold spray, or refrigerated air source)5. Thermometer (optional, for reference)6. Camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recordingIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear chambers side by side on a stable surface. Ensure both chambers are clean, dry, and transparent.2. Humidification: Introduce humid air into both chambers until the air inside appears clear but highly humid (near saturation). Seal the chambers.3. Smoke Introduction: Light the incense and gently introduce a small amount of incense smoke into the left chamber only. The right chamber remains smoke-free.4. Camera Setup: Position the camera facing both chambers. Fix the focus and begin time-lapse recording.5. Cooling Operation: Rapidly and simultaneously cool both chambers using the same cooling method.6. Observation Period: Continue recording as the temperature drops and condensation begins to form inside the chambers.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both chambers appear clear with no visible droplets; the left chamber contains faint visible smoke particles.2. During Cooling: As temperature decreases, fine droplets or fog begin to appear.3. Key Phenomenon: Condensation appears earlier and more densely in the left chamber with incense smoke, while the right chamber shows weaker or delayed condensation.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCloud condensation nuclei are tiny particles in the atmosphere that provide surfaces for water vapor to condense upon. Incense smoke contains abundant aerosol particles that act as CCN. When humid air is cooled to saturation, water vapor condenses more readily where CCN are present. Therefore, under identical cooling conditions, the smoke-filled chamber forms visible cloud droplets more easily than the clean-air chamber.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both chambers have similar humidity before cooling.2. Add only a small, controlled amount of smoke to avoid obscuring observations.3. Cool both chambers simultaneously to ensure fair comparison.4. Handle incense and cooling materials safely.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Mercury Detection Using Thioacetamide Test StripI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Mercury Detection (Thioacetamide Test Strip Method)2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food Hygiene3. Experiment Objective: To detect the presence of mercury ions in food samples by preparing a food extract solution and observing the color change of a thioacetamide-based mercury test strip, and to understand the basic principle of mercury qualitative detection.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentBeaker (100–250 mL), food sample (e.g., rice, fish, or vegetable), distilled water, glass rod or stirring rod, filter paper (optional), thioacetamide-based mercury test strips, original unused test strip (for comparison), gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation of Food Extract: Place a small amount of the food sample into a beaker. Add an appropriate volume of distilled water and stir thoroughly with a glass rod to obtain a food extract solution. If necessary, allow solids to settle or filter to obtain a relatively clear extract.2. Test Strip Immersion: Take one mercury test strip with clean hands or gloves. Immerse the reactive end of the strip into the food extract solution in the beaker, ensuring full contact with the solution.3. Reaction and Removal: Allow the strip to react in the solution for a short time (several seconds). Remove the strip and gently shake off excess liquid.4. Comparison: Place the reacted test strip beside an unused original strip on a clean surface for direct visual comparison.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The original test strip shows its baseline color with no staining.2. After Reaction: If mercury ions are present in the food extract, the immersed test strip shows a visible color change (typically darkening or formation of a brown/black coloration) compared with the original strip. If mercury is absent, little or no color change is observed.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe thioacetamide-based mercury test strip detects mercury ions through a chemical reaction between mercury ions and sulfur-containing functional groups generated from thioacetamide. Mercury ions react to form mercury sulfide or related complexes, which produce a characteristic dark color on the strip. The intensity of the color change qualitatively reflects the presence of mercury in the food extract.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Avoid direct contact with the reactive area of the test strip.2. Use an unused strip as a control for accurate comparison.3. Dispose of used strips and food extracts according to safety and hygiene requirements.

manual: I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Irrigation Water Chloride Content Detection (Silver Nitrate Colorimetric Method)2. Subject: Engineering - Civil & Environmental Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To qualitatively detect the presence of chloride ions in irrigation water by observing the reaction between chloride ions and silver nitrate, and to understand the basic principle of chloride detection in water quality analysis.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (1), test tube rack, dropper or micropipette, silver nitrate solution (standard concentration), chlorinated irrigation water sample, protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Clean the test tube and place it on the test tube rack. Wear protective goggles and gloves.2. Sampling: Use a dropper or pipette to measure 2 ml of the chlorinated irrigation water sample and transfer it into the test tube.3. Reagent Addition (Core Step): Hold the dropper containing silver nitrate solution vertically above the test tube and carefully add 2 drops of silver nitrate solution into the water sample.4. Mixing and Observation: Gently shake the test tube to mix the solution and immediately observe the changes in the liquid.5. Completion: Place the test tube back on the rack and record the observed phenomenon. Dispose of the waste solution according to laboratory regulations.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The irrigation water sample is clear and colorless.2. After Addition of Silver Nitrate: A white turbidity or fine white precipitate appears in the solution. The turbidity becomes more evident after gentle shaking.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on the precipitation reaction between silver ions and chloride ions. When silver nitrate (AgNO3) is added to irrigation water containing chloride ions (Cl-), insoluble silver chloride (AgCl) is formed as a white precipitate. The appearance of white turbidity indicates the presence of chloride ions in the water.Core Reaction Equation: Ag+ + Cl- → AgCl↓The intensity of the turbidity qualitatively reflects the relative chloride content in the irrigation water sample.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Silver nitrate can stain skin and clothing; handle with care.2. Ensure accurate measurement of 2 ml water and exactly 2 drops of reagent for consistency.3. Observe immediately after reagent addition to avoid misinterpretation due to settling of the precipitate.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Strength Comparison Experiment of Lime-Modified ClayI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Strength Comparison Experiment of Lime-Modified Clay2. Subject: Engineering – Geotechnical Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To compare the mechanical strength of pure clay and lime-modified clay through a simple drop test, and to visually understand the strengthening effect of lime on clay.II. Experimental Materials and Equipment1. Pure clay soil (sufficient to form one clod, labeled A)2. Lime-modified clay (clay mixed uniformly with an appropriate amount of quicklime or hydrated lime, formed into one clod, labeled B)3. Balance or measuring container (to ensure similar size and mass of clods)4. Flat, hard ground surface (concrete or stone slab)5. Ruler or marked frame (to ensure same drop height)6. Protective gloves and safety gogglesIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Prepare two soil clods of similar size and mass. Clod A consists of pure clay; clod B consists of clay uniformly mixed with lime and allowed to react and dry to a comparable moisture condition.2. Labeling: Clearly mark the pure clay clod as A and the lime-modified clay clod as B to avoid confusion.3. Height Setup: Select a fixed drop height (for example, 1.0 m) using a ruler or marked reference.4. Core Operation: Hold clod A at the selected height and release it vertically onto the hard ground surface; observe the damage. Repeat the same operation for clod B from the same height and onto the same surface.5. Observation and Recording: Observe and compare the degree of cracking, fragmentation, and integrity of clod A and clod B after impact.6. Cleanup: Collect soil fragments, clean the site, and store remaining materials properly.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Clod A (pure clay): After impact, the clod shows obvious cracking, fragmentation, or even complete disintegration.2. Clod B (lime-modified clay): After impact, the clod remains relatively intact, with fewer cracks and significantly less fragmentation than clod A.3. Comparative Result: Under the same drop height and conditions, clod B shows higher resistance to impact damage than clod A.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Lime reacts with clay minerals and pore water, producing cementitious compounds (such as calcium silicate hydrate and calcium aluminate hydrate).2. These reactions reduce plasticity, decrease water sensitivity, and increase inter-particle bonding within the soil structure.3. As a result, lime-modified clay has higher strength and stiffness than pure clay, which explains why clod B suffers less damage when dropped from the same height.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both clods have similar size, shape, and moisture content to maintain comparability.2. Always drop both clods from the same height and onto the same surface.3. Wear protective equipment to avoid injury from splashing fragments.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate the strength improvement of clay after lime modification using a comparative drop test. Minimum assumptions include gravity-driven free fall, identical drop height, and comparable clod size and moisture.Phased Storyline: (1) Two clearly distinguishable soil clods are presented and labeled; (2) both clods are released from the same height under gravity; (3) impact with the ground causes visible damage; (4) pure clay shows greater fragmentation while lime-modified clay remains more intact. The camera should maintain a stable, wide view to verify height consistency and post-impact damage comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Observation of Parallel Venation in a Corn Leaf (Monocot)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of Parallel Venation in a Corn Leaf2. Subject: Engineering – Agricultural Engineering (Plant Morphology)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate monocot plant morphology by observing the external structure of a corn leaf, focusing on its long, narrow shape and straight, parallel venation from base to tip.II. Experimental MaterialsFresh corn leaf (intact, green), flat table or desk, clean hands (or gloves, optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Select a fresh, undamaged corn leaf. Place it on a clean, flat table surface.2. Placement: Lay the leaf flat with the upper surface facing upward. Align the base and tip clearly along the table.3. Smoothing: Gently smooth the leaf from base to tip using fingers to remove natural curling and make the surface flat.4. Observation: Observe the leaf from directly above. Note the overall long and narrow shape.5. Vein Tracing: Use a finger to trace several veins from the base toward the tip, paying attention to their direction and arrangement.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The corn leaf appears long, narrow, and strap-shaped.2. Numerous veins are visible running lengthwise along the leaf.3. The veins are straight and arranged in parallel lines from the base to the tip.4. No net-like (reticulate) branching of veins is observed.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCorn is a monocotyledonous plant. A key morphological feature of monocots is parallel venation in the leaves. During leaf development, vascular bundles extend longitudinally without forming a reticulate network. By laying the corn leaf flat and observing from above, the straight, parallel distribution of veins can be directly verified, demonstrating a fundamental principle of plant morphology used in agricultural engineering and crop identification.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstrate monocot plant morphology through visual verification of parallel venation in a corn leaf. Minimum assumptions: a real corn leaf, a flat surface, and basic hand interaction without tools. Phased storyline: (1) Introduction of a fresh corn leaf on a table; (2) Gentle smoothing action to flatten the leaf, causing veins to become clearly visible; (3) Stable top-down observation revealing a long, narrow blade; (4) Finger tracing along multiple veins from base to tip, confirming they run straight and parallel with no reticulate branching. Visibility constraints: camera/viewpoint must remain above the leaf, with sufficient lighting to distinguish individual veins clearly.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Visualization of Burgess Concentric Zone Land Use ModelI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visualization of Burgess Concentric Zone Land Use Model2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Architecture & Urban Planning3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the Burgess concentric circle land use model by constructing a simplified city layout that clearly shows the city center and successive land-use zones, and to understand the relationship between urban land value, social structure, and spatial distribution.II. Experimental MaterialsUrban base map or blank canvas (digital or paper), drawing or modeling tools, color markers or digital color fills (yellow, orange, red, pink, light purple, dark purple), labels or legend.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the blank city base map at the center of the workspace. Define a central point representing the city center.2. CBD Construction: Draw the innermost circle around the center and fill it with yellow to represent the Central Business District (CBD).3. Transition Zone: Draw a second ring surrounding the CBD and color it orange, labeling it as the transition zone.4. Working-Class Residential Area: Add the third concentric ring, color it red, and label it as the working-class residential area.5. Middle-Class Residential Area: Draw the fourth ring, color it pink, and label it as the middle-class residential area.6. Upscale Residential Area: Draw the fifth ring, color it light purple, and label it as the upscale residential area.7. Commuter Zone: Draw the outermost ring, color it dark purple, and label it as the commuter zone.8. Final Check: Ensure all rings are concentric, correctly ordered from center to periphery, and clearly labeled.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The city is visually organized into a series of clear concentric circles.2. The CBD occupies the central position, with land-use intensity decreasing outward.3. Residential zones show a gradual transition from lower-income to higher-income groups with increasing distance from the center.4. The commuter zone forms the outer boundary, indicating daily travel into the city center.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe Burgess concentric zone model explains urban land-use structure as a series of rings formed by competition for land and accessibility. The CBD dominates the center due to high accessibility and land value. As distance from the center increases, land value decreases, allowing different social groups and functions to locate in successive zones. This visualization reflects the socio-economic and spatial logic of early industrial cities.VI. Experimental Notes1. Colors must strictly correspond to each zone to avoid misinterpretation.2. Rings should not overlap or break continuity.3. This model is a simplified theoretical representation and does not describe all modern cities.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Burgess Concentric Zone Land Use Model. Minimum assumptions: a monocentric city, land value decreasing with distance from the center, and socio-economic stratification influencing residential location.Expected phased storyline: (1) Establish a single city center; (2) Form a yellow CBD core; (3) Sequentially add outward rings—transition, working-class, middle-class, upscale, and commuter zones—with specified colors; (4) Maintain stable concentric geometry throughout. Key causal transition: decreasing accessibility and land value from center to periphery explains the ordered zoning. Visibility requirement: a top-down or slightly angled view that keeps all rings simultaneously visible for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Urine Citrate Detection (Colorimetric Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Urine Citrate Detection by Colorimetric Method2. Subject: Healthcare – Renal Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the detection of citrate in urine using a colorimetric reagent, understand the basic principle of colorimetric analysis in renal physiology, and master the standard sequence of reagent addition, mixing, and incubation.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsClear glass test tube (1), test tube rack, dropper, urine sample (fresh or simulated, labeled), citrate colorimetric reagent (labeled), timer or clock, disposable gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, dry, clear glass test tube on the test tube rack. Ensure all reagents are clearly labeled and visible.2. Sample Addition: Using a dropper, add a measured amount of urine sample (approximately 2–3 mL) into the test tube.3. Reagent Addition: Using a clean dropper, add the citrate colorimetric reagent dropwise into the same test tube.4. Mixing: Gently mix the contents by lightly tapping or swirling the test tube, avoiding vigorous shaking.5. Incubation: Allow the test tube to stand undisturbed for a brief incubation period (about 1–2 minutes).IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The urine sample appears pale yellow and transparent before reagent addition.2. After Reagent Addition and Mixing: The solution gradually develops a characteristic color (according to the reagent specification), indicating the presence of citrate.3. After Incubation: The color stabilizes and becomes uniform throughout the solution.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on the colorimetric detection of citrate in urine. Citrate in the urine reacts with specific components of the colorimetric reagent to form a colored complex. The intensity or presence of the color is directly related to the citrate concentration. This method is commonly used in renal physiology to assess urinary citrate levels, which are important in evaluating kidney stone risk and metabolic status.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Experiment Title: Iodine–Thiosulfate Redox Titration with Starch Indicator2. Subject: Natural Science – Chemistry – Redox Reactions3. Experiment Objective: To observe the redox reaction between iodine and sodium thiosulfate using starch as an indicator, master the basic titration operation, and understand the principle of using color change to determine a titration endpoint.II. Experimental EquipmentConical flask (250 mL), burette (50 mL) with stand and clamp, funnel, beaker, iodine solution of known concentration, freshly prepared starch indicator solution, sodium thiosulfate solution, glass rod (optional), white background tile or paper for color observation, safety goggles.III. Add 1–2 mL of starch indicator; swirl gently. The solution appears dark blue.Core Titration Operation: Position the burette vertically above the conical flask. While continuously swirling the conical flask by hand, slowly add sodium thiosulfate solution dropwise from the burette.Endpoint Control: As the blue color becomes lighter, slow the addition to single drops, maintaining constant swirling until the blue color just disappears and the solution becomes colorless.Completion: Record the final burette reading. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Blink Reflex to Sudden Air Puff Near the EyeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Blink Reflex Induced by Sudden Air Puff2. Subject: Healthcare – Medicine – Neurophysiology3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the protective blink reflex elicited by a sudden air stimulus near the eye, and to relate the observed response to the underlying neural reflex pathway.II. Experimental EquipmentHandheld rubber air bulb (or similar manual air blower), chair or standing position for the subject, camera positioned in front of the subject (for demonstration), clean environment with normal lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ask the subject to face the camera with eyes open and relaxed. Explain that a brief air puff will be delivered near one eye without touching it.2. Positioning: Hold the air bulb at close range (approximately 5–10 cm) from the side of one eye, ensuring it does not make contact with the face or eyelashes.3. Core Operation: Squeeze the air bulb once to deliver a brief, sudden puff of air toward the eye from the side.4. Completion: Immediately stop the stimulus after the single puff and observe the subject’s response.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The subject’s eyes are open, with no blinking beyond normal spontaneous blinking.2. During Stimulation: At the moment the air puff reaches the eye, the eyelids close rapidly and involuntarily.3. After Stimulation: The eyes reopen shortly after the blink, and the subject returns to a relaxed state.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe blink reflex is a protective, involuntary response mediated by a neural reflex arc. The sudden air puff stimulates sensory receptors of the cornea and surrounding tissues, activating the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V). This sensory input is transmitted to the brainstem, which rapidly activates the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII), causing contraction of the orbicularis oculi muscle and closure of the eyelids. This reflex protects the eye from potential injury.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not touch the eye with the air bulb.2. Use only a brief and gentle air puff to avoid discomfort.3. Ensure the subject is informed and prepared to prevent excessive startle.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: AM Radio Transmission – Microphone Modulating Carrier Amplitude Observed on Oscilloscope2. Subject: Engineering – Communications Engineering3. Experiment Objective: To observe how an audio signal from a microphone modulates the amplitude of a radio-frequency carrier in an AM transmitter, and to visually compare waveform changes when speaking softly versus loudly.II. Experimental EquipmentMicrophone (dynamic or electret), AM transmitter module (with carrier oscillator and amplitude modulator), power supply, short antenna or dummy load, oscilloscope with probe, coaxial cables/leads, lab bench, camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place all equipment on the lab bench. Ensure the AM transmitter is powered off. Fix the camera focus toward the oscilloscope screen and do not adjust it during the experiment.2. Connections: Connect the microphone to the audio input of the AM transmitter. Connect the transmitter output to the antenna or dummy load. Attach the oscilloscope probe to the RF output test point (or across the load) and set the oscilloscope to display the carrier waveform.3. Oscilloscope Setup: Select a time base suitable for viewing the RF carrier and its amplitude envelope. Adjust vertical scale so the waveform is clearly visible.4. Operation – Soft Speech: Power on the transmitter. Speak softly into the microphone. Observe the oscilloscope display and keep speaking for several seconds.5. Operation – Loud Speech: Without changing connections, speak loudly into the microphone. Continue observing the oscilloscope display.6. Completion: Stop speaking, power off the transmitter, and disconnect equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: With no speech, the oscilloscope shows a steady carrier waveform with nearly constant amplitude.2. Soft Speech: When speaking softly, the carrier amplitude varies slightly; a small envelope corresponding to the audio signal appears.3. Loud Speech: When speaking loudly, the carrier amplitude variation becomes much larger; the envelope is clearly pronounced while the carrier frequency remains unchanged.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIn AM (Amplitude Modulation), the instantaneous amplitude of a high-frequency carrier signal is varied in proportion to the instantaneous amplitude of a low-frequency audio signal. The microphone converts sound pressure into an electrical audio signal. This audio signal controls the gain of the transmitter’s modulator stage, causing the carrier’s amplitude envelope to follow the voice signal. Louder speech produces a higher audio amplitude, resulting in a larger modulation depth observed on the oscilloscope, while the carrier frequency remains constant.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Avoid over-modulation, which can distort the envelope.2. Ensure proper grounding of the oscilloscope probe to avoid noise.3. Do not touch RF output points while powered on.4. Keep camera focus fixed throughout recording.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Warm Dyed Water Blob Rising in a Convection TankI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Rising of Warm Dyed Water in a Convection Tank2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science3. Experiment Objective: To simulate atmospheric convection by demonstrating how a warm, less-dense fluid parcel rises in a still environment, helping students understand buoyancy and vertical air motion.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent convection tank (filled with clear water), warm water (slightly higher temperature than tank water), red food dye, syringe or pipette (for injection), thermometer (optional), stable table, good lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the transparent convection tank on a stable table and fill it with clear, room-temperature water. Ensure the water is still, with no visible currents.2. Dye Preparation: Mix a small amount of red dye into warm water, ensuring uniform color. The warm dyed water should be slightly hotter than the tank water.3. Injection Setup: Draw the warm red-dyed water into a syringe or pipette. Carefully insert the tip to the bottom center of the tank without disturbing the water.4. Core Operation: Gently inject a small volume of the warm red-dyed water at the bottom of the tank, then stop injecting and hold still to release it as a coherent blob.5. Observation: Step back and observe the motion of the dyed water after release.6. Completion: Allow the dyed water to rise and gradually disperse. Do not stir the tank. End observation once the parcel loses its clear shape.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The tank water is clear and still; no visible motion is present.2. After Release: The red-dyed water forms a distinct blob near the bottom.3. Rising Stage: The red blob rises upward through the clear water, maintaining a roughly rounded or mushroom-like shape.4. Later Stage: As it rises, the blob gradually spreads and mixes with surrounding water, becoming lighter in color.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates buoyancy and convection. Warm water has a lower density than cooler surrounding water. When the warm red-dyed water is released at the bottom of the tank, the density difference creates an upward buoyant force. This causes the dyed water parcel to rise, similar to a warm air parcel rising in the atmosphere and forming convection currents.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Inject slowly to avoid creating mechanical currents.2. Ensure the temperature difference is moderate; excessive heat can cause rapid mixing.3. Keep the tank undisturbed during observation to maintain a still environment.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Bee Collecting Nectar While Transferring PollenI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Bee Collecting Nectar While Transferring Pollen Between FlowersSubject: Natural Science - BiologyExperiment Objective: To observe and understand how a honeybee collects nectar from flowers of the same species and transfers pollen between flowers, demonstrating the biological process of pollination.II. Experimental MaterialsFlowering plants of the same species (with visible stamens and pistils), honeybees (natural environment or controlled garden), observation notebook, camera or magnifying glass (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Select a group of blooming flowers of the same plant species in a garden or field where honeybees are active.2. Initial Observation: Observe a honeybee approaching and landing on the first flower.3. Core Operation: Watch as the honeybee inserts its proboscis into the flower to collect nectar; note pollen grains sticking to the bee’s legs and body.4. Transfer Observation: Observe the honeybee flying to another flower of the same species and landing on it.5. Continued Observation: Note pollen being brushed onto the stigma of the second flower as the bee collects nectar again.6. Conclusion: Record observations and stop after the bee has visited multiple flowers.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Flowers have pollen on stamens; bee body is initially relatively clean.2. During Nectar Collection: Pollen grains adhere to the bee’s hairy body and legs.3. During Movement: The bee flies between flowers of the same species.4. Resulting State: Pollen is transferred from the bee to the stigma of another flower.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePollination occurs when pollen from the anther of one flower is transferred to the stigma of another flower of the same species. Honeybees collect nectar as food; during this process, pollen adheres to their bodies and is unintentionally transferred between flowers, enabling plant reproduction.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Ammonium Chloride Particulate Formation by Gas DiffusionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Formation of Ammonium Chloride Particulate by Diffusion of Ammonia and Hydrogen Chloride2. Subject: Natural Science – Atmospheric Science (Chemical Processes in the Atmosphere)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the formation of ammonium chloride particulate when ammonia vapor meets hydrogen chloride vapor, and to understand gas diffusion and secondary particulate formation in the atmosphere.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass chamber with two side ports, cotton or glass wool plugs, concentrated ammonia solution (NH3·H2O) as ammonia vapor source, concentrated hydrochloric acid (HCl) as hydrogen chloride vapor source, tweezers, gloves, safety goggles, camera on tripod (fixed focus for time-lapse).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear glass chamber on a stable surface in a well-ventilated area or fume hood. Wear gloves and safety goggles. Fix the camera in front of the chamber and lock focus.2. Gas Source Setup: Moisten one cotton plug with a small amount of ammonia solution and place it at the left port of the chamber. Moisten another cotton plug with concentrated hydrochloric acid and place it at the right port.3. Core Operation: Simultaneously insert both plugs into their respective ports, sealing the chamber. Do not shake the chamber; allow gases to diffuse naturally from opposite sides.4. Observation: Keep the chamber undisturbed and record continuously or by time-lapse. Observe the central region where the gases meet.5. Completion: After observation, remove the plugs in a fume hood, ventilate the chamber, and neutralize residues according to laboratory rules.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The chamber is transparent; both gases are colorless and invisible.2. Diffusion Stage: Ammonia and hydrogen chloride vapors diffuse from opposite sides toward the center.3. Mixing Stage: A white cloud or ring of fine particulate appears where the two gases meet.4. Final State: The white particulate (ammonium chloride) remains suspended briefly, then slowly disperses or settles.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesAmmonia (NH3) and hydrogen chloride (HCl) are colorless gases that diffuse through air. When they meet, they react to form solid ammonium chloride (NH4Cl), which appears as a white particulate cloud. This demonstrates gas diffusion and secondary aerosol formation relevant to atmospheric science.Core Reaction Equation: NH3(g) + HCl(g) → NH4Cl(s)VI. Experimental PrecautionsAvoid direct inhalation of gases; perform in a fume hood. Use minimal reagent amounts. Ensure the chamber is sealed during observation and fully ventilated afterward.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Secondary particulate formation via gas-phase reaction of ammonia and hydrogen chloride, requiring only assumptions of free gas diffusion and immediate salt formation upon contact.Phased storyline: (1) Static transparent chamber with two opposing gas sources; (2) invisible gases diffuse inward over time; (3) upon contact, a visible white particulate band/cloud forms at the mixing interface; (4) particulate lingers and slowly disperses. Visibility constraints: chamber must remain clear, viewpoint fixed, and the mixing zone centrally visible to verify causality and sequence.
